Before implementing, the question to ask is whether all possible failure scenarios have been covered, because one payment change rarely touches only one application, and a solution owner should prioritise the fix and evaluate the options, not chase perfection. Before implementing, the question to ask is whether all possible failure scenarios have been covered, because one payment change rarely touches only one application, and a solution owner should prioritise the fix and

entries.title: Do not document the requirement, decode it
entries.text: Do not document the requirement, decode it Core A high-level need such as letting a customer schedule a payment looks simple, but it has to be decoded into business rules: a payment can be set for a future date, next week or next year, recreated or rescheduled with a new effective date, never scheduled for a date in the past, scheduled for several payment types, and cancelled when it is not processed on the requested date. The same applies to messages: in a request to pay such as pain.013, the execution date should not be shown to the customer when the data element is empty. The BA job is to find the business rule behind the requirement rather than mapping one field to another, and a requirement that cannot be written as a simple rule is not a simple requirement. The BA job is to find the business rule behind the requirement rather than mapping one field to another, and a requirement that cannot be written as a simple rule is not a simple requirement.

entries.title: End-to-end card transaction flow
entries.text: End-to-end card transaction flow Core A card transaction moves through four stages across four parties: authorisation is the issuer approving the payment at the point of sale, clearing is the network exchanging transaction records between acquirer and issuer, settlement is the movement of funds between the banks, and reconciliation matches clearing records, settlement positions and ledger postings so every amount agrees. The issuer, the acquirer, the network and the merchant each play a distinct role at each stage, and a failure at any stage has a different owner and a different fix. Know the stage, and you know who must act. Know the stage, and you know who must act.

entries.title: Debit card versus credit card behaviour
entries.text: Debit card versus credit card behaviour Core A debit card payment draws directly on the customer's account balance, so the funds leave the account at authorisation and settlement moves money the customer already holds. A credit card payment draws on a credit line, so the issuer funds the payment and the customer repays later, which changes settlement timing, interest treatment and the risk the issuer carries. The terminal experience looks identical, but the account and settlement implications are entirely different. The terminal experience looks identical, but the account and settlement implications are entirely different.

entries.title: How the issuer decides to approve or decline
entries.text: How the issuer decides to approve or decline Core When a card is presented, the issuer decides whether to approve or decline: it checks card status, available funds or credit, transaction limits and fraud rules, then returns an approval or a decline with a response code. The outcome depends on all these checks together, so a payment can be declined even when the balance is sufficient, if a fraud rule or a limit is breached. Sufficient funds alone never guarantee approval. Sufficient funds alone never guarantee approval.

entries.title: Card settlement and reconciliation control
entries.text: Card settlement and reconciliation control Core After clearing, the settlement position is the net amount each bank owes or is owed, and the ledger postings must match that position exactly. Reconciliation compares clearing records, settlement positions and ledger postings, and any break between them is investigated rather than written off. A settlement that does not reconcile means money is unaccounted for, which is a control failure even if the customer-facing payment appeared to succeed. A settlement that does not reconcile means money is unaccounted for, which is a control failure even if the customer-facing payment appeared to succeed.

entries.title: Chargeback lifecycle and reason codes
entries.text: Chargeback lifecycle and reason codes Core A chargeback starts when a cardholder disputes a transaction and the issuer raises it with the scheme, and the acquirer and merchant respond with representment evidence while the scheme applies its timelines and reason codes. The financial impact moves between issuer, acquirer and merchant as the case progresses, so knowing the reason code matters: it decides what evidence is needed and who bears the loss at each stage. The reason code is the case, not a label on it. The reason code is the case, not a label on it.

entries.title: NEFT, RTGS and IMPS: three domestic rails
entries.text: NEFT, RTGS and IMPS: three domestic rails Core NEFT, RTGS and IMPS are three domestic rails with different operating models: NEFT settles in batches and suits payments that can wait, RTGS settles each payment individually in central bank money and suits high value payments that must be final, and IMPS settles instantly around the clock and suits payments that must arrive immediately. Compare them on speed, availability, settlement model and customer use case, and use the current scheme rules rather than an old summary. The rail is chosen by the payment's need, not by habit. The rail is chosen by the payment's need, not by habit.

entries.title: The loan lifecycle, application to closure
entries.text: The loan lifecycle, application to closure Core A loan moves from application through decision, agreement, disbursement, servicing, repayment and closure: application collects the request and supporting information, decision assesses credit and affordability, agreement records the terms, disbursement releases the funds, servicing collects repayments and manages changes, and closure confirms the balance is settled and the account is closed. Each stage has its own data, controls and hand-offs, so a failure at one stage does not always show up until a later stage. A loan is a chain, and a weak link anywhere shows up downstream. A loan is a chain, and a weak link anywhere shows up downstream.

entries.title: Approved loan, failed disbursement: tracing the break
entries.text: Approved loan, failed disbursement: tracing the break Core A loan can be approved and still fail to disburse, so trace the path from approval through account validation, the disbursement instruction, the ledger posting and the customer communication, because the break can sit at any of these points. A valid approval with a wrong account, a failed instruction or a missing ledger posting all look the same to the customer, who simply sees that the money has not arrived. Check each stage in order rather than assuming the approval was the problem. Check each stage in order rather than assuming the approval was the problem.

entries.title: Settlement cycles and honest customer timing
entries.text: Settlement cycles and honest customer timing Core A settlement cycle is the period after which funds move between banks, and T+1 or T+2 are only examples of how long that can take. The actual timing depends on the scheme and the product, so always use the scheme and product specific rules rather than a generic T+1 or T+2. Customer communication must state the real timing for that product, because telling a customer the money will arrive tomorrow when the scheme settles in two days creates a complaint that was avoidable. Customer communication must state the real timing for that product, because telling a customer the money will arrive tomorrow when the scheme settles in two days creates a complaint that was avoidable.

entries.title: Payment APIs across the product lifecycle
entries.text: Payment APIs across the product lifecycle Core A payment product exposes several APIs across the lifecycle, not just one for taking payment: the checkout API initiates the payment, the authentication API proves who is paying, the status API reports where a payment stands, the refund API returns money for a completed payment, and the reversal API cancels a payment that should not have completed. Map each touchpoint to the lifecycle stage it serves, so the product never ends up with a payment that can be taken but cannot be refunded or checked. Coverage of the whole lifecycle is what makes a payment product complete. Coverage of the whole lifecycle is what makes a payment product complete.

entries.title: Refund API versus reversal API
entries.text: Refund API versus reversal API Core A refund and a reversal look similar but differ in trigger, timing and ledger effect: a refund returns money for a completed payment, is linked to the original transaction, and posts as a new credit to the customer, while a reversal cancels a payment that should not have completed, is also linked to the original transaction, but unwinds the original posting rather than creating a separate refund. Validate the rail and provider semantics before building either one, because the same word can mean different things on different rails. Build the ledger effect first, and the name will follow. Build the ledger effect first, and the name will follow.

entries.title: Gateway, bank and merchant: who owns what
entries.text: Gateway, bank and merchant: who owns what Core In a card payment the gateway, the bank and the merchant each own a distinct part: the gateway orchestrates the instruction and returns the outcome, the bank authorises and processes the payment and moves the funds, and the merchant is notified of the outcome and must act on it. When a payment fails, knowing which party owns which step decides who must fix it and who must tell the customer, so the boundary between gateway, bank and merchant must be explicit in the design. Unclear ownership turns every failure into a dispute between parties. Unclear ownership turns every failure into a dispute between parties.

entries.title: Finding customers with repeated failed transactions
entries.text: Finding customers with repeated failed transactions Core To find customers with repeated failed transactions, translate the business rule into a time-windowed aggregation: define the window, the failure condition and the threshold, then aggregate the transaction data over that window and validate the data quality before acting on the result. A count that includes test transactions, duplicates or a wrong window will target the wrong customers, so the data quality check is part of the work, not an afterthought. A precise rule plus clean data is the whole method. A precise rule plus clean data is the whole method.

entries.title: AML and CFT controls: what a BA must know
entries.text: AML and CFT controls: what a BA must know Core Anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing controls cover both the customer and the transaction, so map the customer risk controls and the transaction risk controls, the screening outcomes, the case escalation path and the audit trail. An analyst must understand these controls well enough to write requirements that keep the audit trail complete, because a control that cannot be evidenced is treated as if it did not happen. Evidence is the control. Evidence is the control.

entries.title: Handling ambiguous business requirements
entries.text: Handling ambiguous business requirements Core Ambiguity is normal at the start of a requirement, so work it with discovery questions to find what is actually meant, concrete examples to pin down the behaviour, process observation to see how the work is really done, and playback to confirm the understanding with stakeholders. The output is a requirement that is testable, meaning it states an observable outcome, a boundary condition and an acceptance criterion, rather than a vague wish that no one can verify. Ambiguity handled early is cheap; ambiguity found in testing is expensive. Ambiguity handled early is cheap; ambiguity found in testing is expensive.

entries.title: Making requirements testable
entries.text: Making requirements testable Core A requirement is testable when it defines an observable outcome, the boundary conditions, the negative cases and the acceptance criteria. An observable outcome states what can be seen or measured, a boundary condition states where the rule starts and stops, a negative case states what must not happen, and an acceptance criterion states the condition that proves the requirement is met. Without these four, a requirement cannot be verified and a dispute about whether it was delivered cannot be resolved. Without these four, a requirement cannot be verified and a dispute about whether it was delivered cannot be resolved.

entries.title: Resolving conflicting stakeholder requirements
entries.text: Resolving conflicting stakeholder requirements Core When stakeholders disagree, compare the competing requirements on value, risk, urgency, customer impact and dependencies, then facilitate a documented decision. The comparison must be evidence based, so each stakeholder can see why one requirement was chosen over another. Document the decision, who made it and why, because an undocumented compromise will be reopened the next time the same stakeholders meet. Document the decision, who made it and why, because an undocumented compromise will be reopened the next time the same stakeholders meet.

entries.title: Eliciting requirements from non-technical stakeholders
entries.text: Eliciting requirements from non-technical stakeholders Core Non-technical stakeholders describe what they need in business language, not in system language, so use interviews to hear the need, workshops to build shared understanding, observation to see how the work is actually done, examples to pin down the detail, and structured playback to confirm the understanding before it is written down. Playback matters most, because it catches misunderstandings while they are still cheap to fix. Confirm before you write, not after you build. Confirm before you write, not after you build.

entries.title: Resolving a late requirement gap
entries.text: Resolving a late requirement gap Core A late requirement gap is found when a piece of the need was missed, so trace the gap back to where it was lost, whether in discovery, analysis, design, implementation or testing, and agree corrective action with the owner of that stage. Tracing the gap to its origin matters because it decides whether the fix is a small correction or a rework of a whole stage, and it prevents the same gap from recurring. Fix the origin, not just the symptom. Fix the origin, not just the symptom.

entries.title: Creating process and data-flow diagrams
entries.text: Creating process and data-flow diagrams Core Choose the diagram that fits the problem being solved, then validate it: a process diagram must show the actors, the triggers, the decisions, the hand-offs and the data stores, and each of these must be checked against reality rather than assumed. Validate the diagram with the people who do the work, because a diagram that does not match the real process will mislead everyone who relies on it. A diagram is only as good as its validation. A diagram is only as good as its validation.

entries.title: Validating requirements before development
entries.text: Validating requirements before development Core Before development starts, run walkthroughs with stakeholders, consistency checks across the requirement set, testability checks on each requirement and a formal sign-off. A walkthrough catches misunderstandings, a consistency check catches contradictions, a testability check catches requirements that cannot be verified, and sign-off records agreement. Skipping validation does not save time; it moves the cost into development and testing, where fixes are far more expensive. Skipping validation does not save time; it moves the cost into development and testing, where fixes are far more expensive.

entries.title: Requirements Traceability Matrix
entries.text: Requirements Traceability Matrix Core A traceability matrix connects business objectives to requirements, stories, design, tests, defects and release evidence, with each row showing the chain from the objective through the requirement to the test that proves it. Any change can then be traced forward to its impact and any defect traced back to its origin. Without traceability, a team cannot prove that what was built is what was asked for, and cannot assess the impact of a change safely. Without traceability, a team cannot prove that what was built is what was asked for, and cannot assess the impact of a change safely.

entries.title: Stakeholder changes requirements every week
entries.text: Stakeholder changes requirements every week Core Frequent requirement changes are managed with a clear change intake, impact analysis, prioritisation and decision governance. Change intake records what is being asked and why, impact analysis states what the change costs in scope, effort and risk, prioritisation ranks the change against other work, and decision governance records who approved it and why. Without this discipline, weekly changes silently erode the scope and the delivery date. Without this discipline, weekly changes silently erode the scope and the delivery date.

entries.title: Business wants two weeks, development estimates six
entries.text: Business wants two weeks, development estimates six Core When the business wants two weeks and development estimates six, clarify the minimum outcome that would still be valuable, then work through the options. Slice the scope to the smallest useful increment, identify the dependencies that drive the estimate, and present evidence based trade-offs rather than arguing over the number. The decision is then about what to deliver and what to defer, not about whose estimate is right. The decision is then about what to deliver and what to defer, not about whose estimate is right.

entries.title: Senior management asks for a solution, not requirements
entries.text: Senior management asks for a solution, not requirements Core When senior management asks for a solution without requirements, reframe the request around outcomes, constraints, options and decision criteria: ask what outcome is needed, what constraints apply, what options exist and what criteria will decide between them. This turns a request for a specific solution into a decision that can be made on evidence, and it avoids building something that does not solve the real problem. Reframe the ask before you build the answer. Reframe the ask before you build the answer.

entries.title: Business says complete, developers disagree
entries.text: Business says complete, developers disagree Core When the business believes requirements are complete but developers disagree, the gap is usually in interpretation rather than in content. Use concrete examples to show how each side reads the requirement, run walkthroughs to surface the differences, use traceability to show what is covered and what is not, and agree shared definitions for the terms that are being read differently. Close the interpretation gap before development, because it is far cheaper to agree on meaning now than to rebuild later. Close the interpretation gap before development, because it is far cheaper to agree on meaning now than to rebuild later.

entries.title: Digital transformation faces user resistance
entries.text: Digital transformation faces user resistance Core User resistance to a digital change usually has a cause that can be identified, so map the impacts on each group of users, identify the stakeholder groups and their concerns, define the training needs, find champions who will support the change, collect feedback and measure adoption. Resistance that is understood can be addressed; resistance that is dismissed as stubbornness will grow and will damage the change. Diagnose resistance before you try to overcome it. Diagnose resistance before you try to overcome it.

entries.title: Demonstrating measurable BA contribution
entries.text: Demonstrating measurable BA contribution Core An analyst demonstrates contribution by connecting process changes to measurable outcomes: link the change to cost, cycle time, error rates, customer experience and benefits realisation, and measure before and after so the improvement can be shown rather than claimed. Benefits realisation is the final step: it proves that the change delivered the value that justified it, which is what stakeholders remember. Measured value is the analyst's evidence, not a claim. Measured value is the analyst's evidence, not a claim.

entries.title: Managing requirement change mid-sprint
entries.text: Managing requirement change mid-sprint Core A change requested mid-sprint must be assessed before it is agreed: assess the scope of the change, the impact on the sprint goal, the effort required and the dependencies it introduces. Only then decide whether to accept it, defer it or swap it for something else. Accepting a change without this assessment silently breaks the sprint goal and leaves the team accountable for a target it never agreed to. Accepting a change without this assessment silently breaks the sprint goal and leaves the team accountable for a target it never agreed to.

entries.title: Change requested after 70 percent of the sprint
entries.text: Change requested after 70 percent of the sprint Core A change requested when most of the sprint is done needs a careful assessment: establish the reason for the change, the effort it requires, the dependencies it affects and the options the product owner has, and do not silently compromise the sprint goal to absorb it. The product owner decides, with the evidence in front of them, whether the change is worth the disruption or whether it waits for the next sprint. A late change is a decision, not an instruction. A late change is a decision, not an instruction.

entries.title: Two senior stakeholders want opposite outcomes
entries.text: Two senior stakeholders want opposite outcomes Core When two senior stakeholders want opposite outcomes, facilitate an evidence based prioritisation and document the accountable decision. Lay out the value, the risk, the cost and the customer impact of each requirement, let the evidence drive the ranking, and record who made the decision and why. A documented decision ends the debate; an undocumented one will be reopened every time the stakeholders meet. A documented decision ends the debate; an undocumented one will be reopened every time the stakeholders meet.

entries.title: Business process change just before UAT
entries.text: Business process change just before UAT Core A process change just before user acceptance testing must be assessed for requirement impact, test scope, release risk and decision rights: determine which requirements change, which tests must be added or rerun, what risk the change introduces to the release, and who has the authority to approve it. A change approved without this assessment can invalidate the testing that has already been done and put the release date at risk. Never let a late change silently void completed testing. Never let a late change silently void completed testing.

entries.title: User rejects a feature built to signed-off requirements
entries.text: User rejects a feature built to signed-off requirements Core When a user rejects a feature that was built to signed-off requirements, determine whether the issue is a defect, an ambiguity, a missed need or a scope change. A defect means the build does not match the requirement, an ambiguity means the requirement was read differently, a missed need means the requirement was incomplete, and a scope change means the need has moved. Each cause has a different owner and a different fix, so classifying it correctly is the first step. Each cause has a different owner and a different fix, so classifying it correctly is the first step.

entries.title: Planning UAT and preparing test cases
entries.text: Planning UAT and preparing test cases Core User acceptance testing coverage is derived from the business journeys, the acceptance criteria, the roles involved and the exception paths. For each business journey, define the acceptance criteria that prove it works, the roles that must be able to perform it, and the exception paths that must be handled. Test cases built from this coverage test the business outcome rather than the system mechanics, which is what acceptance testing is for. Test cases built from this coverage test the business outcome rather than the system mechanics, which is what acceptance testing is for.

entries.title: BA role in SIT defect discussions
entries.text: BA role in SIT defect discussions Core In system integration testing defect discussions, the analyst assesses reproducibility, requirement traceability, business impact, fix validation and regression. Reproducibility decides whether the defect is real, traceability shows which requirement it breaks, business impact decides its priority, fix validation confirms the fix works, and regression confirms nothing else broke. This assessment keeps defect discussions focused on evidence rather than on opinion. This assessment keeps defect discussions focused on evidence rather than on opinion.

entries.title: BA support during deployment and hypercare
entries.text: BA support during deployment and hypercare Core During deployment and hypercare, the analyst monitors the critical journeys, the exception rates, the unresolved transactions and the stakeholder updates. Critical journeys show whether customers can complete their payments, exception rates show whether the system is handling failures, unresolved transactions show what still needs attention, and stakeholder updates keep everyone informed. Hypercare ends when these measures are stable, not when a fixed number of days has passed. Hypercare ends when these measures are stable, not when a fixed number of days has passed.

entries.title: Requirement, development, testing or environment miss
entries.text: Requirement, development, testing or environment miss Core When intended behaviour diverges from production behaviour, use a layered failure model to locate where it went wrong: check the requirement first, then the development, then the testing, then the environment, and find the layer where the divergence was introduced. Locating the layer matters because it decides whether the fix is a requirement correction, a code change, a test improvement or an environment fix, and it prevents the same miss from recurring. Fix at the layer that introduced the fault. Fix at the layer that introduced the fault.

entries.title: KPI design for a digital banking application
entries.text: KPI design for a digital banking application Core Key performance indicators for a digital banking application should cover adoption, task completion, failure, service, risk and customer outcome measures. Adoption shows whether customers use the feature, task completion shows whether they can finish what they start, failure shows where they are blocked, service shows whether the system performs, risk shows whether controls are holding, and customer outcome shows whether the feature delivered value. A KPI set that covers only one of these gives a misleading picture of health. A KPI set that covers only one of these gives a misleading picture of health.

entries.title: Why customers abandon the payment page
entries.text: Why customers abandon the payment page Core Customers abandon a payment page for reasons that can be found in the evidence: analyse the funnel to see where they drop off, the validation errors they encounter, the latency they experience, the payment options available and the user experience they report. Each of these points to a different fix, so the analysis must separate them rather than treating abandonment as a single problem with a single cause. Abandonment is several problems wearing one label. Abandonment is several problems wearing one label.

entries.title: Why loan approval time rises from hours to days
entries.text: Why loan approval time rises from hours to days Core When loan approval time rises from hours to days, map the process to find the bottleneck: look for queues where applications wait, manual checks that add delay, dependencies on other teams or systems, and rework where applications are sent back for correction. The bottleneck is usually a queue or a manual step rather than the decision itself, so measuring where time is actually spent is more useful than asking people where they think the delay is. Measure the clock, not the opinion. Measure the clock, not the opinion.

entries.title: Why UAT fails despite all test cases passing
entries.text: Why UAT fails despite all test cases passing Core User acceptance testing can fail even when all test cases pass, because passing test cases do not prove the business need is met. Check the test design for gaps, the representativeness of the test data, the expected outcomes for correctness, and whether the unmet business need was ever covered by a test at all. A test suite that passes but does not represent the real business journeys gives false confidence and a failed acceptance. A test suite that passes but does not represent the real business journeys gives false confidence and a failed acceptance.

entries.title: Why the same change is requested every sprint
entries.text: Why the same change is requested every sprint Core When the same change is requested every sprint, the root cause is usually unresolved: look for an unresolved root need that the change does not actually satisfy, weak discovery that missed the real requirement, policy uncertainty that leaves the team guessing, or a lack of decision ownership so no one can say no. Fixing the root cause stops the repeated request; implementing the same change again will not. Repeat requests are a symptom, not a backlog. Repeat requests are a symptom, not a backlog.

entries.title: Translate rules and edge cases for developers
entries.text: Translate rules and edge cases for developers Core Developers need rules and edge cases stated precisely: explain the triggers that start a rule, the conditions that apply, the data involved, the expected behaviour and the failure outcomes. A rule stated as a business sentence leaves the developer guessing about the boundary, while a rule stated with triggers, conditions and failure outcomes can be built and tested without further questions. Precision at the boundary is what makes a rule buildable. Precision at the boundary is what makes a rule buildable.

entries.title: Translate scenarios into testable QA coverage
entries.text: Translate scenarios into testable QA coverage Core Test coverage is built by translating business scenarios into positive, negative, boundary and regression scenarios with expected results. Positive scenarios prove the happy path works, negative scenarios prove invalid input is handled, boundary scenarios prove the limits behave correctly, and regression scenarios prove existing behaviour still works. Each scenario needs an expected result, because a test without an expected result cannot pass or fail. Each scenario needs an expected result, because a test without an expected result cannot pass or fail.

entries.title: Feature complete, but the business problem remains
entries.text: Feature complete, but the business problem remains Core A feature can be technically complete while the business problem remains unsolved, so revisit the hypothesis behind the feature, the actual user behaviour, the process adoption, the operational constraints and the outcome measures. The gap is usually that the feature was built as specified but the hypothesis was wrong, or that users did not adopt it, or that an operational constraint was missed. Measuring the outcome rather than the delivery reveals the gap. Measuring the outcome rather than the delivery reveals the gap.

entries.title: Loan approval time: two hours to two days
entries.text: Loan approval time: two hours to two days Core When loan approval time increases from two hours to two days, analyse queue time, manual reviews, document quality, decision rules and hand-offs. Queue time shows where applications wait, manual reviews show where human effort adds delay, document quality shows where rework is created, decision rules show where the logic is slow, and hand-offs show where work is lost between teams. The fix depends on which of these is actually causing the delay, so measure before changing anything. The fix depends on which of these is actually causing the delay, so measure before changing anything.

entries.title: Why stakeholders repeat the same change request
entries.text: Why stakeholders repeat the same change request Core When stakeholders repeat the same change request, investigate the root need, the decision latency, the incomplete discovery and the feedback loops. The root need may never have been satisfied, the decision may have taken so long that the requester assumed it was ignored, the discovery may have missed the real requirement, or the feedback loop may never have closed the loop with the requester. Each cause has a different fix, and implementing the change again without fixing the cause will only repeat the cycle. Each cause has a different fix, and implementing the change again without fixing the cause will only repeat the cycle.

entries.title: BA ownership without direct authority
entries.text: BA ownership without direct authority Core An analyst often owns delivery outcomes without having direct authority over the teams involved, so drive clarity by stating what is needed and by when, keep decision records so accountability is visible, follow up on actions rather than assuming they will happen, and escalate transparently when a decision or a delivery is blocked. Ownership without authority works through clarity and follow-through, not through control. Authority is borrowed; clarity is owned. Authority is borrowed; clarity is owned.

entries.title: Client says the new process damaged operations
entries.text: Client says the new process damaged operations Core When a client says a new process has damaged their operations, acknowledge the impact first, then establish the facts: provide a safe workaround so the client can keep operating, agree the recovery communications, and investigate what actually changed. Acknowledging the impact does not admit fault, it shows the client is being taken seriously, and it creates the space to find the real cause without the conversation becoming adversarial. Empathy first, evidence second, blame never. Empathy first, evidence second, blame never.

entries.title: Evidence required during a payment surge
entries.text: Evidence required during a payment surge Core During a payment surge, the evidence needed is specific: collect transaction IDs, gateway responses, API logs, timeout rates, timestamps and reconciliation status. Transaction IDs link the evidence to individual payments, gateway responses and API logs show what each system did, timeout rates show where the system is struggling, timestamps show when it happened, and reconciliation status shows whether money is accounted for. Without this evidence, the incident response is guesswork. Without this evidence, the incident response is guesswork.

entries.title: Coordinating business, dev, QA, gateway and support
entries.text: Coordinating business, dev, QA, gateway and support Core Coordinating business, development, QA, gateway and support teams during an incident needs one incident view, clear owners, evidence requests and an update cadence. One incident view prevents each team from working from a different picture, clear owners prevent work from falling between teams, evidence requests ensure the right data is collected, and a regular update cadence keeps everyone aligned. Without this coordination, teams duplicate effort and the incident lasts longer than it should. Without this coordination, teams duplicate effort and the incident lasts longer than it should.

entries.title: Build practical BA projects, not only theory
entries.text: Build practical BA projects, not only theory Core A practical BA portfolio is built from real work rather than from theory alone: create a portfolio with a problem statement, process maps, user stories, an API contract and UAT evidence, so that a reviewer can see the full chain from problem to delivered outcome. Theory shows what was studied; a portfolio shows what was actually done, which is what an employer needs to see. Show the chain, not the certificate. Show the chain, not the certificate.

entries.title: Present project experience with evidence
entries.text: Present project experience with evidence Core Present project experience by structuring the walkthrough around the problem, the role played, the decisions made, the systems involved, the risks managed and the measurable result. This structure shows the scope of the work and the contribution made, rather than a list of tasks. Measurable results matter most, because they prove the work delivered value rather than simply occupying time. Measurable results matter most, because they prove the work delivered value rather than simply occupying time.

entries.title: Walk through a current project and your BA role
entries.text: Walk through a current project and your BA role Core When walking through a current project, structure the walkthrough around context, scope, stakeholders, systems, deliverables, decisions and outcomes. Context sets the scene, scope shows the size of the work, stakeholders show who was involved, systems show the technical landscape, deliverables show what was produced, decisions show judgement, and outcomes show the result. This structure keeps the walkthrough focused and complete, and it prevents it from becoming a list of tasks. This structure keeps the walkthrough focused and complete, and it prevents it from becoming a list of tasks.

entries.title: A pacs.004 return travels the chain in reverse
entries.text: A pacs.004 return travels the chain in reverse Core When a beneficiary bank returns a payment with a pacs.004, the intermediary that received it sends a new pacs.004 back to the originator bank, so the return travels the chain in reverse. The intermediary never keeps the return: it forwards it with the reference to the original payment so the originator bank can match it. In a three-bank chain the rule is uniform: every bank that handled the payment forwards the return to the bank that sent it the payment. In a three-bank chain the rule is uniform: every bank that handled the payment forwards the return to the bank that sent it the payment.

entries.title: How a pacs.004 points back to its payment
entries.text: How a pacs.004 points back to its payment Core A pacs.004 carries the original instruction identification and the original end-to-end identification, and those two references tie it to the payment it returns. The originator bank reads them and matches the return to the payment it sent, even after the return has passed through an intermediary. Without those references a return is only a credit with no story, and reconciliation cannot prove which payment it belongs to. Without those references a return is only a credit with no story, and reconciliation cannot prove which payment it belongs to.

entries.title: A recall must travel the whole chain
entries.text: A recall must travel the whole chain Core When an originator recalls a payment that went through an intermediary, the originator bank sends a camt.056 to the intermediary, which forwards it to the beneficiary bank. The beneficiary bank checks whether the recall is feasible, and if it is, it returns the funds with a pacs.004 to the intermediary, which sends a pacs.004 back to the originator bank. A recall is therefore a chain of messages rather than a single message, and the funds come back only when every bank in the chain acts. A recall is therefore a chain of messages rather than a single message, and the funds come back only when every bank in the chain acts.

entries.title: A pacs.004 can start from either end
entries.text: A pacs.004 can start from either end Core Both the originator payment service provider and the beneficiary payment service provider can initiate a pacs.004, because a return can be started from either end of the payment. The originator side starts one when it recalls or reverses a payment, and the beneficiary side starts one when it rejects or returns a payment it cannot apply. The message is identical in both cases; only the initiating bank and the reason differ. The message is identical in both cases; only the initiating bank and the reason differ.

entries.title: camt.029 closes the recall question
entries.text: camt.029 closes the recall question Core A camt.029 answers a camt.056 recall request by stating whether the recall has been accepted or refused. Readers raise the open question of who sends it, the beneficiary bank or the clearing system, and what it must contain in each case. The answer matters because the originator bank cannot close the recall until that response arrives and confirms whether the funds are coming back. The answer matters because the originator bank cannot close the recall until that response arrives and confirms whether the funds are coming back.

entries.title: Return reason codes are a closed list
entries.text: Return reason codes are a closed list Core When a payment is returned or rejected, the reason code comes from the bank that refused it, and the scheme rulebook lists the codes that bank may use. The open question is whether a payment service provider may add its own codes beyond the rulebook, and a bank that invents one risks the return being rejected by the next bank in the chain. A reason code is therefore a controlled vocabulary, not a free-text field. A reason code is therefore a controlled vocabulary, not a free-text field.

entries.title: What a pacs.002 must carry on a rejection
entries.text: What a pacs.002 must carry on a rejection Core When a pacs.008 is rejected, the pacs.002 reports that rejection, and the open question is which fields it must carry to explain what went wrong. It must identify the original payment and carry the status and the reason code, so the originator bank knows the payment did not settle and why. A pacs.002 without that information leaves the originator guessing, which is why the exact fields required are the question readers ask. A pacs.002 without that information leaves the originator guessing, which is why the exact fields required are the question readers ask.

entries.title: Cover timing: MT103 first, funds later
entries.text: Cover timing: MT103 first, funds later Core In a cover payment the MT103 and the MT202 COV travel separately, so the MT103 can reach the beneficiary bank before the funds leg arrives. The beneficiary bank must then hold the instruction and wait for the cover, because it cannot credit the beneficiary until the funds have settled. This timing gap is a normal feature of the cover method, not an error, though it is also the moment when an amount or reference mismatch is most likely to surface. This timing gap is a normal feature of the cover method, not an error, though it is also the moment when an amount or reference mismatch is most likely to surface.

entries.title: Spotting the MT202 COV at the beneficiary bank
entries.text: Spotting the MT202 COV at the beneficiary bank Core When an MT202 COV reaches the beneficiary bank, the bank must recognise that its purpose is to cover a specific MT103, and the link is the reference and the fields that tie the two messages together. Without that link the cover looks like an ordinary bank-to-bank transfer, and the beneficiary bank cannot match it to the customer payment it is meant to settle. The reference is therefore the bridge between the information leg and the funds leg. The reference is therefore the bridge between the information leg and the funds leg.

entries.title: Addressing the MT202 COV to the funding bank
entries.text: Addressing the MT202 COV to the funding bank Core In a chain, the MT202 COV is addressed to the bank that holds the account from which the funds will settle, and each bank in the chain addresses its own cover leg to the next bank that will fund it. Addressing the cover to the wrong bank breaks settlement, because the funds land in an account that was not expecting them. The address is therefore part of the settlement design, not an administrative detail. The address is therefore part of the settlement design, not an administrative detail.

entries.title: Returning the funds of a rejected cover payment
entries.text: Returning the funds of a rejected cover payment Core When a cover payment is rejected, the funds leg and the information leg have different senders, so the question is who returns the funds and by which message. The bank holding the rejected cover must return the funds to the bank that sent them, so the money travels back along the same correspondent path it came on. A return sent to the wrong bank creates a second exception on top of the first. A return sent to the wrong bank creates a second exception on top of the first.

entries.title: Two ordering parties in one cover payment
entries.text: Two ordering parties in one cover payment Core In a cover payment the ordering customer named in the MT103 and the ordering customer named in the MT202 COV can be different parties, because the MT103 names the customer who instructed the payment while the MT202 COV names the bank moving the funds. Readers ask which one counts as the ordering customer, and the answer is that each message has its own ordering party for its own leg. Treating them as one party is a common source of confusion in cover payments. Treating them as one party is a common source of confusion in cover payments.

entries.title: Field 72: the instruction inside the cover
entries.text: Field 72: the instruction inside the cover Core Field 72 carries sender-to-receiver information, and in a cover payment it tells the next bank what the cover is for and what to do with it. Readers ask repeatedly what field 72 should contain in an MT202 COV, because the field is free text and a wrong instruction can send the funds to the wrong place or delay settlement. The discipline is to put only the instruction the next bank needs, in the form the next bank expects. The discipline is to put only the instruction the next bank needs, in the form the next bank expects.

entries.title: Serial charges: deducted at every step
entries.text: Serial charges: deducted at every step Core In a serial payment the ordering customer bears the charges, and each intermediary bank deducts its own charge from the amount as the payment passes through. The beneficiary therefore receives the amount minus the charges deducted at each step, which is why the credit can be less than the amount sent. An analyst pricing a serial payment must account for every deduction in the chain, not just the first one. An analyst pricing a serial payment must account for every deduction in the chain, not just the first one.

entries.title: Two deductions, one final credit: fields 71A, 71F
entries.text: Two deductions, one final credit: fields 71A, 71F Core When two intermediary banks each deduct a charge, the beneficiary bank works out the final credit from fields 71A and 71F of the MT103. Field 71A states who bears the charges, and field 71F states the amount of each charge deducted, so the credit can be reconciled against the amount the ordering customer sent. Without those fields the beneficiary cannot reconcile the credit against the amount sent. Without those fields the beneficiary cannot reconcile the credit against the amount sent.

entries.title: Charge arithmetic follows the payment method
entries.text: Charge arithmetic follows the payment method Core In a serial payment charges are deducted step by step as the payment passes through each intermediary, while in a cover payment the charges on the information leg and the funds leg are handled separately. The calculation therefore depends on the method, and a payment that mixes the two methods without care can double-charge or under-charge. The analyst must know which method applies before working out what the beneficiary will receive. The analyst must know which method applies before working out what the beneficiary will receive.

entries.title: An MT103 return travels the chain backwards
entries.text: An MT103 return travels the chain backwards Core When an MT103 is returned, the funds come back through the same chain of banks that carried the payment forward, each bank sending the return to the bank that sent it the payment. The charges on the return follow fields 71A and 71F, so the amount that comes back is the amount sent minus the charges already deducted. A return is therefore not a new payment; it is the original payment travelling backwards, and the chain must be able to trace it. A return is therefore not a new payment; it is the original payment travelling backwards, and the chain must be able to trace it.

entries.title: Invalid beneficiary account: the return route
entries.text: Invalid beneficiary account: the return route Core When the beneficiary bank finds the customer account invalid, it returns the payment, and the return must travel back through the intermediary to the originator bank. The beneficiary bank cannot simply keep the funds, and it cannot return them directly to the originator while an intermediary sits in between. An invalid account is one of the most common reasons for a return, and the handling is the same whether the fault is a wrong number, a closed account, or a name that does not match. An invalid account is one of the most common reasons for a return, and the handling is the same whether the fault is a wrong number, a closed account, or a name that does not match.

entries.title: When a clearing house cannot carry a recall
entries.text: When a clearing house cannot carry a recall Core Some clearing houses do not support the camt.056 recall message, so the originator bank and the clearing system cannot send a recall to the beneficiary bank for a payment that has already settled. The Estonian clearing house is a real example: it does not support the recall message, so a settled SCT payment cannot be recalled through that route. An analyst must know which clearing systems support a recall before promising a customer that a payment can be taken back. An analyst must know which clearing systems support a recall before promising a customer that a payment can be taken back.

entries.title: A recall after the beneficiary has spent the funds
entries.text: A recall after the beneficiary has spent the funds Core When a payment has been executed and the beneficiary has already spent the funds, a camt.056 can still be sent to ask the beneficiary bank to return the money, but the beneficiary bank must ask its customer whether it agrees. If the funds are no longer there, the recall cannot be completed by message alone, and the customer must take action against the beneficiary. Once the money has been spent, a recall is a request, not a reversal. Once the money has been spent, a recall is a request, not a reversal.

entries.title: Recall in favour of a third-party beneficiary
entries.text: Recall in favour of a third-party beneficiary Core When a recall is made in favour of a third-party beneficiary, for example a bank acting as debtor agent, the question is who receives the recall and who must act on it. The recall is sent to the first agent in the chain, the bank that must return the credit, and that bank then passes the recall onward. The third party never receives the recall directly; it receives the result through the bank that acts for it. The third party never receives the recall directly; it receives the result through the bank that acts for it.

entries.title: A rejected recall and a misused GVC code
entries.text: A rejected recall and a misused GVC code Core A camt.056 recall request can itself be rejected, and readers ask what that rejection looks like and what the reason code means. One real case is a recall returned with a pacs.004 carrying the reason code GVC, which is not a code that should be used for a return, so the handling was wrong. A reason code must match the message and the situation, and a code used in the wrong place creates a second exception. A reason code must match the message and the situation, and a code used in the wrong place creates a second exception.

entries.title: camt.026 reports, camt.056 recalls
entries.text: camt.026 reports, camt.056 recalls Core A camt.056 requests a recall of a payment, asking the beneficiary bank to return funds that have already been credited. A camt.026 reports that a payment cannot be applied, telling the sender that the instruction could not be processed. The two are often confused because both relate to a payment that did not complete, but they do different jobs: one asks for money back, the other reports that money could not be applied. The two are often confused because both relate to a payment that did not complete, but they do different jobs: one asks for money back, the other reports that money could not be applied.

entries.title: Is pacs.004 mandatory for a return?
entries.text: Is pacs.004 mandatory for a return? Core When a payment must be returned, the question is whether a pacs.004 is mandatory or the return can be made another way. The pacs.004 is the ISO 20022 message designed for returns in the SEPA interbank space, and it carries the link to the original payment that lets every bank in the chain match it. Using another route breaks that link, which is why the pacs.004 is the expected message for a return. Using another route breaks that link, which is why the pacs.004 is the expected message for a return.

entries.title: Screen both legs of a cover payment
entries.text: Screen both legs of a cover payment Core An MT103 and its MT202 COV are both subject to sanction screening, and the screening must happen before the payment is credited to the beneficiary. Readers ask what the screening process looks like for a cover payment, because the information leg and the funds leg are screened separately and a hit on either leg stops the payment. A bank that screens only the MT103 and not the cover, or the reverse, leaves a gap that a regulator will find. A bank that screens only the MT103 and not the cover, or the reverse, leaves a gap that a regulator will find.

entries.title: When the MT103 and the MT202 COV disagree
entries.text: When the MT103 and the MT202 COV disagree Core In a cover payment the MT103 and the MT202 COV must agree on amount and on the references that link them, and a mismatch between the two creates an exception that stops settlement. The discrepancy can be a different amount, a missing reference, or details that do not line up, and the bank must investigate before it credits the beneficiary. A mismatch is therefore not a minor data error; it is a break in the link between the information leg and the funds leg. A mismatch is therefore not a minor data error; it is a break in the link between the information leg and the funds leg.

entries.title: Recalling a serial MT103 follows the chain
entries.text: Recalling a serial MT103 follows the chain Core A serial MT103 can be recalled, but the recall must travel the same chain of banks that carried the payment forward, because each bank in the chain holds part of the payment. The originator bank sends the recall to the next bank in the chain, and each bank passes it on until it reaches the beneficiary bank, which decides whether the funds can be returned. A recall that skips a bank cannot work, because the bank that was skipped still holds the funds. A recall that skips a bank cannot work, because the bank that was skipped still holds the funds.

entries.title: Paying a bank that is not a SWIFT member
entries.text: Paying a bank that is not a SWIFT member Core When the beneficiary bank is not a SWIFT member, the MT103 cannot be sent to it directly, so the payment must reach it through a bank that is a member and can forward the instruction. The forwarding bank becomes an intermediary in the chain, and the payment follows the same serial or cover logic as any other payment with an intermediary. Non-membership does not stop the payment; it adds a step to the chain. Non-membership does not stop the payment; it adds a step to the chain.

entries.title: An MT103 with field 57 left empty
entries.text: An MT103 with field 57 left empty Core When an MT103 arrives with field 57 empty, the message names no beneficiary bank, so the receiving bank must work out where the payment should go from the other fields. The empty field is not necessarily an error: it can mean the payment is to be handled by the receiving bank itself, or that the beneficiary bank is identified elsewhere in the chain. The analyst must read the whole message before deciding whether the empty field is a gap or a deliberate omission. The analyst must read the whole message before deciding whether the empty field is a gap or a deliberate omission.

entries.title: Parent pays for subsidiaries via MT101
entries.text: Parent pays for subsidiaries via MT101 Core A parent company can pay on behalf of its subsidiaries using an MT101, and the question is how the instruction names the subsidiary as the ordering customer for each transaction. The MT101 carries a general instruction sequence and a per-transaction sequence, and the subsidiary appears as the ordering customer in the per-transaction sequence. The parent's bank must then report each transaction under the correct subsidiary, so the accounting and the screening both land on the right party. The parent's bank must then report each transaction under the correct subsidiary, so the accounting and the screening both land on the right party.

entries.title: MT103 STP: option A only
entries.text: MT103 STP: option A only Core An MT103 STP is a straight-through-processing version of the MT103, and it only allows option A for fields such as 52, 54 and 57. Option A carries the party identifier and the BIC, so the receiving system can identify the bank without human help. Any other option leaves the bank to work out who the party is by hand, which is why those options are not allowed in an STP message. Any other option leaves the bank to work out who the party is by hand, which is why those options are not allowed in an STP message.

entries.title: A credit notification is not an MT103
entries.text: A credit notification is not an MT103 Core An MT103 instructs the receiving bank to debit the sender's account and pay the beneficiary, so it is an instruction to move money. When a bank only wants to say that an account has already been credited, it uses an MT910 confirmation of credit or an MT950 or MT940 statement instead. Sending an MT103 for a credit that has already happened confuses an instruction with a notification, and the receiving bank may try to debit an account that should not be debited. Sending an MT103 for a credit that has already happened confuses an instruction with a notification, and the receiving bank may try to debit an account that should not be debited.

entries.title: Fields 55 and 56: intermediary and reimbursement
entries.text: Fields 55 and 56: intermediary and reimbursement Core Field 56 names the intermediary institution, the bank that receives the payment from the sender and forwards it to the account with institution in field 57. Field 55 names a third reimbursement institution, used when the funds are reimbursed through a bank that is neither the sender nor the receiver. When a serial chain gains an intermediary, field 56A is simply added, and when the receiver is itself the receiver's correspondent there is no need to name it in field 56 at all. When a serial chain gains an intermediary, field 56A is simply added, and when the receiver is itself the receiver's correspondent there is no need to name it in field 56 at all.

entries.title: MT900: confirmation of a debit
entries.text: MT900: confirmation of a debit Core When a bank debits an account on the instruction of an MT103, it can confirm the debit with an MT900, a confirmation of debit. The MT900 is a separate message, not part of the MT103 itself, and whether one is sent depends on the agreement between the two banks. A payment can therefore settle correctly without any MT900 being exchanged. A payment can therefore settle correctly without any MT900 being exchanged.

entries.title: Account relationships decide serial or cover
entries.text: Account relationships decide serial or cover Core A Canadian bank paying a United States beneficiary held its United States dollars with Wells Fargo, while the beneficiary held its account with Citibank New York. Because the sending bank had no account relationship with Citibank, the correct route was a cover payment: an MT103 sent directly to Citibank and an MT202 COV sent to Wells Fargo. If the sending bank had held an account with the beneficiary's bank, a single serial MT103 would have been enough. If the sending bank had held an account with the beneficiary's bank, a single serial MT103 would have been enough.

entries.title: The cover amount must never fall short
entries.text: The cover amount must never fall short Core It is forbidden to take charges from an MT202 COV, so the cover amount must never be lower than the amount announced in the MT103. If an intermediary needs to be paid for its part in the chain, it asks the sending bank to pay through an MT191 or debits the account directly under the agreement between the banks. A cover that arrives short of the announced amount is therefore an exception, not a normal deduction. A cover that arrives short of the announced amount is therefore an exception, not a normal deduction.

entries.title: RMA: authorisation before the MT103 arrives
entries.text: RMA: authorisation before the MT103 arrives Core Before one bank can send an MT103 to another over SWIFT, the receiving bank must set up an RMA, a relationship management authorisation, for that sender. Without an RMA the receiving bank's system will not accept the message, which is why a beneficiary bank is asked to establish one before a payment is sent. The RMA is therefore a precondition for the payment, not a formality that can be sorted out afterwards. The RMA is therefore a precondition for the payment, not a formality that can be sorted out afterwards.

entries.title: Sequence B of the MT202 COV must mirror the MT103
entries.text: Sequence B of the MT202 COV must mirror the MT103 Core In sequence B of an MT202 COV, only the ordering and beneficiary customer information in fields 50a and 59a is mandatory, and the other fields are optional. When the bank does provide a field such as field 72 or field 59, it must match the same field in the MT103 exactly, or the field must be left empty. Some banks reject a cover whose sequence B does not match the announcement, so a mismatch stops the funds even when the amounts agree. Some banks reject a cover whose sequence B does not match the announcement, so a mismatch stops the funds even when the amounts agree.

entries.title: SSI: the routing table banks share
entries.text: SSI: the routing table banks share Core Banks tell each other how to send them funds in each currency through standing settlement instructions, exchanged as MT670 and MT671 messages and stored in payment engine databases. An SSI names the correspondent of the receiver and any intermediaries on the route, so the sending bank can build the MT103 and the cover from the database instead of asking every time. A sender who does not know the receiver's correspondent must find it out through SWIFT services or by asking the receiver directly. A sender who does not know the receiver's correspondent must find it out through SWIFT services or by asking the receiver directly.

entries.title: Several SSIs: the sender picks the shortest route
entries.text: Several SSIs: the sender picks the shortest route Core A bank can publish several standing settlement instructions for one currency, marking one as preferred, but the preferred route is an option, not an order. The sender may use a shorter route, even one that passes through a bank named in a non-preferred instruction, because the aim is for the funds to reach the beneficiary. If the beneficiary is paid faster on the shorter route, no one in the chain will complain. If the beneficiary is paid faster on the shorter route, no one in the chain will complain.

entries.title: Field 57a points at a different bank in each leg
entries.text: Field 57a points at a different bank in each leg Core In a serial MT103, field 57a names the bank that holds the beneficiary's account, and field 56 names the intermediary that forwards the payment to it. In an MT202 COV the roles shift: field 58a names the beneficiary bank, while field 57a names the correspondent bank of the beneficiary bank. Reading field 57a the same way in both messages is a common error, because the same field number points at a different bank in each leg. Reading field 57a the same way in both messages is a common error, because the same field number points at a different bank in each leg.

entries.title: The MT202 COV is itself a serial payment
entries.text: The MT202 COV is itself a serial payment Core Looked at on its own, an MT202 COV is a serial payment: the sender instructs the receiver to debit the sender's account and credit the next bank in the chain. Each bank in the cover chain debits the previous bank's account and instructs the next bank, until the funds reach the beneficiary bank. The cover is therefore not a different kind of movement; it is the same serial mechanism carrying the funds leg of a customer payment. The cover is therefore not a different kind of movement; it is the same serial mechanism carrying the funds leg of a customer payment.

entries.title: MT190 and MT191: the charges leg between banks
entries.text: MT190 and MT191: the charges leg between banks Core When one bank owes another bank charges or interest on a payment, the claim travels in an MT191, a request for payment of charges, and the advice travels in an MT190. These messages exist because charges must not be deducted from a cover payment, so an intermediary that is owed money asks for it separately instead of taking it from the funds. A reader who sees an MT191 in a chain is therefore looking at the charges leg, not the payment itself. A reader who sees an MT191 in a chain is therefore looking at the charges leg, not the payment itself.

entries.title: No intermediary may change the currency
entries.text: No intermediary may change the currency Core The sender decides the currency of a transaction, and no intermediary may change it on the way. If the beneficiary's account is in a different currency, the conversion happens as a separate foreign exchange step, and the beneficiary is credited in the currency of the account. A payment sent in United States dollars to a United States dollar account that arrives short because an intermediary converted it twice has gone wrong, and the banks in the chain must be challenged on it. A payment sent in United States dollars to a United States dollar account that arrives short because an intermediary converted it twice has gone wrong, and the banks in the chain must be challenged on it.

entries.title: Cross-border timing: when a delay is a problem
entries.text: Cross-border timing: when a delay is a problem Core A transfer in a major currency such as the United States dollar or the euro usually arrives in 48 to 72 hours, while a transfer in a less common local currency takes longer because the currency is harder to buy. A large amount can also slow a payment down, because it may need extra checks before it is released. If the money has not arrived after two weeks, there is definitely a problem, and the sending bank should be asked to trace it, since it knows every party in the chain. If the money has not arrived after two weeks, there is definitely a problem, and the sending bank should be asked to trace it, since it knows every party in the chain.

entries.title: 71A BEN: the beneficiary bears every charge
entries.text: 71A BEN: the beneficiary bears every charge Core When field 71A carries BEN, every charge in the chain is borne by the beneficiary, and each bank deducts its charge from the amount as the payment passes through. The sender does not prepay the downstream charges, because the beneficiary is the one who pays them. A bank copy that shows SHA where the sender instructed BEN is therefore a discrepancy worth querying, since the two codes give the beneficiary a different amount. A bank copy that shows SHA where the sender instructed BEN is therefore a discrepancy worth querying, since the two codes give the beneficiary a different amount.

entries.title: The charges equation: 32A, 33B, 71G, 71F
entries.text: The charges equation: 32A, 33B, 71G, 71F Core Field 32A is the amount that settles between banks, field 33B is the amount the ordering customer instructed, field 71G is the receiver's charges prepaid by the sender, and field 71F is each sender's charge deducted along the way. The relationship always holds: 32A equals 33B plus 71G minus all the 71F charges. Field 71A itself is set by the bank that generates the MT103 and cannot be changed by later banks, which can only add a 71F when they take a charge. Field 71A itself is set by the bank that generates the MT103 and cannot be changed by later banks, which can only add a 71F when they take a charge.

entries.title: Field 57 options B, C and D: what each carries
entries.text: Field 57 options B, C and D: what each carries Core Field 57 offers four options, and option A, with a BIC, is the one that allows straight-through processing. Option B carries a party identifier, generally an account number, with the location of the account, and a BIC must never be passed in option B: if the BIC is to be used, option A is the right choice. Option D needs no routing code at all and can simply carry the bank's name and address, while the /C/ or /D/ code before an account number is part of the standard but almost never used in practice. Option A is therefore the default whenever a BIC is available, and the other options are for identifiers a BIC cannot express. Option A is therefore the default whenever a BIC is available, and the other options are for identifiers a BIC cannot express.

entries.title: A CHIPS UID in field 57A
entries.text: A CHIPS UID in field 57A Core In option A of field 57, the line before the BIC is the party identifier, and for a United States payment that identifier can be the beneficiary bank's CHIPS UID. The CHIPS UID identifies the bank in the United States clearing system, while the BIC identifies it on SWIFT, so the two sit together in the same field. Using the BIC alone is also valid, but the UID removes any doubt about which clearing account should be used. Using the BIC alone is also valid, but the UID removes any doubt about which clearing account should be used.

entries.title: Field 53B: pinning down the account to debit
entries.text: Field 53B: pinning down the account to debit Core A bank can hold more than one account with the same correspondent in the same currency, and field 53B exists to say exactly which account must be debited. Using option B tells the receiver that the sender has many accounts with it and wants a specific one used to settle the transaction. Field 53 itself is optional in an MT103, and it does not always contain the sender's nostro account, because the field has three options that can carry different information. Field 53 itself is optional in an MT103, and it does not always contain the sender's nostro account, because the field has three options that can carry different information.

entries.title: Field 70: codes, references and the 16-character limit
entries.text: Field 70: codes, references and the 16-character limit Core Field 70 carries remittance information, and several references can be given if they are separated by a double slash, but one code such as /RFB/ or /INV/ cannot serve two references of the same kind. The reference that follows /RFB/ is limited to 16 characters, so a longer description must continue on the following lines of the field instead of stretching the reference. A field 70 that repeats a code or overruns the limit is not a valid instruction, even though no system may reject it automatically. A field 70 that repeats a code or overruns the limit is not a valid instruction, even though no system may reject it automatically.

entries.title: FFC: routing funds past the named beneficiary
entries.text: FFC: routing funds past the named beneficiary Core When the funds must be credited to an account other than the beneficiary's own account, the instruction travels as /FFC/, for further credit, in field 72, sender to receiver information. The beneficiary bank reads the code and passes the funds on to the account named after it, instead of crediting the beneficiary directly. Without the code, the bank has no instruction to look beyond the beneficiary named in field 59. Without the code, the bank has no instruction to look beyond the beneficiary named in field 59.

entries.title: UETR in field 121: the reference that traces a payment
entries.text: UETR in field 121: the reference that traces a payment Core The unique end-to-end transaction reference, the UETR, is carried in field 121 of block 3 of the message header, not in the body of the MT103. When a payment is late or a bank cannot trace it, the UETR is the reference to give the bank, because every bank in the chain can use it to follow the payment across the network. A copy of an MT103 on its own proves nothing about whether the money moved; the UETR and the sending bank's records are what settle the question. A copy of an MT103 on its own proves nothing about whether the money moved; the UETR and the sending bank's records are what settle the question.

entries.title: Field 50K: a name may span several lines
entries.text: Field 50K: a name may span several lines Core Option K of field 50a allows the ordering customer's name and address in up to four lines of 35 characters each. The name does not have to fit on the first line: it can sit on one line with the address on the rest, or run over two or three lines with the address on what remains. The standard does not restrict the name to the first line, so a name split across lines is valid. The standard does not restrict the name to the first line, so a name split across lines is valid.

entries.title: The announcement must name the cover's source
entries.text: The announcement must name the cover's source Core In a cover payment the MT103 announcement should state in field 53 which correspondent will send the cover, so the beneficiary bank knows where the funds will come from. When the cover arrives from a bank the announcement never mentioned, the beneficiary bank cannot match the two legs and will not credit the beneficiary. The fix sits with the sender, whose bank must correct the announcement so the two legs agree. The fix sits with the sender, whose bank must correct the announcement so the two legs agree.

entries.title: An MT103 with no beneficiary name
entries.text: An MT103 with no beneficiary name Core An MT103 can arrive showing only the beneficiary's IBAN and address in field 59, with no name at all. Field 59 is meant to identify the beneficiary, so a missing name leaves the beneficiary bank unable to confirm that the account belongs to the person the payment was meant for. The bank may hold the payment and ask for confirmation instead of crediting it, and the sender's bank is the one that must supply the missing name. The bank may hold the payment and ask for confirmation instead of crediting it, and the sender's bank is the one that must supply the missing name.

entries.title: MT101 fields 20 and 21R: two references, two owners
entries.text: MT101 fields 20 and 21R: two references, two owners Core Field 20 is the sender's reference, assigned by the bank that sends the MT101 to identify the payment. Field 21R is the ordering customer's reference, assigned by the customer who ordered the payment, and it stays the same across every message sent for one order. The two references can coincide when the sender is also the ordering customer, but they belong to different parties, and field 21R is optional while field 20 is mandatory. The two references can coincide when the sender is also the ordering customer, but they belong to different parties, and field 21R is optional while field 20 is mandatory.

entries.title: Parent pays, subsidiary is named to the beneficiary
entries.text: Parent pays, subsidiary is named to the beneficiary Core When a parent company sends an MT101 to pay on behalf of a subsidiary, the parent company stands as the sender, not the subsidiary. The beneficiary is told the payment is from the subsidiary through the Instructing Party field, which names the subsidiary even though the parent sent the instruction. The beneficiary therefore sees the parent as the sender and the subsidiary as the party the payment is really from. The beneficiary therefore sees the parent as the sender and the subsidiary as the party the payment is really from.

entries.title: Drawing on the parent's account needs authority
entries.text: Drawing on the parent's account needs authority Core A subsidiary cannot simply use its parent company's account to pay: an authorisation is required before the subsidiary may draw on the parent's account. In the MT101 the subsidiary appears as the Instructing Party in field 50L, while the parent company appears as the ordering customer in field 50H, because the parent owns the account that will be debited. The same need for authorisation applies whenever the sender of an instruction is not the owner of the account being debited. The same need for authorisation applies whenever the sender of an instruction is not the owner of the account being debited.

entries.title: One MT101 to a concentrating bank
entries.text: One MT101 to a concentrating bank Core A large corporate with accounts at many banks can send a single MT101 to one concentrating bank, and that bank forwards the instruction to each bank that holds an account to be debited. The alternative is for the corporate to prepare a separate MT101 for every bank, which is slower and harder to manage. The forwarding service is a genuine value-added service, and the concentrating bank charges for it. The forwarding service is a genuine value-added service, and the concentrating bank charges for it.

entries.title: Field 28D: splitting one order across MT101s
entries.text: Field 28D: splitting one order across MT101s Core An MT101 message is limited to 10,000 characters, so an order with many transactions must be split across several MT101 messages, numbered in field 28D as 1 of 5, 2 of 5, and so on. Banks are configured to hold a chained message until every message in the chain has arrived, because processing one element alone could pay the wrong amounts. Banks also set their own limits on how many transactions they will accept in one order, so a very large order should be agreed with the bank before it is sent.
