Banks also set their own limits on how many transactions they will accept in one order, so a very large order should be agreed with the bank before it is sent.

entries.title: Same bank, both accounts: one MT101 suffices
entries.text: Same bank, both accounts: one MT101 suffices Core If the same bank holds both the debtor's account and the beneficiary's account, the payment never leaves the bank, so no interbank message is needed. A single MT101 is enough: the bank debits the debtor's account and credits the beneficiary's account on its own books. An MT103 is only required when the beneficiary's bank is different from the debtor's bank. An MT103 is only required when the beneficiary's bank is different from the debtor's bank.

entries.title: MT940: one closing balance per statement
entries.text: MT940: one closing balance per statement Core A statement split across several MT940 messages must use the intermediate closing balance, tag 62M, in every message except the last. Only the final message carries the final closing balance, tag 62F, because there is only one closing balance for the whole statement. A client system that receives a 62F in an intermediate message may treat the statement as finished and fail to generate the messages that follow. A client system that receives a 62F in an intermediate message may treat the statement as finished and fail to generate the messages that follow.

entries.title: MT940 intermediate balance dates: match the last entry
entries.text: MT940 intermediate balance dates: match the last entry Core When a statement is split across several MT940 messages, the intermediate opening balance tag 60M and the intermediate closing balance tag 62M should ideally show the date of the last entry in that message. In practice receivers care most that the balances themselves are correct, and the dates that truly matter are those of the opening balance, the closing balance, the closing available balance and the forward available balance. If the intermediate dates can be fixed easily, they should be. If the intermediate dates can be fixed easily, they should be.

entries.title: A long statement arrives as several MT940s
entries.text: A long statement arrives as several MT940s Core A single MT940 can carry only a limited number of entries, so a statement with many entries is split across several MT940 messages, one after another. Each message carries a statement number and a sequence number, and the sequence number rises with each new message, so the receiver can put the statement back together in order. The chain can run to a very large number of sequences, which is more than enough in practice. The chain can run to a very large number of sequences, which is more than enough in practice.

entries.title: pacs.002: a status report with no entry of its own
entries.text: pacs.002: a status report with no entry of its own Core A pacs.002 reports the outcome of a pacs.008; it moves no money, so it normally needs no accounting entry of its own. When it carries a negative acknowledgement, the postings made for the original payment are undone exactly, debit and credit reversed, restoring the books to their pre-payment position. Booking the status report itself as a debit or credit would count the same payment twice. Booking the status report itself as a debit or credit would count the same payment twice.

entries.title: Credit notification: camt.054 or MT900, sender decides
entries.text: Credit notification: camt.054 or MT900, sender decides Core When a bank tells its customer that a credit has landed, it may use a camt.054 in ISO 20022 or an MT900 in MT format, and both do the same job. No rule compels one format over the other, so the sender picks the form it will use. The receiving side must therefore be ready to read either format when the advice arrives. The receiving side must therefore be ready to read either format when the advice arrives.

entries.title: SDD: silence after pacs.007 is normal, not failure
entries.text: SDD: silence after pacs.007 is normal, not failure Core Under the SDD scheme the debtor bank sends no scheme response once it has the pacs.007 collection instruction, so silence after that point says nothing about the outcome. When the collection comes back, it arrives as a pacs.004 return or refund, and the creditor bank must process it without any option to refuse. The creditor therefore builds its processing around handling returns, rather than waiting for the debtor bank to seek agreement. The creditor therefore builds its processing around handling returns, rather than waiting for the debtor bank to seek agreement.

entries.title: pacs.004: the initiator decides return or refund
entries.text: pacs.004: the initiator decides return or refund Core A pacs.004 can carry either a return or a refund, and the two are distinct business events sharing one message type. The debtor bank starts a return, while the debtor starts a refund, so reading the initiator identifies which event the message carries. That identification matters because the two events run under different rules and different time limits. That identification matters because the two events run under different rules and different time limits.

entries.title: SDD Core refunds: 8 weeks, or 13 months if no mandate
entries.text: SDD Core refunds: 8 weeks, or 13 months if no mandate Core In SDD Core a debtor may claim a refund within 8 weeks where a valid mandate stands behind the collection. The 13 month window opens only where no valid mandate exists at all, so the two periods must never be confused. The creditor holds the mandate, which is why the creditor must produce it when a refund claim is disputed. The creditor holds the mandate, which is why the creditor must produce it when a refund claim is disputed.

entries.title: MT950 intraday runs only when both sides agree
entries.text: MT950 intraday runs only when both sides agree Core An MT950 is normally the end of day statement, yet it can also be produced intraday alongside the MT940. The single condition is agreement between the account servicing bank and the account owner. That agreement sets what the receiver should expect to see during the day. That agreement sets what the receiver should expect to see during the day.

entries.title: MT950: field 61 repeats, field 62F closes once
entries.text: MT950: field 61 repeats, field 62F closes once Core Every transaction on an MT950 sits in its own repeating field 61, so twenty transactions mean twenty field 61 blocks. The closing balance in field 62F appears a single time, at the very end of the statement. That balance must agree with the opening balance plus all field 61 entries, and checking the arithmetic is the fastest completeness test. That balance must agree with the opening balance plus all field 61 entries, and checking the arithmetic is the fastest completeness test.

entries.title: MT940: field 61 moves the money, field 86 explains it
entries.text: MT940: field 61 moves the money, field 86 explains it Core In an MT940, field 61 is the statement line, carrying the date, the amount and the entry type for each transaction. Field 86 sits beside that line and carries the information to the account owner, the narrative behind the movement. Field 61 alone shows that money moved; field 86 shows why, and reconciliation needs both together. Field 61 alone shows that money moved; field 86 shows why, and reconciliation needs both together.

entries.title: MT940 balances: 62M, 64 and 65 answer different questions
entries.text: MT940 balances: 62M, 64 and 65 answer different questions Core Field 62M is the interim closing balance, struck when the statement was cut during the day. Field 64 is the closing available balance, the funds actually available at day end, while field 65 is the forward available balance, the funds expected on a future date. Confusing them overstates or understates liquidity, so each balance must be read for the question it answers. Confusing them overstates or understates liquidity, so each balance must be read for the question it answers.

entries.title: MT940: field 28C is the first completeness check
entries.text: MT940: field 28C is the first completeness check Core Field 28C carries the statement number and the sequence number, pinning down exactly which statement this is and where it sits in the run. A missing statement, or one arriving out of order, shows as a gap in the 28C sequence before any transaction is examined. That makes 28C the first completeness check on every MT940 received. That makes 28C the first completeness check on every MT940 received.

entries.title: Small banks ride on large banks' correspondent networks
entries.text: Small banks ride on large banks' correspondent networks Core Building and maintaining a correspondent network is costly and slow, so a small bank often opens a foreign currency account with a large bank in its own country that already holds a correspondent in the currency's country. That large bank then acts as intermediary for the small bank's cross-border payments, while the real funds still end up held in the currency's country. Strictly the large bank is the small bank's correspondent, but in a cross-border transfer it is usually called the intermediary bank. Strictly the large bank is the small bank's correspondent, but in a cross-border transfer it is usually called the intermediary bank.

entries.title: Settlement instructions: how banks publish correspondents
entries.text: Settlement instructions: how banks publish correspondents Core Banks tell each other who their correspondents are through Standing Settlement Instructions, exchanged as SWIFT MT670 and MT671 messages, and receiving banks store them in their payment engines. The MT671 goes out to all SWIFT institutions, whether or not they hold a direct relationship with the sender. Where a bank has several correspondents in one currency it lists them all, leaving the sender to choose among them. Where a bank has several correspondents in one currency it lists them all, leaving the sender to choose among them.

entries.title: Mirror nostro moves transaction by transaction
entries.text: Mirror nostro moves transaction by transaction Core Every movement on the real nostro is mirrored one transaction at a time, never in a daily batch. When the nostro is credited, the correspondent advises the holder, for example with an MT910 or MT950, and the mirror is updated from that advice. When the bank instructs its correspondent to debit the nostro, the mirror is updated at once, and the two entries always carry the same amount with opposite signs. When the bank instructs its correspondent to debit the nostro, the mirror is updated at once, and the two entries always carry the same amount with opposite signs.

entries.title: Why the mirror nostro always shows the opposite sign
entries.text: Why the mirror nostro always shows the opposite sign Core A debit on the real nostro appears as a credit on the mirror, and a credit on the real account appears as a debit on the mirror, always for the same amount. The mirror reflects the real account, so the two sides sit opposite by design rather than by coincidence. Reading the mirror balance and its movements therefore tells a bank exactly what the real account should show. Reading the mirror balance and its movements therefore tells a bank exactly what the real account should show.

entries.title: FX tenor counts from the trade, if before cut-off
entries.text: FX tenor counts from the trade, if before cut-off Core An FX tenor such as Today, Tomorrow or Spot counts from the day the deal is traded, provided the trade happens before the FX cut-off time. Traded today before the cut-off, a Today tenor settles today, a Tomorrow tenor settles tomorrow, and Spot settles in two days or more. A trade after the cut-off settles a day later, because once the cut-off passes the bank is already working on the next day. A trade after the cut-off settles a day later, because once the cut-off passes the bank is already working on the next day.

entries.title: Treasury keeps the nostro funded, never moves money
entries.text: Treasury keeps the nostro funded, never moves money Core A treasury team moves no money itself; it watches balances on the correspondent accounts and buys or sells foreign exchange to hold enough funds for the day's payments. When it buys currency in the FX market, the funds land in the correspondent bank account in the foreign country, and the mirror account simply reflects that credit. The mirror does nothing on its own; it only records what happened on the real account. The mirror does nothing on its own; it only records what happened on the real account.

entries.title: Cover leg: same country means local clearing can settle it
entries.text: Cover leg: same country means local clearing can settle it Core In a cross-border payment the cover leg moves funds between the sender's correspondent and the receiver's correspondent, and where both correspondents sit in the same country a local clearing system can settle that leg. The payment message still travels over SWIFT, but the money itself moves locally. The local route costs less than moving the funds over the SWIFT network. The local route costs less than moving the funds over the SWIFT network.

entries.title: Euro leg in Europe: SEPA beats MT202 COV
entries.text: Euro leg in Europe: SEPA beats MT202 COV Core When a bank outside Europe instructs its correspondent in France to pay a customer of a German bank in euros, it need not use an MT202 COV. The correspondent can pay through SEPA or another local system instead, and in practice that local route is the one used most often. It also costs less than sending the funds over the SWIFT network. It also costs less than sending the funds over the SWIFT network.

entries.title: Withdrawing foreign cash the bank holds at home
entries.text: Withdrawing foreign cash the bank holds at home Core A customer holding a USD account with a bank in France can ask for the funds in physical USD cash, even though the real dollars sit with the bank's correspondent in the USA. The bank keeps an estimated stock of USD cash on hand, sized on customer demand, and sources it from customers selling USD for euros or from another bank. It hands over the cash and debits the same amount from the customer's USD account. It hands over the cash and debits the same amount from the customer's USD account.

entries.title: Documentary collections: banks intermediate, never promise
entries.text: Documentary collections: banks intermediate, never promise Core In a documentary collection the collecting bank and the remitting bank act only as intermediaries between the drawer and the drawee. Unlike a documentary credit, the collecting bank owes the drawer no payment even when the documents are in order. It releases the documents to the drawee when the drawee pays what is due, and the payment undertaking found under a letter of credit simply does not exist here. It releases the documents to the drawee when the drawee pays what is due, and the payment undertaking found under a letter of credit simply does not exist here.

entries.title: Card payments: the order money actually moves
entries.text: Card payments: the order money actually moves Core Paying by card moves money in an order that surprises many people. First the card is used to pay, then the issuer sends the statement, then the merchant is paid by the acquirer at settlement, and finally the cardholder pays the issuer. The acquirer settles with the merchant every day across all transactions, while the cardholder's payment to the issuer comes only after the statement arrives. The acquirer settles with the merchant every day across all transactions, while the cardholder's payment to the issuer comes only after the statement arrives.

entries.title: Card interest: timing decides the free credit window
entries.text: Card interest: timing decides the free credit window Core The interest-free credit period depends on where in the billing cycle the payment fell, and it can reach about 45 days for a payment made at the start of a cycle. When the cycle ends, the issuer sends the statement, and the cardholder then has a set period, usually about 21 days, to pay. Paying the full statement amount inside that window means no interest, while paying less leaves interest charged on the balance. Paying the full statement amount inside that window means no interest, while paying less leaves interest charged on the balance.

entries.title: Interchange: the acquirer's fee to the issuer
entries.text: Interchange: the acquirer's fee to the issuer Core Interchange is what the acquirer pays the issuer per card transaction, known too as the wholesale fee or interexchange fee. It is the issuer's transaction fee in clearing and settlement, typically running to 75 to 85 percent of the merchant service charges. The merchant bears this cost through the fees charged on the transaction, not the cardholder. The merchant bears this cost through the fees charged on the transaction, not the cardholder.

entries.title: Scheme fees: Mastercard per deal, Visa by membership
entries.text: Scheme fees: Mastercard per deal, Visa by membership Core The card schemes collect fees from merchants alongside the processor, and each scheme charges in its own way. The processing firm usually takes what it is owed straight from the merchant's account. Mastercard charges per transaction, while Visa charges yearly or quarterly memberships, so a merchant's scheme cost depends on which cards its customers use and how much volume goes through each scheme. Mastercard charges per transaction, while Visa charges yearly or quarterly memberships, so a merchant's scheme cost depends on which cards its customers use and how much volume goes through each scheme.

entries.title: Settlement method: who moves the funds
entries.text: Settlement method: who moves the funds Core In an ISO 20022 credit transfer the settlement method is the field that assigns settlement to one bank in the chain. INDA puts settlement on the instructed agent, so the next bank moves the funds, while INGA puts it on the instructing agent, so the sending bank moves the funds itself. Read the field first in any funding dispute, because it fixes which bank must hold the liquidity, which account is debited, and how both sides reconcile. Read the field first in any funding dispute, because it fixes which bank must hold the liquidity, which account is debited, and how both sides reconcile.

entries.title: UPI feels instant; settlement is not
entries.text: UPI feels instant; settlement is not Core UPI compresses the customer experience into seconds, debit seen at once, merchant receipt confirmed almost immediately, while the banks still settle with each other later under the scheme settlement cycle. Customer leg and interbank settlement are two separate events, and the bank funds the liquidity and reconciliation exposure between them. In any failure, separate the two events first and ask which one broke: the customer leg or the settlement leg. In any failure, separate the two events first and ask which one broke: the customer leg or the settlement leg.

entries.title: D-1 submission: four readiness checks
entries.text: D-1 submission: four readiness checks Core Bringing direct debit submission forward to D-1 is an operational commitment, not a diary change. Four things must support the earlier date, the scheme calendar, the file cut-off, the bank processing window and operational capacity, or collections fail at the first step. Verify all four before moving the date, because a date the infrastructure cannot meet turns into rejects, complaints and refunds. Verify all four before moving the date, because a date the infrastructure cannot meet turns into rejects, complaints and refunds.

entries.title: Bad intermediary data, rejected downstream
entries.text: Bad intermediary data, rejected downstream Core An instruction can name an intermediary that cannot serve the destination currency and holds no settlement relationship for that corridor, and the payment dies downstream. The failure is then unreadable: message mapping, routing reference data and routing logic all look equally guilty. Start from the agent chain data, validate every intermediary against the corridor, repair the reference data, and track repair rates so the bad intermediary is caught before its next payment. Start from the agent chain data, validate every intermediary against the corridor, repair the reference data, and track repair rates so the bad intermediary is caught before its next payment.

entries.title: Request to Pay: the date cannot be vague
entries.text: Request to Pay: the date cannot be vague Core Without a requested execution date a SEPA Request to Pay has no payment date, so one must be derived, chosen by the customer, or validated against a rule. Unless derivation, choice and validation are all defined, the same request settles on different dates in different systems. Execution then follows the agreed date, and a date that fails validation is rejected before it ever reaches the scheme. Execution then follows the agreed date, and a date that fails validation is rejected before it ever reaches the scheme.

entries.title: Control order is a risk decision
entries.text: Control order is a risk decision Core Running payment controls sequentially or in parallel is a risk decision, not a performance tweak: it changes latency, risk coverage and behaviour under load. Sequential controls are slower but easy to reason about, since each waits for its predecessor, while parallel controls are faster but demand explicit rules for one control failing while another passes. Map control dependencies first, because a control that assumes a predecessor has run will pass bad payments the moment the order changes. Map control dependencies first, because a control that assumes a predecessor has run will pass bad payments the moment the order changes.

entries.title: The purpose code gap that breaks payments
entries.text: The purpose code gap that breaks payments Core A purpose code that is optional at the customer and mandatory downstream is a defect waiting for a payment. Name the downstream system that needs it, give enrichment a named owning source, and validate early enough to catch a missing code before the payment reaches that system. And define the repair behaviour up front, who fixes it, how fast, and what happens to the payment while it waits. And define the repair behaviour up front, who fixes it, how fast, and what happens to the payment while it waits.

entries.title: When Intermediary Agent 2 data goes stale
entries.text: When Intermediary Agent 2 data goes stale Core Reference data without an owner decays, and Intermediary Agent 2 is the proof: nobody maintains it, so it quietly points payments at a bank that no longer serves the corridor. The control set is fourfold, a named owner, a validation rule, an update process, and a routing control that stops a payment whose intermediary data is out of date. Leave any of the four out and the same bad intermediary keeps reappearing until a rejection or a repair exposes it. Leave any of the four out and the same bad intermediary keeps reappearing until a rejection or a repair exposes it.

entries.title: A mandate is a lifecycle, not a record
entries.text: A mandate is a lifecycle, not a record Core Think of a mandate as a lifecycle, created, amended when a customer changes bank accounts, and cancelled, with a reference and evidence at every step. Scatter that evidence, a paper scan in a shared drive, an online consent in another system, an amendment as a free-text note, and a collection rejected for a missing or invalid mandate becomes unexplainable. Give billing one view of each mandate, its current state and the evidence that proves it. Give billing one view of each mandate, its current state and the evidence that proves it.

entries.title: The mandate reference never changes
entries.text: The mandate reference never changes Core A mandate reference is generated once and stays with the mandate from creation through amendments to cancellation. Every amendment and cancellation is recorded against it with an audit history, so any collection traces back to the mandate that authorised it. Reuse it, change it or lose it and the mandate cannot be proven, and its collections cannot be defended. Reuse it, change it or lose it and the mandate cannot be proven, and its collections cannot be defended.

entries.title: A collection file is a scheme submission
entries.text: A collection file is a scheme submission Core Treat a collection file as a regulated scheme submission, not a spreadsheet job: the same errors return every month, a cancelled customer still collected, an amount changed after the file was built, a file submitted after the scheme deadline. The discipline is the sequence, build from current mandate and billing data, validate, win creditor PSP acceptance, submit inside the scheme window. Skip a step and the cost arrives as refunds, complaints and rework. Skip a step and the cost arrives as refunds, complaints and rework.

entries.title: After submission, deletion stops working
entries.text: After submission, deletion stops working Core Once a file is with the creditor PSP, cancelling a collection is a scheme process, not a delete key. Cancellation follows the process for the collection state at that moment, and a collection already in processing can only be stopped on the defined cancellation path. Billing must know the exact lifecycle point where deletion stops working and cancellation takes over, because that point decides whether the customer is debited. Billing must know the exact lifecycle point where deletion stops working and cancellation takes over, because that point decides whether the customer is debited.

entries.title: Same word, different mechanism
entries.text: Same word, different mechanism Core Cancellation and revocation are different mechanisms that happen to sound alike: different parties start them, at different times, for collections in different states. A member cancelling a membership expects no further collection, a billing clerk revoking a collection expects it never to leave the building, and a creditor PSP receiving a cancellation request expects a scheme message with a response. Choose by collection state, because the wrong mechanism debits the member anyway or gets the request rejected by the bank. Choose by collection state, because the wrong mechanism debits the member anyway or gets the request rejected by the bank.

entries.title: Settled money is reversed, never erased
entries.text: Settled money is reversed, never erased Core A reversal is its own transaction, not a deletion and not a debtor refund claim: a separate, linked entry returning money already settled, used when a duplicate collection can no longer be cancelled or revoked because the money has moved. It carries the original references, is initiated by the creditor, and posts as its own accounting entry so reconciliation pairs it with the original instead of finding a hole. Deleting settled entries breaks reconciliation, so the duplicate is reversed, never erased. Deleting settled entries breaks reconciliation, so the duplicate is reversed, never erased.

entries.title: Core and B2B: the risk points differ
entries.text: Core and B2B: the risk points differ Core Core and B2B differ exactly where risk is decided: who may use them, what refund rights the debtor holds, and what the debtor bank must verify before the first collection. A business collected under Core holds a refund right the creditor may not expect, while under B2B there is no such right but the mandate must be verified first. Running one process for both hides those differences, so record the scheme on each mandate and follow that scheme's current rulebook. Running one process for both hides those differences, so record the scheme on each mandate and follow that scheme's current rulebook.

entries.title: One transfer, three stacked charges
entries.text: One transfer, three stacked charges Core Take the cited example, a 140 euro transfer carrying an 11.39 percent fee, and the corridor cost structure becomes visible: the fee is not one charge but transfer fee plus exchange margin plus intermediary charges along the route. Splitting the total into components is what lets a customer compare corridors and an analyst say which part is avoidable. These figures describe that cited example only, not every transfer on the corridor, so present them as one case, never as the corridor rate. These figures describe that cited example only, not every transfer on the corridor, so present them as one case, never as the corridor rate.

entries.title: RJCT before settlement: repair, do not return
entries.text: RJCT before settlement: repair, do not return Core An RJCT on a pacs.002 is a pre-settlement verdict: the status report says the instruction failed, and no money has moved. The reason code names the failure precisely, technical, such as a schema or format error, or business, such as a sanctions flag, and each kind has its own owner. The remedy is repair at source and resubmission as a new instruction, new message ID, same UETR, so tracking stays continuous. The remedy is repair at source and resubmission as a new instruction, new message ID, same UETR, so tracking stays continuous.

entries.title: After settlement, only a return moves money
entries.text: After settlement, only a return moves money Core Settlement closes the pacs.002 path for good: a status report never moves money, so a settled payment cannot be fixed by reporting. The funds must come back through a pacs.004, a real settlement instruction in reverse, travelling the return chain through every bank the original passed. Return charges may come off along the way, so the amount returning can differ from the amount sent, and the UETR ties both legs together for reconciliation. Return charges may come off along the way, so the amount returning can differ from the amount sent, and the UETR ties both legs together for reconciliation.

entries.title: Beneficiary bank sends the money back itself
entries.text: Beneficiary bank sends the money back itself Core A beneficiary bank that credits an account and then finds it closed or frozen does not wait to be asked. It becomes the return originator and sends the pacs.004 back along the chain in reverse. Charges may be deducted at hops, so the sender recovers the original minus charges, and the return is matched to the original payment by UETR. Charges may be deducted at hops, so the sender recovers the original minus charges, and the return is matched to the original payment by UETR.

entries.title: Uncertain party details: ask, do not kill
entries.text: Uncertain party details: ask, do not kill Core Ultimate debtor or creditor details that look wrong but are not proven wrong call for a question, not a rejection, because rejecting outright can kill a legitimate payment. Park the payment under a clear status, request the additional information back up the chain, and give the sender a bounded window to answer. Clean facts release it, confirmed problems mean rejection or return depending on settlement state, and a missed deadline falls back to the policy default. Clean facts release it, confirmed problems mean rejection or return depending on settlement state, and a missed deadline falls back to the policy default.

entries.title: A timeout is an unknown, not a failure
entries.text: A timeout is an unknown, not a failure Core A timeout reports nothing about the outcome, and a blind retry on an unknown can double-pay. Freeze the payment, then work the evidence, UETR, EndToEndId and TxId across the tracker and hop logs, late responses, and statements against camt.054 notifications. Act only on the true state found: resubmit if it truly failed, recall or claim if it settled incorrectly. Act only on the true state found: resubmit if it truly failed, recall or claim if it settled incorrectly.

entries.title: Cover: instruction one way, money another
entries.text: Cover: instruction one way, money another Core The cover method splits the payment in two: the pacs.008 carries customer details to the beneficiary bank, while the pacs.009 with settlement method COVE moves the funds through correspondents, the pair linked by one UETR. A sanctions hold on either leg stops the whole payment, because the beneficiary bank may credit the customer only when both legs reconcile. A cover that arrives alone parks as an unmatched item until its instruction completes the pair. A cover that arrives alone parks as an unmatched item until its instruction completes the pair.

entries.title: India to USA: trace the failed payment
entries.text: India to USA: trace the failed payment Core Cross-border tracing works leg by leg, never as one rail: a SWIFT pacs.008 moves across correspondents, then Fedwire completes final US dollar settlement. Start from the UETR in the tracker, locate the last successful hop, and read the status message there, because its reason code names the failure. Then test the corridor suspects, a missing purpose code, a sanctions hold, an invalid routing number, or an FX or cut-off gap, and close the case with the right message, a pacs.004 return or a camt.056 recall. Then test the corridor suspects, a missing purpose code, a sanctions hold, an invalid routing number, or an FX or cut-off gap, and close the case with the right message, a pacs.004 return or a camt.056 recall.

entries.title: Timeout: pull the recall brake
entries.text: Timeout: pull the recall brake Core A payment timed out mid-chain with its true state unknown is exactly when a recall earns its name as an emergency brake: send the request down the chain and stop it before it completes. The brake has one limit, it cannot undo a completed credit. Where the credit already completed, switch to the return flow via pacs.004, and update the customer at each step, because silence turns incidents into escalations. Where the credit already completed, switch to the return flow via pacs.004, and update the customer at each step, because silence turns incidents into escalations.

entries.title: A return is a payment in reverse
entries.text: A return is a payment in reverse Core Treat a pacs.004 as what it is, a real payment in reverse: settled funds moving backward through the same chain, carrying its own charges and its own references. It applies when the beneficiary bank finds a closed or frozen account, a duplicate payment, or a wrong beneficiary after settlement. Its return chain element preserves the original chain so every intermediary knows its place, and returns deserve the same operational controls as outward payments. Its return chain element preserves the original chain so every intermediary knows its place, and returns deserve the same operational controls as outward payments.

entries.title: Spot the at-risk payment before the call
entries.text: Spot the at-risk payment before the call Core At-risk has a precise meaning: no status update within the expected window for that corridor and amount, drawn from the tracker, pacs.002 statuses and internal hop timestamps. Every flagged payment needs a named owner, operations, the relationship manager, or investigations, and action before the deadline, reroute, chase the intermediary, or warn the customer early. A dashboard of unowned flags is decoration; a flag works only with an owner and a next action. A dashboard of unowned flags is decoration; a flag works only with an owner and a next action.

entries.title: Investigations run on rails, not instinct
entries.text: Investigations run on rails, not instinct Core A payment investigation is a fixed sequence: intake and triage, identify the payment, verify the true status, check compliance, contact the correspondent, and resolve. Give every case type an SLA and an escalation matrix, because investigations without deadlines become backlogs. And contact the correspondent with structured queries and full references, never free-text emails that go nowhere. And contact the correspondent with structured queries and full references, never free-text emails that go nowhere.

entries.title: Small breaks, one $2M surprise
entries.text: Small breaks, one $2M surprise Core Small uncleared items accumulated for months, looking harmless, until rising volumes exposed a 2 million dollar discrepancy just before an audit. The cause was timing: two systems derived the transaction value date with different logic. Aligning that logic cleared 80 percent of breaks automatically, which is the lesson to keep: fix the process that creates the break, never optimise the manual workaround, and run reconciliation as an early-warning system. Aligning that logic cleared 80 percent of breaks automatically, which is the lesson to keep: fix the process that creates the break, never optimise the manual workaround, and run reconciliation as an early-warning system.

entries.title: A surname parked a 28M dirham LC
entries.text: A surname parked a 28M dirham LC Core Sanctions screening is a false-positive business: about 95 percent of alerts are false positives, yet each one delays real business, and a fuzzy match on a common surname parked a legitimate 28 million dirham letter of credit for 8 working days. The answer is risk triage, exact matches and high-risk corridors first, with matching thresholds tuned per corridor and name frequency instead of one global setting. Judge the screening flow on its KPIs, the false-positive rate and the average hold time, and measure and report both. Judge the screening flow on its KPIs, the false-positive rate and the average hold time, and measure and report both.

entries.title: SDN block holds $500K; SAR filed
entries.text: SDN block holds $500K; SAR filed Core A sanctions list match stops the payment at once: it is held immediately and no funds move while the review is open. The analyst escalates to the compliance officer with the match evidence attached, and true-match verification decides the path, release if false, block if true. Where the activity meets the threshold a Suspicious Activity Report is filed, and every step is documented, because the decision trail is what regulators will ask for. Where the activity meets the threshold a Suspicious Activity Report is filed, and every step is documented, because the decision trail is what regulators will ask for.

entries.title: APP fraud: $85K lost, ruled authorised
entries.text: APP fraud: $85K lost, ruled authorised Core Authorised push payment fraud exploits the gap between a valid payment and a deceived customer. A scammer posing as a bank representative won remote access to the victim computer, and the wire left from the victim's own login and device, so the bank classified it as authorised and refused reimbursement. The defences are confirmation of payee, friction on first-time payees, warnings at the point of payment, and behavioural detection, and the regulatory trend is shifting liability back toward banks. The defences are confirmation of payee, friction on first-time payees, warnings at the point of payment, and behavioural detection, and the regulatory trend is shifting liability back toward banks.

entries.title: Chase the cause upstream, not the symptom
entries.text: Chase the cause upstream, not the symptom Core Start from the symptom and walk upstream, because the most visible error is rarely the root cause and a payment timeout is often a downstream effect of something earlier. Trace the full end-to-end lifecycle from where the message was created, hop by hop with timestamps and message copies. Here the culprit was a small deviation from payment message standards, which compounds downstream, so validate messages against the standard at every boundary, not just at entry. Here the culprit was a small deviation from payment message standards, which compounds downstream, so validate messages against the standard at every boundary, not just at entry.

entries.title: The parameter everyone assumed was filled
entries.text: The parameter everyone assumed was filled Core One unchecked assumption can survive QA, staging and a small rollout, then fail at full volume: a parameter assumed to always return a value sometimes came back empty. Partner API calls failed, reconciliation mismatched, and rebuilding partner trust took longer than the three-hour fix. Validate every input, above all the ones assumed always present, and add contract tests with the partner covering empty and null variants of every field. Validate every input, above all the ones assumed always present, and add contract tests with the partner covering empty and null variants of every field.

entries.title: Mule accounts: read the network, not the case
entries.text: Mule accounts: read the network, not the case Core A mule network is a pattern, not an account: small inward transfers from unrelated sources, funds moved out within minutes of credit, minimal balance retention, and common device or IP linkage. One account is a case, linked accounts are a network, so freeze suspect accounts on debit first, then run EDD and KYC reviews and escalate to investigations. Recalibrate detection rules so the pattern is caught earlier next time, without punishing genuine customers. Recalibrate detection rules so the pattern is caught earlier next time, without punishing genuine customers.

entries.title: 250,000 euros held on a name mismatch
entries.text: 250,000 euros held on a name mismatch Core A 250,000 euro payment sat uncredited for three days because the beneficiary bank flagged a name mismatch. A pacs.002 showing Pending means the beneficiary bank is holding the payment, not rejecting it, so open with an investigation query for the exact mismatch detail. Correct and verify the name and the bank applies the funds; if it cannot be resolved the payment returns via pacs.004, so validate beneficiary details at initiation, including confirmation of payee where the corridor supports it. Correct and verify the name and the bank applies the funds; if it cannot be resolved the payment returns via pacs.004, so validate beneficiary details at initiation, including confirmation of payee where the corridor supports it.

entries.title: The cut-off moved; nobody told the fintech
entries.text: The cut-off moved; nobody told the fintech Core Code can be perfect and dashboards green while transactions fail, because the bank moved its transaction cut-off time and the fintech kept sending on the old settlement window. Requests were accepted, then processed in a later cycle, breaking user expectations without a single error. Most production incidents in finance are coordination failures of this kind, cut-off changes, holiday calendars, or report timings that moved without notice, so keep cut-off and calendar configuration synced with every bank partner. Most production incidents in finance are coordination failures of this kind, cut-off changes, holiday calendars, or report timings that moved without notice, so keep cut-off and calendar configuration synced with every bank partner.

entries.title: Five ways the SDD timeline can break
entries.text: Five ways the SDD timeline can break Core On a normal due date the due date, settlement date and debit date are the same, but the timeline breaks when calendars do not align. Five scenarios test it for a single due date: the creditor PSP closed, TARGET or the CSM closed, the debtor PSP closed, both PSPs closed, and a new national holiday declared after planning. In each case the BA must ask which parties are open, what activity needs to happen and which calendar applies, rather than assuming which date moves, because a good SDD timeline is designed for the broken assumptions, not only for the happy flow. In each case the BA must ask which parties are open, what activity needs to happen and which calendar applies, rather than assuming which date moves, because a good SDD timeline is designed for the broken assumptions, not only for the happy flow.

entries.title: Stop a mistaken collection by its lifecycle stage
entries.text: Stop a mistaken collection by its lifecycle stage Core When a creditor realises a collection was made by mistake, the right mechanism depends on where the collection sits in its lifecycle. While it is warehoused with the creditor PSP and has not entered the inter-PSP flow, the creditor revokes it, and once it is in the clearing flow but before settlement, the creditor requests cancellation through the PSP or CSM process. After clearing and settlement, only a reversal can reimburse the debtor for the erroneous collection, and one generic cancel requirement cannot cover all three because the stage, initiator, mechanism and responsibilities differ, with refund the remaining step after settlement. After clearing and settlement, only a reversal can reimburse the debtor for the erroneous collection, and one generic cancel requirement cannot cover all three because the stage, initiator, mechanism and responsibilities differ, with refund the remaining step after settlement.

entries.title: SDD retry: D+5 is a window, not a penalty
entries.text: SDD retry: D+5 is a window, not a penalty Core When a direct debit fails for insufficient funds, retries are confined to the D+5 window of inter-PSP business days, and D+5 is a window, not a penalty or a fine. A scheduler that retries in first-in-first-out order can keep failing, because retry logic is also seasonal: salary credits land on specific dates, and salary accounts hold a balance on those dates. The better requirement checks the balance daily and collects when the account can fund the debit, rather than assuming the scheduler is the optimum solution. Who owns a retry failure, the BA, the developer or the product owner, is a stakeholder agreement, not a technical fact. Who owns a retry failure, the BA, the developer or the product owner, is a stakeholder agreement, not a technical fact.

entries.title: SDD resubmission: define the timing rule first
entries.text: SDD resubmission: define the timing rule first Core When a collection is rejected, the originator can resubmit it only once the resubmission timing rule is clear, so before asking for the rule, the BA should ask what the rule must answer: how it aligns the original timing so the resubmission improves on the original outcome. The method compares the clean-state timeline of a complete collection with the rejection reason and the proposed resubmission timeline, and tests if the earliest resubmission point is tied to the original collection date. Once the rule is clear it goes into the backlog so the feature can be built quickly, and the BA should first see how the business operation works in practice, face to face. Once the rule is clear it goes into the backlog so the feature can be built quickly, and the BA should first see how the business operation works in practice, face to face.

entries.title: Read the reason code, then investigate the failure
entries.text: Read the reason code, then investigate the failure Core A pacs.004 return tells a bank that a payment was returned, but on its own it does not say why it failed, while the pacs.002 carries the return reason code, and only when the two are reconciled does the bank know whether to flag, retry, investigate, replace or reject the payment. Gap analysis compares the instruction against its structure, the investigation against its evidence, the business rules against their procedure, and the return reason against its expected outcome. It measures the delta between the process the bank has and the process it needs, because a faulty gap analysis steers the technical team toward the wrong process. It measures the delta between the process the bank has and the process it needs, because a faulty gap analysis steers the technical team toward the wrong process.

entries.title: Reject or repair: decide from the business context
entries.text: Reject or repair: decide from the business context Core A payment rejected for a format fault is not always a rejection, because the right response depends on where the fault sits, whether the original instruction is intact, who owns the defect, and whether the agreement permits a correction. When the bank's own pacs.008 is wrong, fix the mapping and repair and resubmit after status and duplicate checks, and when the customer pain.001 is wrong and the agreement allows correction, repair within the agreement and keep the audit trail, while a customer pain.001 fault with no agreement gets a rejection with a clear reason. A format fault is a diagnosis to make first, not a verdict, and the business context decides whether the payment is repaired or rejected. A format fault is a diagnosis to make first, not a verdict, and the business context decides whether the payment is repaired or rejected.

entries.title: Instant cross-border: speed is only one piece
entries.text: Instant cross-border: speed is only one piece Core Instant cross-border payments are not only about speed, because several pieces must work together for the whole journey to be efficient. Clearing, processing and settlement must become more efficient, FX conversion must be transparent to the customer, and payment status must be traceable, while richer remittance information supports AML and fraud checks, and common messaging standards and APIs make systems interoperable. When these pieces combine, transaction time and end-user costs fall, which is the real transformation. When these pieces combine, transaction time and end-user costs fall, which is the real transformation.

entries.title: TARGET calendar governs the interbank SDD leg
entries.text: TARGET calendar governs the interbank SDD leg Core SDD counting runs on Inter-PSP Business Days, defined as TARGET Business Days, so a national holiday elsewhere leaves the TARGET schedule and the collection validity untouched. TARGET drives Due Date, D-1 and settlement for the interbank journey, while each PSP applies its own Business Day calendar only to customer-facing service. Treating a national holiday calendar as the SDD Business Day calendar is the classic error, and the TARGET calendar is the one that controls the interbank leg. Treating a national holiday calendar as the SDD Business Day calendar is the classic error, and the TARGET calendar is the one that controls the interbank leg.

entries.title: SDD presentation window runs D-14 to D-1
entries.text: SDD presentation window runs D-14 to D-1 Core D-14 marks the earliest Inter-PSP Business Day for presenting a collection to the Inter-PSP Space, and it doubles as the pre-notification date, by which the debtor must be told about the collection at least 14 calendar days ahead of the Due Date. Receipt by the debtor PSP through the CSM must fall inside that span, with D-1 as the latest permitted day, and for a 15 October Due Date the window is 1 October to 14 October, while the debtor pre-notification in the example went out on 15 September. Confusing D-14 with a submission deadline misreads the rule, since D-14 opens the window and D-1 closes it. Confusing D-14 with a submission deadline misreads the rule, since D-14 opens the window and D-1 closes it.

entries.title: Untraced payments turn queries into investigations
entries.text: Untraced payments turn queries into investigations Core A processed cross-border payment can still show no credit by mid-morning because it may have failed silently, queued, stalled on missing details, or stopped for compliance checks, and without a live trace one customer query becomes hours of back-and-forth, reconciliation and investigation. Visibility comes from three elements working together: the UETR, ISO 20022 structured data, and connected systems and processes. A payment without a trace leaves a customer question unanswered, while a tracked payment reconciles faster, clears exceptions sooner, and avoids duplication, failed credits and manual rework. A payment without a trace leaves a customer question unanswered, while a tracked payment reconciles faster, clears exceptions sooner, and avoids duplication, failed credits and manual rework.

entries.title: Failed instant payments: find the outcome first
entries.text: Failed instant payments: find the outcome first Core When an instant payment fails, the debit can land immediately while the beneficiary receives nothing, so the first task is to establish the cause: a timeout, an account issue, a technical problem, a compliance issue, or insufficient funds. Failed payments split into two kinds: genuinely rejected ones, where the money returns to the payer, and stuck ones, which need investigation, sometimes with the receiving bank helping to return the money. The same payment can even end differently in different countries, so the operative question is not only whether money left, but what the outcome is and where the money now sits. The same payment can even end differently in different countries, so the operative question is not only whether money left, but what the outcome is and where the money now sits.

entries.title: Compliance must run at instant payment speed
entries.text: Compliance must run at instant payment speed Core A payment reaching the beneficiary in 10 seconds still needs AML, sanctions and fraud controls, because instant means compliance must work at payment speed, not that controls disappear. The difficulty is that screening for AML, sanctions and fraud often runs longer than the instant window allows, yet newer technology is making screens smarter and automated, with same-day handling and, in some cases, real-time checks. Once the check sits inside the journey instead of blocking it, instant payments become instant, intelligent and compliant. Once the check sits inside the journey instead of blocking it, instant payments become instant, intelligent and compliant.

entries.title: Interoperability demands more than connectivity
entries.text: Interoperability demands more than connectivity Core Interoperability goes beyond connecting two systems with an API, because messaging, processing rules, clearing, settlement, compliance and day-to-day operations must also line up. A payment bridge joins two payment ecosystems in business and technical terms, where each side may run its own instant rail, currency and rules, and the bridge works as shared standards, scheme rules and cooperation between systems dictate. ISO 20022 supplies the common language, UETR supplies traceability, OCT Inst supplies rules for the Euro leg, and together they move interoperable instant payments across borders closer. ISO 20022 supplies the common language, UETR supplies traceability, OCT Inst supplies rules for the Euro leg, and together they move interoperable instant payments across borders closer.

entries.title: UETR: one reference for the whole payment journey
entries.text: UETR: one reference for the whole payment journey Core The UETR, the Unique End-to-End Transaction Reference, is a 36-character RFC 4122 identifier issued by the initiating bank and unchanged from originator to beneficiary. It lets a bank follow the journey from end to end, pinpoint where the payment sits at any moment, and carry the relevant details forward along the way, while also helping banks manage liquidity, exceptions and reconciliation. When the beneficiary thinks the money has not arrived, the UETR lets them claim, trace and prove the payment, which is why a payment lacking a UETR travels with no track at all. When the beneficiary thinks the money has not arrived, the UETR lets them claim, trace and prove the payment, which is why a payment lacking a UETR travels with no track at all.

entries.title: OCT Inst and the non-euro leg in 60 seconds
entries.text: OCT Inst and the non-euro leg in 60 seconds Core OCT Inst is already live and processes cross-border payments in 60 seconds, handling both the payment and the settlement, with both legs settled through the Euro system. The non-euro leg runs wholly outside the Euro area, governed by non-euro rules, standards and bank policies, with conversion completed before the beneficiary is paid, so the beneficiary receives exactly the amount expected. Speed is not the test here, reliability and rule-following are. Speed is not the test here, reliability and rule-following are.

entries.title: One-Leg Out: OCT Inst clears in 10 seconds
entries.text: One-Leg Out: OCT Inst clears in 10 seconds Core One-Leg Out means a payment starts in Europe and goes outside it, with a euro leg plus a leg outside the euro area, and the One-Leg Out Instant Credit Transfer, OCT Inst, clears such cross-border payments in 10 seconds. As part of SEPA, OCT Inst follows the SEPA rule set, and clears and settles through the Euro leg, while payments can be made around the clock, every day of the year. Speed is not the point, an efficient, consistent and compliant process is. Speed is not the point, an efficient, consistent and compliant process is.

entries.title: Two rules collide after the SCT Inst limit is removed
entries.text: Two rules collide after the SCT Inst limit is removed Core When the EU Instant Payments Regulation removed the EUR 100K scheme-level maximum for SCT Inst, the old routing rule that sent payments above EUR 100K to TARGET2 lost the scheme limit it was built on. A bank can now set its own customer limits, so Customer A with a EUR 300K limit can send EUR 200K instantly while the unchanged routing rule still sends anything above EUR 100K to TARGET2, which means two live rules produce different outcomes for the same payment. The BA must surface the conflict, trace why each rule exists, and take the choice to the Product Owner or Business Owner, because only the business can decide which outcome it wants once the scheme constraint is gone. The BA must surface the conflict, trace why each rule exists, and take the choice to the Product Owner or Business Owner, because only the business can decide which outcome it wants once the scheme constraint is gone.

entries.title: Performance requirements start from business demand
entries.text: Performance requirements start from business demand Core Monthly volume describes scale, but peak behaviour describes performance demand, so a BA who only records today's volumes has not defined what the platform must support. With payment traffic peaking between 7 AM and 10 AM and five clients in the pipeline who could add 10 million transactions a month, the BA must establish when they onboard, how certain the forecast is, what their peaks look like, whether they create new bursts, and whether the workload itself changes with more validations, API calls, real-time processing, and concurrency. The answer is a six-part view of current demand, peak behaviour, future demand, planning horizon, workload characteristics, and measurable requirements that cover response time, processing conditions, volume, and peak TPS, because a platform that performs today can still fail tomorrow if growth was never considered. The answer is a six-part view of current demand, peak behaviour, future demand,

entries.title: Repair at scale needs a threshold, not a habit
entries.text: Repair at scale needs a threshold, not a habit Core Sending failed transactions to a repair queue works when only a few fail, but when 90 percent of a remittance file needs repair, Operations cannot manage the volume and the customer cannot reconcile what was processed, what was not, and what must be corrected. The working rule is size-based: files with fewer than 20 transactions carry no threshold and send problem items to repair while valid items continue, while files with 20 or more apply a 5 percent threshold, so up to 5 percent repair goes to repair and anything above it rejects the whole file for correction and resubmission. No transaction is released before the threshold is checked, because releasing some items first and then discovering the whole file should have been rejected leaves a partially processed file that cannot be undone cleanly. No transaction is released before the threshold is checked, because releasing some items first and then discovering the whole file should

entries.title: A holiday calendar is an end-to-end operating decision
entries.text: A holiday calendar is an end-to-end operating decision Core A payment engine can be open while the rest of the payment journey is not, so asking whether the engine is open is the wrong question when the USA is open, France is closed, and a French bank holds the account receiving an international USD payment. Core banking and account booking, compliance controls, customer reporting, and the nostro funding feed must remain available, because a credit that never appears in intraday reporting leaves a cash management customer acting on an incomplete cash position. Internal reporting, regulatory reporting, and the nostro reconciliation feed may be able to wait under agreed controls, but the BA must not decide that alone: the Reporting Product Manager defines reporting criticality and Operations defines the reconciliation catch-up. Internal reporting, regulatory reporting, and the nostro reconciliation feed may be able to wait under agreed controls, but the BA must not decide that alone:

entries.title: Trace the chain before blaming the payment engine
entries.text: Trace the chain before blaming the payment engine Core A payment routed to the wrong intermediary bank looks like a payment engine fault until the BA traces the full routing chain from instruction through routing decision, settlement directory, Swift reference data, intermediary selection, and routing. The fault may sit in an incorrectly updated settlement directory or in Swift reference data for a correspondent bank that was never updated, which means a correct routing rule can still produce the wrong intermediary from bad data. The investigation must establish what was expected, what actually happened, where the two diverged, which component decided, and what data it used, then move from symptom to investigation to root cause to corrective action instead of asking each team in turn whether it is their problem. The investigation must establish what was expected, what actually happened, where the two diverged, which component decided, and what data it used, then move from symptom to

entries.title: Intermediary Agent 2: optional, until it is not
entries.text: Intermediary Agent 2: optional, until it is not Core In a pacs.008 cover payment, Intermediary Agent 2 is optional in the message definition, shown as 0..1, so a reader can conclude it can always be left out. But the beneficiary bank may need the intermediary chain to understand the expected cover path, and without it the payment can be held for cover information, sent to investigation, or rejected. Message cardinality answers a design question, so the working test is not whether the field is mandatory but whether the business scenario needs it, who consumes it, and what happens if it is missing. Message cardinality answers a design question, so the working test is not whether the field is mandatory but whether the business scenario needs it, who consumes it, and what happens if it is missing.

entries.title: Blockchain networks: keys, ledger and controls
entries.text: Blockchain networks: keys, ledger and controls Core Every node in the network is a validated participant holding cryptographic keys, so encryption and mutual awareness work much as they do under bilateral key exchange. Settlement rests on a distributed ledger maintained by each participant and refreshed with every transaction, with accounting posted to participant accounts held inside that ledger, and a network under CSM control leaves settlement to the CSM. Compliance remains a live discussion, yet sanctions and similar controls are expected to operate alongside near real time processing without slowing it. Compliance remains a live discussion, yet sanctions and similar controls are expected to operate alongside near real time processing without slowing it.

entries.title: Multilateral clearing dominates, bilateral stays rare
entries.text: Multilateral clearing dominates, bilateral stays rare Core Multilateral clearing dominates because netting collapses many payments into a few positions and saves a huge number of transactions. Bilateral clearing stays rare, gaining appeal only where the banks involved are very large. Banks also favour a single connection to the clearing and settlement mechanism to reach every other bank, and the mechanism manages credit risk for all participants. Banks also favour a single connection to the clearing and settlement mechanism to reach every other bank, and the mechanism manages credit risk for all participants.

entries.title: Settlement flows through the CSM central bank account
entries.text: Settlement flows through the CSM central bank account Core The mechanism is a company, not a bank, and it settles through an account it holds with the central bank. Banks ending in a net debit position transfer funds into that account. The mechanism then credits the accounts of banks in net credit positions, so settlement flows through central bank money with the CSM in the middle. The mechanism then credits the accounts of banks in net credit positions, so settlement flows through central bank money with the CSM in the middle.

entries.title: How the CSM tracks flows and computes positions
entries.text: How the CSM tracks flows and computes positions Core The mechanism sees every flow in both directions, receiving transactions from all banks to each bank and from each bank to all the others, so it can track how many each bank sent and received. A cut-off fixes the time limit after which no further transactions enter that cycle, and netting then starts on what is available. Amounts carried in the messages let the mechanism compute each participant position. Amounts carried in the messages let the mechanism compute each participant position.

entries.title: How short positions are checked before settlement
entries.text: How short positions are checked before settlement Core Risk control rests on procedures that keep participants funded on the account used for settlement. The mechanism also reviews short participants at intervals to confirm they can meet their obligations. The final check still falls immediately before settlement, so a bank unable to cover its short position is caught before settlement completes. The final check still falls immediately before settlement, so a bank unable to cover its short position is caught before settlement completes.

entries.title: Direct participants carry indirect participant risk
entries.text: Direct participants carry indirect participant risk Core Accountability for risk arising from indirect participants sits with the direct participant. In practice the indirect participant funds an account held with the direct participant, and before the direct participant sends a debit on its behalf it draws the money from that account, rejecting the transaction when funds are insufficient. For a credit the direct participant credits the indirect participant account and forwards the transaction. For a credit the direct participant credits the indirect participant account and forwards the transaction.

entries.title: Validating a SWIFT MX message with the MDR
entries.text: Validating a SWIFT MX message with the MDR Core Validation of a SWIFT MX message follows the ISO 20022 standard. The authoritative place to read how a given message is validated is its Message Definition Report, which sets out the message content and its validation rules. Those reports are free to download from the ISO 20022 website. Those reports are free to download from the ISO 20022 website.

entries.title: Beneficiary credit deadline after pacs.008
entries.text: Beneficiary credit deadline after pacs.008 Core Once pacs.008 arrives, the creditor agent must put the funds at the beneficiary disposal on the settlement day. The Payment Services Directive leaves the beneficiary bank no float, so the credit cannot slip past that day. The settlement day itself is therefore the maximum window. The settlement day itself is therefore the maximum window.

entries.title: MT101 also starts domestic corporate payments
entries.text: MT101 also starts domestic corporate payments Core Corporates initiate domestic payments with MT101 just as they initiate cross-border ones, covering real time gross settlement, electronic funds transfer, automated clearing house and cheque payments. The commercial logic is that the corporate enterprise resource planning system generates one standard format to initiate all payables. A single MT101 format therefore starts every kind of payment a corporate makes. A single MT101 format therefore starts every kind of payment a corporate makes.

entries.title: Concentrating bank forwards the same MT101
entries.text: Concentrating bank forwards the same MT101 Core In the concentration cases the bank forwards the MT101 it received instead of originating a new one. It pulls out the MT101 due to each destination bank and processes its own instruction, the one where it stands as debtor bank. The same instruction therefore travels onward, split per destination where needed. The same instruction therefore travels onward, split per destination where needed.

entries.title: Can MT101 carry a SEPA payment?
entries.text: Can MT101 carry a SEPA payment? Core A SEPA payment can travel on an MT101, but the message cannot hold all the information a pain.001 can carry. Whether a bank processes MT101 as a SEPA payment turns entirely on that bank's own capabilities, so not every bank will do it. Where the information fits, MT101 works for SEPA; where it does not, pain.001 is the right message. Where the information fits, MT101 works for SEPA; where it does not, pain.001 is the right message.

entries.title: Account servicing institution: debit then MT103
entries.text: Account servicing institution: debit then MT103 Core The account servicing institution is the bank holding the account to be debited. On receiving the MT101 it processes the instruction against that account. It then issues an MT103 to move the funds onward, so the MT101 instructs the debit and the MT103 carries the money. It then issues an MT103 to move the funds onward, so the MT101 instructs the debit and the MT103 carries the money.

entries.title: Creditor bank need not check the mandate
entries.text: Creditor bank need not check the mandate Core SEPA applies the creditor driven mandate flow, so the creditor bank carries no obligation to check a pacs.003 against an active mandate. The creditor bank may still validate if it chooses, but the scheme does not require it. That contrasts with a debtor driven flow, where the debtor side holds the mandate. That contrasts with a debtor driven flow, where the debtor side holds the mandate.

entries.title: Open loop versus closed loop: who runs each
entries.text: Open loop versus closed loop: who runs each Core Open loop systems are run by financial service providers regulated within the national payment system environment. Closed loop systems are usually run by non-financial service providers, and the payment is used for goods or services. A clothing store voucher for a pair of shoes worth R1000 shows the closed loop pattern. A clothing store voucher for a pair of shoes worth R1000 shows the closed loop pattern.

entries.title: Can a private individual pay by promissory note?
entries.text: Can a private individual pay by promissory note? Core In some countries, such as France, only businesses can issue promissory notes, so a private individual cannot use one to pay. Elsewhere the law may permit private individuals to issue them, yet banks stay silent about them and steer people toward bank loans, which are legally and financially more interesting for the banks. A bank or finance company may therefore refuse a personal promissory note even where the law allows it. A bank or finance company may therefore refuse a personal promissory note even where the law allows it.

entries.title: Push or pull: follow the money, not the device
entries.text: Push or pull: follow the money, not the device Core Push and pull describe the movement of the instruction and the funds, never the technology behind the payment. A PayPal reserve debit sent straight to the beneficiary counts as push. Paying by card through PayPal counts as pull: the beneficiary is credited right away after a balance check, while the bank account behind the card is debited one or two days later. A credit transfer started directly from a bank account counts as push, with the account debited right away. A credit transfer started directly from a bank account counts as push, with the account debited right away.

entries.title: Wallet and bank account: moving your own money
entries.text: Wallet and bank account: moving your own money Core Moving funds between a mobile wallet and a bank account means moving money between two accounts belonging to the same customer. Push transactions should be enough for these moves. A wallet to bank transfer should start only when the wallet holds sufficient funds, and a bank to wallet transfer only when the bank account holds sufficient funds. A wallet to bank transfer should start only when the wallet holds sufficient funds, and a bank to wallet transfer only when the bank account holds sufficient funds.

entries.title: SEPA Cards done, SEPA Cash still ongoing
entries.text: SEPA Cards done, SEPA Cash still ongoing Core The SEPA Cards Framework stands complete across the SEPA area, with Visa and Mastercard as the two main card networks and interoperability that was already working accelerated by SEPA. Major projects that began in 2007 to 2010 are complete, so people in Europe can now use their bank cards in any SEPA country regardless of the country that issued the card. The SEPA Cash initiative remains a work in progress, because cash is a sensitive area and standardising practices everywhere in SEPA is a real challenge. The SEPA Cash initiative remains a work in progress, because cash is a sensitive area and standardising practices everywhere in SEPA is a real challenge.

entries.title: GPA versus FIN: system messages or user traffic
entries.text: GPA versus FIN: system messages or user traffic Core The General Purpose Application carries system messages only: a user writing to SWIFT, or SWIFT writing to a user, never one user writing to another. The FIN Application carries messages from one user to another, and alongside that it covers the user-to-user range MT1xx through MT9xx, the system messages MT0xx, plus other service messages such as acknowledgements. The distinction is therefore about who a message can travel between, not the network itself. The distinction is therefore about who a message can travel between, not the network itself.

entries.title: Interchange pays for the issuer guarantee
entries.text: Interchange pays for the issuer guarantee Core Card networks do not charge interchange. The fee compensates the issuer, who takes on all the risk, authorises the transaction and guarantees payment to the merchant. That guarantee is what interchange pays for. That guarantee is what interchange pays for.

entries.title: When AI agents pay for customers
entries.text: When AI agents pay for customers Advanced An AI agent that pays on behalf of a customer follows six steps: understand, verify, evaluate, authorize, execute and confirm. The use cases range from paying bills to paying vendor invoices, and the authorisation step is the control that makes the whole flow safe. entries.text: Good engineering protects real people Advanced The post is about a house that stood strong while everything around it was destroyed, with prayers for the people of Nepal.
