entries.title: Gathering requirements for a third-party payment gateway
entries.text: Gathering requirements for a third-party payment gateway Advanced A retailer sells online and in store and wants to add a third-party payment gateway so customers can pay by card and by instant payment at checkout, but the requirements are still a set of general wishes: fast, secure and easy to integrate. Start from the customer and finance outcomes, not from the provider brochure: list the payment methods, currencies, channels and customer journeys in scope, and for each one define the expected flow, authorisation, capture, refund, partial refund, void, chargeback handling and settlement timing. Then define the API capabilities, the request and response contracts, the error handling, the security, the retries and the reconciliation, so the provider can be compared on evidence rather than on marketing. Then define the API capabilities, the request and response contracts, the error handling, the security, the retries and the reconciliation, so the provider can be compared on evidence

entries.title: SIT passes but the production API fails
entries.text: SIT passes but the production API fails Advanced A merchant payment API integration passes system integration testing cleanly, with every test case returning the expected response, yet it fails in production. Contain the impact first by stopping new submissions if the failure rate is rising, telling the partner what is known and what is not, and confirming which payments have a financial effect and which do not. Then compare the environments side by side in a fixed order: endpoint and configuration, credentials and scopes, certificates and expiry dates, network routes and firewall rules, feature flags, downstream dependency versions and production data. The difference between test and production is usually in one of these, and comparing them in a fixed order finds it faster than guessing. The difference between test and production is usually in one of these, and comparing them in a fixed order finds it faster than guessing.

entries.title: Validating a payment API
entries.text: Validating a payment API Advanced A fintech partner is integrating with a bank's payment API to submit customer credit transfers on behalf of its merchants. In testing, the API returns a successful HTTP response, but the merchant's downstream order record is not created, and in one case the payment is debited while the merchant dashboard still shows the order as unpaid. Start from the contract, not from the code: the API definition must state, for each endpoint, what a success response promises, receipt, validation, acceptance or completion, and what the caller must do next in each case. Then review authentication, schema, mandatory fields, business validation, response codes, idempotency and observability, because a success response that promises completion when it only means receipt will mislead every caller. Then review authentication, schema, mandatory fields, business validation, response codes, idempotency and observability, because a success response that promises completion

entries.title: Defining request and response expectations
entries.text: Defining request and response expectations Advanced A bank is publishing a Payment API for corporate customers and retail partners, and the first draft of the contract is a list of fields with no rules. It does not say which fields are required and which are optional, what happens when a field is missing, which error code means what, whether a success response means the payment completed, or how a caller should safely retry. Define every field with its name, type, cardinality, validation rule and error code, and state explicitly which fields are required, which are optional, and which are conditionally mandatory by rail, destination or product. Where a field is optional under the message schema but the bank's reporting or product needs it, say so in the contract and state the source the bank will use and the derivation rule. Where a field is optional under the message schema but the bank's reporting or product needs it, say so in the contract and state the source the bank will use and

entries.title: Two-week BA sprint for a Payment API integration
entries.text: Two-week BA sprint for a Payment API integration Advanced A retailer needs a Payment API integration delivered in a two-week sprint. The checkout must submit payment instructions to the bank, receive a clear acceptance or rejection, and create the order only when the payment outcome is known. Start the sprint with discovery compressed into the first two days: confirm the business outcome, the checkout journey, the payment types in scope, the expected volumes and the response contract. The contract definition matters most, so agree in writing what each response means, so that an acceptance response is never mistaken for completion, and define the status enquiry path the retailer uses when a payment outcome is unclear. The contract definition matters most, so agree in writing what each response means, so that an acceptance response is never mistaken for completion, and define the status enquiry path the retailer uses when a payment outcome is unclear.

entries.title: Redesigning a KYC onboarding journey
entries.text: Redesigning a KYC onboarding journey Advanced A bank wants more new retail customers to complete digital onboarding, but only a small share of started applications reach an active account. Customers abandon the journey at document upload and at identity verification, and many who do finish are later held for manual review because documents are unclear or data does not match. Start with evidence, not opinions, and measure the funnel stage by stage: started, identity details entered, document uploaded, identity verified, screening complete, account opened and first transaction. Then map the friction, the document collection, the validation, the screening, the exception handling and the conversion measures, so the redesign targets the stages where customers actually drop off. Then map the friction, the document collection, the validation, the screening, the exception handling and the conversion measures, so the redesign targets the stages where customers actually drop off.

entries.title: Change affects multiple applications and teams
entries.text: Change affects multiple applications and teams Advanced A bank must change its instant euro payments to match the current scheme rules: there is no longer a scheme-level maximum amount for SCT Inst, execution must complete within 10 seconds, and verification of payee is mandatory for instant euro payments. The change touches the mobile app, the payment engine, the sanctions and fraud services, the clearing adapter, the ledger and the customer notifications. Build the impact analysis as a map, not as a list of opinions: start from the change and walk upstream to find which channels, products and customer journeys can submit an instant euro payment, which limits and validations apply today, and which of those must change, then walk downstream to find the systems, data, interfaces, controls, tests, operations and release dependencies that are affected. Build the impact analysis as a map, not as a list of opinions: start from the change and walk upstream to find which channels, products

entries.title: Critical requirement appears one day before deployment
entries.text: Critical requirement appears one day before deployment Advanced A bank is one day from deploying an upgrade to its instant euro payment service. UAT is signed off, regression evidence is filed, the deployment window is booked and the communications to customers are ready, and late in the afternoon the compliance team raises a requirement nobody recorded. First classify the item precisely as a defect against an agreed requirement, a safety or compliance obligation, or genuinely new scope, and confirm the obligation at its source, for example verification of payee is mandatory for instant euro payments from 9 October 2025 under Regulation (EU) 2024/886, and SCT Inst execution has a 10-second maximum with no scheme-level maximum since the 2025 rulebook change. Then triage defect versus new scope, quantify the risk and obtain a formal go or no-go decision, because a mandatory compliance obligation cannot be deferred the way new scope can. Then triage defect versus new scope, quantify the

entries.title: Critical UAT failure rate at test start
entries.text: Critical UAT failure rate at test start Advanced A bank is starting user acceptance testing for a new SEPA direct debit collection service. On the first morning the failure rate is critical: most test collections are rejected, mandate references cannot be found, and the test schedule shows collections submitted on the wrong day. Begin with a triage that separates the failure causes into four buckets, environment, test data, build and requirements, and check the environment first: whether the UAT build is the intended version, whether the endpoints, credentials and scheme adapters point at the right test systems, and whether the feature flags are set as the release notes state. Only then decide whether to continue, fix and restart, or stop, because continuing a test on a broken environment wastes the testers' time and produces evidence that cannot be trusted. Only then decide whether to continue, fix and restart, or stop, because continuing a test on a broken environment wastes the

entries.title: Incorrect EMI for a small customer subset
entries.text: Incorrect EMI for a small customer subset Advanced A bank receives complaints from a small group of loan customers that their monthly EMI is wrong. Most customers are unaffected, which makes the problem harder, not easier, so start by defining the affected population precisely: list every complaining account and search for others with the same characteristics, so the fix covers silent cases as well as complaints. For each affected loan, capture the full calculation inputs: principal, sanctioned rate, rate change history with effective dates, tenure, schedule generation rules, rounding policy, part-payment history and customer data. The pattern only emerges when the cases are compared, because the affected loans share a characteristic, such as a particular rate change date, that the unaffected loans do not. The pattern only emerges when the cases are compared, because the affected loans share a characteristic, such as a particular rate change date, that the unaffected loans do not.

entries.title: Designing discovery for a new product
entries.text: Designing discovery for a new product Advanced A bank wants to launch an instant payment product for small business customers, and the product sponsor has asked the team to make payments faster. The request has no named user group, no baseline, no target speed and no statement of the problem customers actually face today. Start by naming the target users precisely, for example small businesses that pay domestic suppliers on fixed weekly cycles, and exclude segments the product will not serve in the first release, then write a problem statement in the form of who suffers, what it costs them and how often, and gather evidence such as payment volumes, current settlement times, supplier discount losses and support contacts. Then define the hypotheses, the constraints, the minimum viable product and the success metrics, so discovery ends with a decision rather than with a longer list of ideas. Then define the hypotheses, the constraints, the minimum viable product and the success metrics,

entries.title: Optimising an inefficient legacy process
entries.text: Optimising an inefficient legacy process Advanced A bank runs a legacy supplier payment process that has grown by accretion over a decade. A corporate customer sends a payment file, operations staff print exception lists, re-key corrected details into three different screens, phone the customer for missing information, and then release the file late in the day. Begin by observing the work as performed, not as documented: follow real files from intake to release, time each step, and record every workaround, hand-off and re-key, then quantify the pain with measures the business can compare, such as straight-through processing rate, repair rate by defect type, average and worst-case cycle time per step, rework hours, error rate after release and customer contacts per file. Then design the target process, validate the controls and the operational impacts, and only then change the process. Then design the target process, validate the controls and the operational impacts, and only then

entries.title: Message flow after the clearing system
entries.text: Message flow after the clearing system Advanced After the clearing system, the message flow continues with the pacs.008 reaching the beneficiary bank and the pacs.002 reporting the status back, and the question is how those messages fit together once the clearing system is in the middle. The clearing system sits between the originator bank and the beneficiary bank, so the pacs.008 passes through it and the pacs.002 returns through it. An analyst drawing the flow must include the clearing system as a party, not as a pipe, because it sends and receives messages of its own. An analyst drawing the flow must include the clearing system as a party, not as a pipe, because it sends and receives messages of its own.

entries.title: Deducted, rejected, and the funds must return
entries.text: Deducted, rejected, and the funds must return Advanced When the originator bank deducts the amount from the customer but the payment never reaches the beneficiary because the clearing system rejected it, the funds must be returned, and the question is which messages carry that return inside the clearing system. The clearing system holds the funds it rejected, so the return starts there and travels back to the originator bank, which credits the customer. The customer sees a deduction with no payment, and the return is what makes the customer whole. The customer sees a deduction with no payment, and the return is what makes the customer whole.

entries.title: Language never blocks an MT103
entries.text: Language never blocks an MT103 Advanced When the beneficiary bank is in a country whose language is not English, the MT103 is still processed from its structured fields, which are coded and do not depend on the language of the country. The names and addresses in the message may be in the local language, but the fields that drive processing, such as the account number, the currency, and the amount, are numeric or coded. Processing therefore does not stop at a language barrier; it follows the fields. Processing therefore does not stop at a language barrier; it follows the fields.

entries.title: Reaching a bank with no direct relationship
entries.text: Reaching a bank with no direct relationship Advanced A customer can transfer funds to a bank that has no account with the sending bank, because the payment travels through correspondent and intermediary banks that do hold accounts with each other. The sending bank passes the instruction to its correspondent, which passes it onward until it reaches a bank that holds an account for the beneficiary bank. The chain exists precisely to connect banks that have no direct relationship. The chain exists precisely to connect banks that have no direct relationship.

entries.title: Direct relationship: is an intermediary needed?
entries.text: Direct relationship: is an intermediary needed? Advanced When the ordering bank and the beneficiary bank already hold accounts with each other, the question is whether an intermediary bank should still be used for an international payment. A direct relationship can carry the payment without an intermediary, which is faster and cheaper, but an intermediary may still be used for a currency, a corridor, or a compliance reason. The choice is a design decision, not a rule, and it depends on the corridor and the banks involved. The choice is a design decision, not a rule, and it depends on the corridor and the banks involved.

entries.title: A misspelt name in field 50 can return a payment
entries.text: A misspelt name in field 50 can return a payment Advanced When the ordering customer name in field 50 is misspelt, the MT103 can be returned to the originator bank, and the question is which message carries that return. The misspelling matters because screening and reconciliation match on the name, and a name that does not match the account can look like a different party. The return is therefore a data-quality failure, not a funds failure, and it is fixed by correcting the name and resending. The return is therefore a data-quality failure, not a funds failure, and it is fixed by correcting the name and resending.

entries.title: Beneficiary short after intermediary charges
entries.text: Beneficiary short after intermediary charges Advanced When an ordering customer pays an employee with an MT103 and an intermediary bank deducts its charges, the beneficiary receives less than the amount sent, and the shortfall is the charge, not an error. The beneficiary bank credits the amount that arrives after the deductions, and the ordering customer must explain the difference to the employee. The situation is a normal consequence of the serial method, and it is why the charge-bearer field matters before the payment is sent. The situation is a normal consequence of the serial method, and it is why the charge-bearer field matters before the payment is sent.

entries.title: Faster Payments and BACS: not SEPA messages
entries.text: Faster Payments and BACS: not SEPA messages Advanced The messages exchanged between banks in UK Faster Payments and in BACS are different from the messages used in SEPA, and readers ask for the flow in each system. The SEPA message set is a good starting point, because the concepts of initiation, clearing, and status reporting are the same, but the actual messages and the clearing systems differ. An analyst who understands the SEPA flow can learn the UK flows by mapping each SEPA message to its UK equivalent, rather than starting from nothing. An analyst who understands the SEPA flow can learn the UK flows by mapping each SEPA message to its UK equivalent, rather than starting from nothing.

entries.title: CHAPS as the sterling leg of a cross-border payment
entries.text: CHAPS as the sterling leg of a cross-border payment Advanced CHAPS is the UK high-value payment system, and the question is whether it can be used for cross-border payments. CHAPS settles sterling payments between UK banks in central bank money, and a cross-border payment that needs sterling settlement in the UK can use it as the domestic leg. The cross-border leg itself still needs a correspondent or a scheme to carry the payment out of the UK, so CHAPS is one leg of the journey, not the whole journey. The cross-border leg itself still needs a correspondent or a scheme to carry the payment out of the UK, so CHAPS is one leg of the journey, not the whole journey.

entries.title: Why BACS outlasts Faster Payments for bulk pay
entries.text: Why BACS outlasts Faster Payments for bulk pay Advanced Faster Payments settles in seconds, yet BACS remains the preferred way to pay for many UK businesses, and the reason is that BACS is built for bulk, scheduled, low-cost payments such as salaries and supplier runs. Faster Payments is built for single, urgent payments, and it costs more per payment and carries limits that bulk runs do not want. The two systems therefore serve different needs, and the older one survives because it fits the bulk use case better. The two systems therefore serve different needs, and the older one survives because it fits the bulk use case better.

entries.title: How Wise settles without SWIFT on each leg
entries.text: How Wise settles without SWIFT on each leg Advanced Wise moves money internationally without using SWIFT codes for every payment, because it holds local accounts in the countries it serves and settles each leg domestically. A customer paying from one country to another funds a local account in the sending country, and Wise pays the beneficiary from its local account in the receiving country, so no cross-border SWIFT message is needed for the legs. The model works because Wise nets the flows across its customers, and it is a different design from the correspondent banking chain. The model works because Wise nets the flows across its customers, and it is a different design from the correspondent banking chain.

entries.title: Cover currency and fields 52, 53 and 54
entries.text: Cover currency and fields 52, 53 and 54 Advanced In a cover payment the MT103 and the MT202 can carry different currencies, and the question is how the currency of each leg is decided and what fields 52, 53 and 54 carry. Field 52 identifies the ordering institution, field 53 identifies the sender's correspondent, and field 54 identifies the receiver's correspondent, so together they describe the chain of banks that will fund the payment. The currency of the cover leg follows the correspondent account it settles in, which is why the two legs can differ. The currency of the cover leg follows the correspondent account it settles in, which is why the two legs can differ.

entries.title: SEPA dispute, cancellation and recall: three acts
entries.text: SEPA dispute, cancellation and recall: three acts Advanced In SEPA, a dispute, a cancellation, and a recall are three different actions, and the question is how each one works and which message carries it. A recall is requested with a camt.056 and answered with a camt.029, a return is made with a pacs.004, and a cancellation stops a payment before it settles. The three are often confused because they all undo a payment, but they apply at different stages and they use different messages. The three are often confused because they all undo a payment, but they apply at different stages and they use different messages.

entries.title: Paying a bank with a non-connected BIC
entries.text: Paying a bank with a non-connected BIC Advanced Some banks hold a BIC with the digit 1 in position 8, which marks it as non-connected: it is a SWIFT participant but cannot receive messages directly. The MT103 announcement and the MT202 COV are then sent to a live BIC, which forwards the funds to the non-connected bank over an internal network, usually with a normal serial MT103. The same pattern appears in bank groups where SWIFT communication is centralised at the head office and the head office forwards payments to subsidiaries and branches. The same pattern appears in bank groups where SWIFT communication is centralised at the head office and the head office forwards payments to subsidiaries and branches.

entries.title: Why a bank waits to buy the payment currency
entries.text: Why a bank waits to buy the payment currency Advanced A bank does not buy the currency of every payment the moment it is instructed, because it does not know in advance how much foreign currency it will need. It collects orders until a cut-off time and then decides whether to buy, sell or do nothing, based on the balance of orders and the funds already sitting in its nostro accounts. A payment can therefore wait for the bank's currency position to be settled, even when the instruction itself is complete. A payment can therefore wait for the bank's currency position to be settled, even when the instruction itself is complete.

entries.title: Five returns over a wrong field 57A
entries.text: Five returns over a wrong field 57A Advanced A payment sent to Australia was returned five times over six weeks, each time with the note that the beneficiary bank's SWIFT code had to appear in field 57A. The code had been placed in field 72 and in field 52A, where the receiving bank could see it, but that did not satisfy the validation: field 57A is the field the receiving bank reads to find the account with institution. The beneficiary bank had also been taken over and its SWIFT code had changed, so the sender had to use the new code in field 57A before the payment could be applied. The beneficiary bank had also been taken over and its SWIFT code had changed, so the sender had to use the new code in field 57A before the payment could be applied.

entries.title: UETR: the thread through a pass-through payment
entries.text: UETR: the thread through a pass-through payment Advanced When a payment passes through a correspondent bank, that bank sees two payments: the incoming payment from the sender and the outgoing payment to the next bank. The two legs are linked by the unique end-to-end transaction reference, the UETR, which travels unchanged from one message to the next and is carried in field 121 of block 3. No bank in the chain may modify field 121, because changing it would break the link that lets every bank reconcile the payment it received with the payment it sent. No bank in the chain may modify field 121, because changing it would break the link that lets every bank reconcile the payment it received with the payment it sent.

entries.title: A future-dated MT103 cannot be discounted
entries.text: A future-dated MT103 cannot be discounted Advanced An MT103 can be value-dated far in the future, but that does not turn it into an instrument a bank will discount. An MT103 is an instruction to pay, not a proof of financial commitment: when the due date arrives, execution depends on the payer account holding sufficient funds. If the payer does not pay, the beneficiary has no recourse, and neither does a bank that discounted it, unless it signed a separate contract with the payer. If the payer does not pay, the beneficiary has no recourse, and neither does a bank that discounted it, unless it signed a separate contract with the payer.

entries.title: The accounting inside an MT101
entries.text: The accounting inside an MT101 Advanced Accounting is done on the MT101 itself, in part: the debtor's account is debited and the funds are placed on an intermediary account inside the bank. When the MT103 is generated to move the money onward, the funds are debited from that intermediary account and forwarded to the destination. The MT101 therefore does the customer-side accounting, and the MT103 does the interbank settlement. The MT101 therefore does the customer-side accounting, and the MT103 does the interbank settlement.

entries.title: Bank to bank dollars settle inside the USA
entries.text: Bank to bank dollars settle inside the USA Advanced When a French bank sends USD to a German bank, it tells its US correspondent to debit the nostro and credit the German bank's account with that bank's own US correspondent. Settlement completes in a single domestic step, since both accounts sit in the USA. The sender finds the German bank's US correspondent in its Standing Settlement Instructions and states it in the MT103. The sender finds the German bank's US correspondent in its Standing Settlement Instructions and states it in the MT103.

entries.title: Letter of credit settlement: MT103 or MT103 plus cover
entries.text: Letter of credit settlement: MT103 or MT103 plus cover Advanced A letter of credit is issued with an MT700, but the standard does not fix how it must be settled, so the parties agree the payment instrument between themselves. In general the settlement runs through a serial MT103, or through an MT103 together with an MT202 COV. Either route moves the funds under the credit once the documents have been accepted. Either route moves the funds under the credit once the documents have been accepted.

entries.title: France before SEPA: PNS and TBF, then CORE for retail
entries.text: France before SEPA: PNS and TBF, then CORE for retail Advanced Before SEPA, France already ran EBA systems for interbank payments alongside high value systems called PNS and TBF. CORE, the retail clearing system, arrived after SEPA to process XML format files and improve retail payment services. The market infrastructures changed greatly with the SEPA project, with old and new systems sitting side by side for a time. The market infrastructures changed greatly with the SEPA project, with old and new systems sitting side by side for a time.

entries.title: RuPay: scheme and clearing house in one
entries.text: RuPay: scheme and clearing house in one Advanced On RuPay, clearing and settlement run between domestic and other network partners, with RuPay acting as both the card scheme and the clearing house. In India the clearing house role sits with NPCI, which operates RuPay. When issuer and acquirer are both RuPay members, they clear their transactions through RuPay itself rather than through a separate clearing house. When issuer and acquirer are both RuPay members, they clear their transactions through RuPay itself rather than through a separate clearing house.

entries.title: MT103 cannot supply what pacs.008 demands
entries.text: MT103 cannot supply what pacs.008 demands Advanced MT to MX coexistence creates a data gap: an MT103 may carry no structured address, yet pacs.008 requires town name and country code. The missing town cannot be invented, guessing writes false data onto the payment and a blank fails validation. Handle the gap with explicit translation rules, enrichment from a trusted source, and exception governance for every field the old message cannot supply. Handle the gap with explicit translation rules, enrichment from a trusted source, and exception governance for every field the old message cannot supply.

entries.title: Routing must survive a limit cut
entries.text: Routing must survive a limit cut Advanced Good routing rules are written for the bad day, not the quiet one: a correspondent can cut an intraday credit limit without warning, and an engine that keeps feeding the same corridor will queue payments and generate rejects it cannot explain. Build the rules with eligibility checks, fallback routes, a defined decision order, and an audit trail naming the affected payments and the reason. A routing decision nobody can reconstruct is a control failure, not a routing outcome. A routing decision nobody can reconstruct is a control failure, not a routing outcome.

entries.title: Ten million a month: test the peak, not the average
entries.text: Ten million a month: test the peak, not the average Advanced Five new clients at ten million transactions a month add roughly 330,000 transactions a day on average, but averages hide the risk: payroll and supplier files arrive in concentrated morning windows, so the peak dwarfs the average. With the busiest hour already at about 70 percent of measured capacity, the only question that matters is whether the peak fits. Convert the growth into throughput, concurrency, queue depth, storage, monitoring and resilience requirements before the clients go live. Convert the growth into throughput, concurrency, queue depth, storage, monitoring and resilience requirements before the clients go live.

entries.title: An extra hour moves every deadline
entries.text: An extra hour moves every deadline Advanced A cut-off is not a single time but the end of a deadline chain, channel cut-offs, scheme windows, liquidity checks and operational staffing. Adding an hour moves the whole chain, and the customer promise has to survive at the new time. Judge the extension on four things, downstream scheme windows, liquidity for the extra hour, staffing to run it, and exception handling for payments that still miss the new cut-off. Judge the extension on four things, downstream scheme windows, liquidity for the extra hour, staffing to run it, and exception handling for payments that still miss the new cut-off.

entries.title: One corridor, one owner, end to end
entries.text: One corridor, one owner, end to end Advanced A European buyer paying an Indian exporter crosses four legs, a domestic euro rail, a cross-border bridge, an FX conversion and a domestic Indian rail, and each participant reports only its own leg. With no owner of the end-to-end state, a late payment turns into a chain of calls, exporter to buyer, buyer to bank, bank to bridge operator, and nobody can say where the money is. Give the corridor a named owner for the whole journey, with every leg mapped to its rail, FX step, settlement and compliance check. Give the corridor a named owner for the whole journey, with every leg mapped to its rail, FX step, settlement and compliance check.

entries.title: Credited already? The recall is only a request
entries.text: Credited already? The recall is only a request Advanced Once the beneficiary bank has credited the customer, the sender bank has no power to command the money back; it can only request it. The sender sends a camt.056 cancellation request, the beneficiary bank tests whether the funds are still available and answers with a camt.029, and a pacs.004 moves the money only on acceptance. A rejection leaves the sender with a commercial claim outside the payment rails, so the camt.056 must go out fast, while the funds are still there. A rejection leaves the sender with a commercial claim outside the payment rails, so the camt.056 must go out fast, while the funds are still there.

entries.title: Two legs settled, two returns needed
entries.text: Two legs settled, two returns needed Advanced A cover payment settles twice over, the pacs.008 instruction and the pacs.009 cover that moved funds between correspondents. Returning the customer payment unwinds only the first leg; the cover needs its own pacs.004, matched to the original cover by UETR and settlement references. Both legs post to the Nostro ledger, so reconciliation must pair all four messages, instruction, cover, return of instruction, and return of cover. Both legs post to the Nostro ledger, so reconciliation must pair all four messages, instruction, cover, return of instruction, and return of cover.

entries.title: Debited, failed, and the books disagree
entries.text: Debited, failed, and the books disagree Advanced A 5,000 euro SEPA credit transfer debited the account yet failed between engine and clearing, so the books and reality disagree. Before touching anything, establish the true state across core banking, payment engine, ISO 20022 messages, clearing, settlement and accounting, and rule out duplicates. Then reverse the debit or re-release the payment, post correcting entries with a clear audit trail, and bring every system to the same outcome. Then reverse the debit or re-release the payment, post correcting entries with a clear audit trail, and bring every system to the same outcome.

entries.title: Duplicate payouts: 90 percent recovered
entries.text: Duplicate payouts: 90 percent recovered Advanced Duplicates demand containment before diagnosis: freeze the retry and payout batch so no more duplicates are created while the team investigates. Then identify the full population by reference or idempotency key, reverse the duplicates systematically, and track recovery until every case is closed. The cause here was a retry firing twice after a timeout through an idempotency gap, and the permanent fix is idempotency keys on every payout plus real-time reconciliation flagging double credits. The cause here was a retry firing twice after a timeout through an idempotency gap, and the permanent fix is idempotency keys on every payout plus real-time reconciliation flagging double credits.

entries.title: acks=1: acknowledged, then lost
entries.text: acks=1: acknowledged, then lost Advanced With acks=1 only the leader acknowledges, so a broker dying before replication loses the message, yet the payment had already been charged and the retry charged a second time. Nothing alerted because each component behaved as designed; the failure lived in the interaction. Fix the guarantees, acks=all with idempotent producers and dedup keys on every payment, add the transactional outbox pattern so the business record and the event cannot diverge, and keep reconciliation as the backstop. Fix the guarantees, acks=all with idempotent producers and dedup keys on every payment, add the transactional outbox pattern so the business record and the event cannot diverge, and keep reconciliation as the backstop.

entries.title: 125,000 pounds, no trace: prove first
entries.text: 125,000 pounds, no trace: prove first Advanced A 125,000 pound international payment left the sender and never arrived, with no rejection, no return and no confirmation. Before acting, prove what happened: pull the UETR, check the tracker for the last confirmed hop, and ask whether the money sits with an intermediary, in a compliance review, or stuck in a queue. Never re-send until the original is accounted for, because a duplicate is worse than a delay, and keep both sender and expectant beneficiary updated. Never re-send until the original is accounted for, because a duplicate is worse than a delay, and keep both sender and expectant beneficiary updated.

entries.title: Processed, timed out, then re-submitted
entries.text: Processed, timed out, then re-submitted Advanced A core banking API processed the transaction, then timed out before responding, so caller retry logic re-submitted a completed transaction. The missing controls were idempotency keys, a smart timeout strategy, and a reconciliation layer. The fix is idempotency keys on every mutating call, a pending-state transaction model that checks state before acting, and a standing rule that on any timeout the true state is queried first, asking what actually happened to the money. The fix is idempotency keys on every mutating call, a pending-state transaction model that checks state before acting, and a standing rule that on any timeout the true state is queried first, asking what actually happened to the money.

entries.title: UPI debit landed, credit never did
entries.text: UPI debit landed, credit never did Advanced A UPI debit committed locally while the credit acknowledgement timed out, a partial commit across two systems: the sender account debited, the receiver never credited. A retry hit duplicate-suppression logic and the message parked in a queue, leaving one system committed and the other uncertain. The mitigations are globally unique transaction references, idempotent processing at each bank, compensating transactions such as auto-reversal, and settlement-level balancing at the end of the cycle. The mitigations are globally unique transaction references, idempotent processing at each bank, compensating transactions such as auto-reversal, and settlement-level balancing at the end of the cycle.

entries.title: Direct debit rejects routed to a third-party account
entries.text: Direct debit rejects routed to a third-party account Advanced A debtor bank normally returns a rejected collection to the creditor bank, authorising it to debit the originator's account, but a collection can instead be booked to a designated third-party account. The third-party account is funded to meet regulatory obligations and to follow rejected payments through the general ledger, and it can be used only if the originator's instructions allow it, the account was opened and funded first, and it is opened and maintained by the creditor bank. Building it as a system requirement is a sensitive decision that needs product owner and business owner agreement, with checks for the returning customer, fraud signs and valid repayment flows. A BA cannot necessarily refuse a requirement, yet challenging it remains the BA responsibility. A BA cannot necessarily refuse a requirement, yet challenging it remains the BA responsibility.

entries.title: Late consent after a camt.056 cancellation
entries.text: Late consent after a camt.056 cancellation Advanced A negative camt.029 can arrive while a payment engine is still processing a set of 500 payments, and a beneficiary consent can then arrive after the expected timeframe, while the pacs.004 return that follows can be made per payment or grouped by customer, reason, value or compliance cause. The remaining payments have no universal answer: return them, complete them, or reject the late consent by accepting or overriding the rule, so each bank must define when a late consent can be accepted and when it cannot, and record the message, the consent and the retention rules that apply. Treating a late consent as merely late misses the point, since it can still reflect sound business behaviour. Treating a late consent as merely late misses the point, since it can still reflect sound business behaviour.

entries.title: Cut-offs are set backwards from the deadline
entries.text: Cut-offs are set backwards from the deadline Advanced A cut-off time is a calculated risk decision, not a time on the clock, and it starts from the downstream deadline, subtracting screening time, buffer, processing capacity, file size, treasury funding and expected rejections. In the worked example a 4:00 PM downstream deadline minus a 15-minute buffer minus 20 minutes of screening gives a 3:25 PM customer cut-off, with guaranteed service until 3:00 PM, best effort until 3:25 PM and next-day service after that. A payment BA should ask what time the payment must be out of the file, whether the deadline is hard, and whether tiers are needed in the requirements. A payment BA should ask what time the payment must be out of the file, whether the deadline is hard, and whether tiers are needed in the requirements.

entries.title: ISO 20022 readiness: close the eight gaps first
entries.text: ISO 20022 readiness: close the eight gaps first Advanced ISO 20022 migration is a transformation of the payments business model, not a message format change, and readiness fails where processes are not aligned to customer payment journeys, hand-offs are unplanned, business teams are untrained, systems cannot hold high data quality, and compliance, fraud and AML teams are not aligned. Limited resources, missing governance and weak coordination across stakeholders leave the gap between business and technology in place even after execution starts. A migration plan must close these eight gaps before it can claim the business is ready. A migration plan must close these eight gaps before it can claim the business is ready.

entries.title: Interlinking: instructions, status and complaints
entries.text: Interlinking: instructions, status and complaints Advanced Interlinking connects payment systems across countries so a payment can be tracked end to end once it is debited, and the open question is whether the customer-side acceptance of payment instructions can travel the same way, and then complaints and investigations too. If instructions, status and complaints all travel on the interlinked rails, the hardest cross-border problem, not knowing where a payment is, starts to close. That is why interlinking is a way of thinking about payments, not only a connectivity project. That is why interlinking is a way of thinking about payments, not only a connectivity project.

entries.title: A pacs.004 does not decide the debtor credit by itself
entries.text: A pacs.004 does not decide the debtor credit by itself Advanced A pacs.004 only says a payment was returned, so crediting the debtor on receipt is an event-to-action shortcut that skips the questions that matter: what the return is for, who initiated it, whether the original was a pacs.008 or a pacs.009, why it was returned, and what happened to the original payment. When the pacs.004 relates to a rejected pacs.009 cover payment, the related pacs.008 cannot be assumed rejected, since the cover may have failed for lack of correspondent funds, wrong beneficiary correspondent or bank details, or a cover rejection for incorrect bank information. The correct procedure investigates the reason, establishes the status of the pacs.008 and any open exception, and only then chooses between re-initiating the pacs.009, returning funds to the debtor, re-initiating the pacs.008, or another defined action. The correct procedure investigates the reason, establishes the status of the pacs.008 and any

entries.title: A return code gap usually sits between systems
entries.text: A return code gap usually sits between systems Advanced Mapping AC06 for a blocked account to MS03, reason not specified, looks like a one-line change until the BA asks how core banking communicates the condition, what the payment engine actually understands, and which conditions should produce AC06 at all. Core banking may know the account is blocked for a KYC restriction, a debit block, dormancy, or another restriction, while the engine only understands that the account is blocked, and national data-protection requirements may forbid passing the specific reason downstream. The real gap is found by comparing what the ecosystem understands today with what the requirement expects, then tracing the chain from core banking through business interpretation, country rule, and mapping to the return code, and deciding which system changes and who agrees the mapping. The real gap is found by comparing what the ecosystem understands today with what the requirement expects, then tracing the

entries.title: Blockchain for payments: four open questions
entries.text: Blockchain for payments: four open questions Advanced Transparency means every node sees transaction detail, and control over confidential fields is still being built. A business relationship links each node with every other node, which simplifies maintenance of the shared ledger. Formats will vary with the algorithm each network uses, so one universal message and ledger format is ambitious yet not impossible. A single network spanning domestic and cross-border payments is achievable if the industry aligns on common standards. A single network spanning domestic and cross-border payments is achievable if the industry aligns on common standards.

entries.title: Status responses: CSM on RTGS, beneficiary bank abroad
entries.text: Status responses: CSM on RTGS, beneficiary bank abroad Advanced The sender of a status response depends on the rail the payment travelled. On a real time gross settlement system the clearing and settlement mechanism sends pacs.002, pacs.004 and camt.029 to the originator. On a cross-border payment the beneficiary bank, or instructed bank, sends them. On a cross-border payment the beneficiary bank, or instructed bank, sends them.

entries.title: The central bank view of indirect participation
entries.text: The central bank view of indirect participation Advanced From the central bank standpoint the risk is liquidity: whether the indirect participant can meet its financial obligations. Ensuring that funding is normally the direct participant business, since the direct participant must confirm the indirect participant holds enough before sending debit payments. The central bank sees only the direct participant, even when the payment belongs to the indirect participant, and oversees the direct participant as a whole rather than dealing with the indirect participant. The central bank sees only the direct participant, even when the payment belongs to the indirect participant, and oversees the direct participant as a whole rather than dealing with the indirect participant.

entries.title: Scheme cycles for direct and indirect participants
entries.text: Scheme cycles for direct and indirect participants Advanced Cycle sign-up belongs to the direct participant alone, so a direct participant enrolled for cycle 00 receives those transactions yet sends nothing to an indirect participant that did not enrol. Forwarding runs on a timetable the two agree separately, for instance once at the end of the day, and stays independent of the cycles. In classic SEPA only the direct participant exchanges files with the clearing and settlement mechanism. In SCT Inst some indirect participants connect directly to the mechanism and files move immediately, so no cycles exist there. In SCT Inst some indirect participants connect directly to the mechanism and files move immediately, so no cycles exist there.

entries.title: Reading pacs.008 for direct or indirect payment
entries.text: Reading pacs.008 for direct or indirect payment Advanced Two agents in pacs.008 reveal the participation model behind a payment. Where the payer is a direct participant, both instructing agent and debtor agent name that direct participant. Where the payer is indirect, the instructing agent still names the direct participant while the debtor agent names the indirect participant. Where the payer is indirect, the instructing agent still names the direct participant while the debtor agent names the indirect participant.

entries.title: TAG 21 of MT101 stays out of the MT103
entries.text: TAG 21 of MT101 stays out of the MT103 Advanced TAG 21 of an MT101 never maps into the MT103 that follows. It serves reporting to the ordering customer about the MT101, letting that customer reconcile the reporting automatically with the original transaction. TAG 21 stops there and never travels to the next party in the chain. TAG 21 stops there and never travels to the next party in the chain.

entries.title: How the debtor bank picks the cheapest rail
entries.text: How the debtor bank picks the cheapest rail Advanced A debtor bank looks for the cheapest way to reach the beneficiary on time. When the receiver sits in the same country the payment goes through the local clearing and settlement mechanism or the local real time gross settlement system, and when the receiver sits abroad it goes through SWIFT. Routing rules set up in the payment engine apply that choice automatically, including for bulk MT101 and pain.001 files. Routing rules set up in the payment engine apply that choice automatically, including for bulk MT101 and pain.001 files.

entries.title: Routing e-mandates without a CSM in the middle
entries.text: Routing e-mandates without a CSM in the middle Advanced A creditor bank needs a player in between to route e-mandate messages to debtor banks, but that player does not have to be a clearing and settlement mechanism. The operating model defines two services for this: routing and validation, each delivered by a service provider, and either service can come from a debtor bank, a creditor bank or a CSM. Market players such as GoCardless and EquensWorldline provide this kind of routing service, and a search for SEPA e-mandate providers finds more names. Market players such as GoCardless and EquensWorldline provide this kind of routing service, and a search for SEPA e-mandate providers finds more names.

entries.title: Cancelling SEPA payments: the right message each time
entries.text: Cancelling SEPA payments: the right message each time Advanced In the SEPA Credit Transfer scheme camt.056 is the message used to request cancellation of an SCT transaction. For SDD Core reversals the creditor bank sends pacs.007 against funds mistakenly debited. Corporations may also send camt.055 through their bank to cancel a pain.008: an unexecuted transaction is cancelled, while an executed one is reversed by the bank with pacs.007 instead. Corporations may also send camt.055 through their bank to cancel a pain.008: an unexecuted transaction is cancelled, while an executed one is reversed by the bank with pacs.007 instead.

entries.title: Write Requirements for Same-Day Cross-Border Payments for SMEs
entries.text: Write Requirements for Same-Day Cross-Border Payments for SMEs Requirement analysis A mid-sized bank wants to offer same-day cross-border payments to its small and medium enterprise customers, who today wait two to three days for supplier payments to arrive. The current process relies on manual checks, emailed instructions and a correspondent chain that the customer cannot track. In this lab you act as the business analyst who turns that business problem into a clear, testable set of requirements. You will define the objectives and the scope, identify the stakeholders, record the assumptions and dependencies, and write the business rules that govern cutoffs, charges and value dates. You will then separate functional requirements from non-functional requirements, so that the development team knows what the solution must do and how well it must do it. By the end of the lab you will have a requirements pack that a sponsor can sign off and a development team can build from without

entries.title: Redesign the Payment Exception Repair Process
entries.text: Redesign the Payment Exception Repair Process Process modelling When a payment cannot be processed straight through, it lands in an exception queue where operations staff must repair it, return it or reject it. In many banks that queue is slow, opaque and full of rework, because nobody has mapped the process end to end. In this lab you model the as-is exception repair process, measure where time is lost, and design a to-be process that clears most exceptions on first touch. You will draw a BPMN diagram with clear swimlanes, add sequence diagrams for the system interactions, and model the exception flows for the most common failure types. You will also define the controls, the handoffs and the service levels for each step. By the end of the lab you will have a process design that operations can run, technology can build, and management can measure. entries.title: Map MT103 to pacs.008 for a Migration
entries.text: Map MT103 to pacs.008 for a Migration Data and messaging Migrating from MT103 to pacs.008 is a data exercise before it is a technology exercise, and the quality of the mapping decides whether payments arrive intact. In this lab you build a source-to-target mapping for a real migration scope, starting from a canonical data model and working down to field level rules. You will decide which fields are mandatory, optional or defaulted, write the transformation rules for party data, addresses, remittance information and charges, and define the validation rules that catch bad data before it leaves the bank. You will also record data lineage, so that any field in the outgoing pacs.008 can be traced back to its source. By the end of the lab you will have a mapping sheet that developers can build from and testers can verify against. entries.title: Specify a Payment Initiation API for a Corporate Channel
entries.text: Specify a Payment Initiation API for a Corporate Channel API analysis A corporate banking channel needs an API that lets treasury systems initiate payments directly, without a person typing each instruction into a screen. The API must be easy to integrate, safe against duplicate payments, and clear about what went wrong when a request fails. In this lab you analyse and specify a payment initiation API from the business need down to the contract. You will define the endpoints, the HTTP methods, the request and response schemas, the authentication model, the error codes, and the rules for idempotency, correlation IDs, timeouts and retries. You will also write the OpenAPI contract that the corporate integration team builds against. entries.title: What is a payment?
entries.text: What is a payment? A payment is the transfer of value from one party to another in order to settle an obligation. When you buy a coffee, pay rent, send a salary, or settle a supplier invoice, you are making a payment. The obligation can come from a purchase, a loan, a tax, a salary agreement, or any commitment where one party owes value to another. The payment discharges that obligation, fully or partly, and creates a record that the debt has been reduced or cleared. In a modern banking context, a payment almost always involves accounts held with regulated institutions and a set of instructions that tell those institutions what to move, from whom, to whom, and for what reason. The instructions travel as a payment message, while the actual value moves through accounts and settlement

entries.title: What is a payment rail?
entries.text: What is a payment rail? A payment rail is the infrastructure that carries a payment from one party to another. Think of it like a railway track. The train is the payment instruction, and the rail is the set of systems, rules, and connections that let the train reach its destination safely. A rail includes the network that moves the message, the clearing system that exchanges instructions between banks, the settlement system that moves value between banks, and the scheme rules that define cut off times, value dates, and liability when something goes wrong. Common examples help make this concrete. In India, UPI, IMPS, NEFT, and RTGS are different rails with different speeds, limits, and settlement models. In the United States, Fedwire, ACH, and FedNow are separate rails. In Europe, SEPA

entries.title: What is the difference between a payment instruction and settlement? Why does the distinction matter in system design?
entries.text: What is the difference between a payment instruction and settlement? Why does the distinction matter in system design? The payment instruction is the **pacs.008** or the **pain.001** that tells the bank to move money. Settlement is the actual movement of funds between banks that discharges the obligation. They are different events and they can happen at different times. When a customer submits a payment, the hub creates a pacs.008 and sends it through the clearing system. The clearing system processes it and returns a **pacs.002** with a status. When the status is ACSC, settlement has happened. Until then, the payment is only an instruction. entries.title: What is the difference between a branch, a subsidiary and an entity in payment routing?
entries.text: What is the difference between a branch, a subsidiary and an entity in payment routing? These three words describe different legal structures, and they change how a payment moves. A branch is part of the same legal entity as the head office. A London bank with a branch in Singapore is one legal entity, so money moving between London and Singapore is an internal transfer, not a payment between two banks. A subsidiary is a separate legal entity owned by the parent bank. A UK bank with a subsidiary in India is two legal entities, so a payment between them is a real payment that must go through proper channels and be recorded as an intercompany transaction. An entity is the general word for a legal unit of the bank, and a large bank can have hundreds of entities across different countries.

entries.title: What is a payment factory model and why do large banks use it?
entries.text: What is a payment factory model and why do large banks use it? A payment factory is a model where a large bank centralises all payment processing into one shared service instead of letting each business unit run its own payments. In a bank like JP Morgan, the corporate banking team, the retail team and the private banking team all send their payment instructions to the same factory. The factory handles validation, routing, clearing and exceptions the same way for everyone. The benefit is scale and consistency. One team maintains the payment logic, one set of controls applies to all payments, and a change to a regulation is made once, not in five different systems. The factory also gives the bank a single view of all payment volumes, which helps treasury manage liquidity and helps risk

entries.title: How does a bank join a clearing system as a direct participant versus using an indirect clearer? What changes operationally?
entries.text: How does a bank join a clearing system as a direct participant versus using an indirect clearer? What changes operationally? A **direct participant** connects to the clearing system itself, holds a **settlement account** at the central bank, and settles its own payments. The bank must meet the clearing system's technical, financial, and operational requirements, hold enough collateral, and staff an operations team that can manage the connection, the queue, and the settlement account through the day. The bank has full control over its payments, its cut-off management, and its liquidity. An **indirect participant** uses a direct participant, called a clearer, to settle on its behalf. The bank sends its payments to the clearer, and the clearer settles them through its own central bank

entries.title: What is straight-through processing and what breaks it?
entries.text: What is straight-through processing and what breaks it? Straight-through processing, or STP, means a payment goes from instruction to settlement without any human touching it. The instruction arrives, the system validates it, routes it, sends it to clearing and confirms settlement, all automatically. STP is the goal for large banks because it is fast, cheap and consistent. A bank like Standard Chartered aims for a high STP rate, often above 95 percent for standard payments. What breaks STP is anything that needs a human decision. A missing field, for example a beneficiary name that does not match the account, stops the payment. A sanctions hit stops it. A payment above a limit needs manual approval. entries.title: What is straight through processing, and how do you design a payment system to maximise it? What is a realistic STP rate?
entries.text: What is straight through processing, and how do you design a payment system to maximise it? What is a realistic STP rate? Straight through processing means a payment goes from initiation to settlement without any manual touch. To design for it, you need four things. First, **complete data at initiation**. The channel must capture every mandatory field before the payment is accepted, so nothing is missing downstream. Second, **automated validation**. The hub checks the account, the balance, the sanctions lists and the message format without human help. Third, **clean routing rules**. The hub decides the clearing system, the settlement method and the charge option from static data, not from someone reading the payment. The sending bank receives the ACSC, updates the payment status, and tells the customer the payment has arrived. entries.title: What is Fedwire?
entries.text: What is Fedwire? Fedwire is the United States real time gross settlement system operated by the Federal Reserve. It is the system through which banks settle large value payments in central bank money, one transaction at a time, with immediate finality. When a bank sends a payment through Fedwire, the Federal Reserve debits the sending bank master account and credits the receiving bank master account, and the payment is final at that moment. There is no netting and no waiting for an end of day batch. Fedwire is used for high value and time critical payments: interbank transfers, settlement of securities transactions, corporate treasury payments, and large customer payments where certainty matters. entries.title: What is CHIPS?
entries.text: What is CHIPS? CHIPS, the Clearing House Interbank Payments System, is a private sector US payment system operated by The Clearing House, and it is the main system for large value US dollar payments. It is used heavily for international payments: when a bank outside the US sends dollars to a bank inside the US, the payment very often clears through CHIPS. It also handles domestic large value transfers between US banks. CHIPS is a net settlement system, which is its defining difference from Fedwire. In CHIPS, payments are not settled one by one in central bank money as they arrive. Instead, they are queued, offset against each other where possible, and settled on a net basis through a prefunded account at the Federal Reserve. entries.title: What is Faster Payments (UK)?
entries.text: What is Faster Payments (UK)? Faster Payments is the United Kingdom real time payment system, launched in 2008 and operated by Pay.UK. It lets people and businesses send sterling payments between UK bank accounts in seconds, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. It is the system behind most everyday instant payments in the UK: paying a friend, paying a bill, or a business paying a supplier. When you make an instant transfer from your UK banking app, it is almost certainly travelling over Faster Payments. The system works through participating banks and payment service providers. The payer bank sends the payment instruction, the system validates and routes it, the beneficiary bank credits the account and confirms, and the payer sees the result within seconds. entries.title: What is CHAPS?
entries.text: What is CHAPS? CHAPS, the Clearing House Automated Payment System, is the United Kingdom high value payment system, operated by the Bank of England. It is the UK equivalent of Fedwire: a real time gross settlement system in which each payment is settled individually and immediately in central bank money, with finality at the moment of settlement. It is used for payments where value, certainty and timing matter most, such as house purchases, large corporate payments, and settlement between financial institutions. A CHAPS payment is typically high value, and there is no upper limit in principle, although banks set their own limits and charges. entries.title: What is RTGS?
entries.text: What is RTGS? RTGS stands for Real Time Gross Settlement. It is a system in which each payment is settled individually, in real time, in central bank money, as soon as it is submitted and validated. There is no batching and no netting: every payment is processed on its own, and the funds move from the sending bank's account at the central bank to the receiving bank's account immediately. The word gross is important. It means each payment is settled for its full value, not netted against other payments. If a bank sends ten payments of 10 lakh rupees each, RTGS settles ten separate transfers of 10 lakh rupees. entries.title: What is RTGS in India and what is the minimum amount?
entries.text: What is RTGS in India and what is the minimum amount? RTGS, the Real Time Gross Settlement system, is India's high value payment system operated by the Reserve Bank of India. It settles each transaction individually and in real time, rather than netting transactions together in a batch. The word gross means each payment is settled for its full amount, one by one, in central bank money. RTGS is designed for large value, time critical payments such as interbank transfers, government securities settlements, and large corporate payments. The minimum amount for an RTGS transaction is 2 lakh rupees. There is no maximum amount, so transactions worth crores of rupees can be settled through RTGS. entries.text: A corporate client needs to send a £250,000 payment to a supplier in the UK today. How do you decide between CHAPS and Faster Payments, and what happens step by step once you choose? The first check is the amount and the value date. **Faster Payments** has a per-transaction limit that varies by bank, usually around £250,000 to £1 million, and it settles in seconds. **CHAPS** has no upper limit and settles in central bank money on the same day, but it costs more and runs to a cut-off, usually around 5 PM. For £250,000 the bank checks its own Faster Payments limit first. If the payment fits, Faster Payments is the default because it is cheaper and instant for the customer. entries.text: A corporate client submits a payment at 4:45 PM for same-day settlement through CHAPS. The CHAPS cut-off is 5 PM. Walk me through what happens if the payment misses the cut-off. The cut-off is a hard deadline set by the clearing system, not by the bank. If the instruction reaches the **Bank of England RTGS** after the cut-off, it is rejected for same-day settlement. The bank cannot force it through. The first thing the **payment hub** does is check the status. If the payment was submitted before the cut-off but is still being processed, the hub tries to release it in time. If it misses, the payment is not lost, but the value date moves to the next working day. The bank then has three jobs. entries.title: How does Faster Payments settle between banks if the customer sees the money instantly? Explain the deferred net settlement behind it.
entries.text: How does Faster Payments settle between banks if the customer sees the money instantly? Explain the deferred net settlement behind it. The customer experience and the bank-to-bank settlement are two different things. When a customer sends a **Faster Payment**, the beneficiary bank credits the customer within seconds. That is the customer leg, and it is instant. But the banks do not settle with each other at that moment. Instead, Faster Payments uses **deferred net settlement**. Each bank's payments are recorded through the day, and at set times, usually three times a day, the central system nets all the payments between each pair of banks and settles only the net amount. entries.text: A Fedwire payment is sent in the US. How does Fedwire settle, and how is it different from CHIPS? **Fedwire** is the **Federal Reserve's** real-time gross settlement system. Each payment settles individually, in central bank money, the moment it is sent. The sending bank's **Federal Reserve account** is debited and the receiving bank's account is credited immediately. There is no netting and no delay. Fedwire is used for high-value, time-critical payments, and it is final the moment it settles. entries.title: What is a nostro FX conversion?
entries.text: What is a nostro FX conversion? A nostro FX conversion is a currency conversion that a bank performs using the funds held in its own nostro account, rather than buying the currency in the market at the moment of the payment. For example, if BNP Paribas holds US dollars in its nostro account with Wells Fargo, and it needs to pay USD 367,574.90 to Banco Santander, it can use the dollars already in the account, with no FX trade needed. If instead it holds only euros in Paris and needs to pay dollars, it must sell euros and buy dollars, and that trade is settled by delivering dollars into the Wells Fargo nostro account. entries.title: A cross border payment was processed with the wrong FX rate. The customer received less than they should have. How do you investigate and fix it?
entries.text: A cross border payment was processed with the wrong FX rate. The customer received less than they should have. How do you investigate and fix it? The first step is to find the **source of truth** for the FX rate. In a bank, the treasury system publishes rates, and the payment hub must use the same rate the customer was quoted. If the hub used a different rate, the customer was overcharged or undercharged. Check the **rate timestamp** on the payment record and compare it against the treasury rate at that moment. Then check the **rate type**. A customer rate includes a margin, a wholesale rate does not, and mixing them up is a common error. Next, check the **currency pair direction**. EUR to USD is not the same as USD to EUR, and inverting the pair is a classic mapping bug. Also check

entries.title: Walk me through a clean cross-border payment end to end, from the corporate customer instruction to the beneficiary credit. How do the instruction and the money move together?
entries.text: Walk me through a clean cross-border payment end to end, from the corporate customer instruction to the beneficiary credit. How do the instruction and the money move together? A clean cross-border payment has two parallel tracks, the instruction track and the money track, and both must complete for the payment to land. The corporate customer sends a **pain.001** to their bank. The bank validates it, checks sanctions, checks the balance, and sends a **pain.002** acceptance. The bank then sends a **pacs.008** instruction to the beneficiary bank, carrying the full customer and remittance details. At the same time, the funds move through the correspondent chain. If the cover method is used, a **pacs.009** with settlement method COVE moves the money between correspondents through their

entries.title: Walk through a clean FX conversion on a cross-border payment. How does the rate get locked and the beneficiary receive exactly the quoted amount?
entries.text: Walk through a clean FX conversion on a cross-border payment. How does the rate get locked and the beneficiary receive exactly the quoted amount? A clean FX conversion starts with the **rate being locked** at the moment the customer confirms the payment. The customer sees the rate, the amount in the source currency, and the amount in the target currency, and agrees. The bank executes the FX trade immediately, buying the target currency at the locked rate. The payment hub then sends the **pacs.008** in the target currency to the beneficiary bank. The beneficiary bank credits the account in the target currency, and the customer receives exactly the amount that was quoted. The bank sends a **pacs.002** with ACSC status, and the end-of-day **camt.053** shows the debit in the source currency

entries.title: What is SWIFT?
entries.text: What is SWIFT? SWIFT is the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication. It is a global messaging network used by banks and financial institutions to send secure instructions and information to each other. When a bank in India needs to tell a bank in the United Kingdom to pay a beneficiary, it often sends that instruction over SWIFT. More than 11,000 institutions in over 200 countries are connected, and they exchange millions of messages every day, covering customer payments, bank to bank transfers, trade finance, securities, and treasury operations. The most important fact about SWIFT, and the one beginners most often get wrong, is that SWIFT is a messaging system, not a payment system. It carries instructions, not money. It holds no accounts and it settles nothing. When

entries.title: What is SWIFT gpi?
entries.text: What is SWIFT gpi? SWIFT gpi is the Global Payments Innovation initiative, a service that makes cross border payments faster, more transparent, and more traceable. Before gpi, a cross border payment could take several days, the customer had no idea where the money was, and the final amount was uncertain because each intermediary could deduct charges without warning. Gpi was built to fix those three problems by setting service level rules for member banks, requiring same day processing, end to end tracking, and transparency on fees and foreign exchange. The core of gpi is the tracker. Every gpi payment carries a Unique End to End Transaction Reference, known as the UETR, which stays with the payment from the debtor agent to the creditor agent. Each bank in the chain confirms when it

entries.title: What is a nostro account?
entries.text: What is a nostro account? A nostro account is an account that a bank holds with a foreign bank, in the foreign bank's currency. The word nostro is Latin for ours, and it is used from the perspective of the bank that owns the account. So if an Indian bank holds a US dollar account with a bank in New York, the Indian bank calls that account its nostro account. The purpose of a nostro account is to make payments in that foreign currency. When the Indian bank's customer pays a supplier in the United States, the Indian bank instructs its New York correspondent to debit its nostro account and pay the beneficiary. The nostro account is prefunded, meaning the Indian bank keeps a balance there so payments can go out immediately without waiting for funds to arrive. Managing nostro accounts is a

entries.title: What is a payment versus a cover in correspondent banking?
entries.text: What is a payment versus a cover in correspondent banking? The serial and cover methods below are shown in their pre-migration MT form, because that form shows each method most clearly. Since coexistence ended on 22 November 2025, the same payment travels as a pacs.008 in serial, and as a pacs.008 plus a pacs.009 COV in cover. In correspondent banking, the payment and the cover are two different messages that together move money across borders, and the distinction matters most in the serial and cover methods. The payment message, usually an MT103, carries the full payment details to the beneficiary bank, including the debtor, the creditor, the amount, and the remittance information. The cover message, usually an MT202 COV, carries only the settlement instruction between banks, telling the

entries.title: What is a nostro fee?
entries.text: What is a nostro fee? A nostro fee is any charge a correspondent bank levies for holding and operating a nostro account on behalf of another bank. The most common nostro fees are a monthly account maintenance fee, a per transaction fee for each payment or receipt processed through the account, a fee for statements and reporting, and a fee for investigations or repairs. The correspondent may also charge for liquidity services, such as an overdraft facility, and for FX conversion when it converts funds in the account. Nostro fees are set out in the account tariff agreed when the account is opened, and they are usually billed monthly. The account holder can pay the invoice by a separate payment, or authorise the correspondent to debit the nostro account directly. In practice, many nostro

entries.title: What is SWIFT gpi in detail?
entries.text: What is SWIFT gpi in detail? SWIFT gpi, or Global Payments Innovation, is a service launched by SWIFT in 2017 to make cross border payments faster, more transparent, and easier to track. Before gpi, a sender had no way to know where a payment was, how much had been deducted, or when it would arrive. Gpi changes that by giving every payment a unique end to end transaction reference, the UETR, and by requiring every gpi bank in the chain to confirm receipt, to confirm credit, and to report any charges deducted. The payment is tracked from the sender bank to the beneficiary bank, and the sender can see each step, including the time each bank received the payment and the amount it passed on. Gpi also sets service level agreements, so banks must confirm credit within a set time, and it

entries.title: What is gpi Case Resolution?
entries.text: What is gpi Case Resolution? Gpi Case Resolution is the SWIFT gpi service that helps banks solve problems with a gpi payment quickly, by giving them a shared case file linked to the payment UETR. When a payment is delayed, missing, or incorrect, the sender bank can open a case in the gpi Tracker, and it can send a message to the bank that currently holds the payment, asking for an update. The receiving bank must respond within the gpi SLA, and all messages in the case are stored in one place, so no one has to search through emails or phone notes. The case can cover many issues, including a payment that has not been credited, a wrong amount, a missing beneficiary, or a request for a refund. Case Resolution replaces the old MT195 and MT196 investigation messages for gpi payments, although

entries.title: What is a nostro account and how does a bank use it day to day?
entries.text: What is a nostro account and how does a bank use it day to day? A nostro account is an account a bank holds with another bank in a foreign currency. For example, a UK bank like Standard Chartered holds a US dollar nostro account with a bank in New York. When the UK bank needs to pay US dollars to a beneficiary, it instructs its nostro agent in New York to pay from that account. The nostro account is funded in advance, so the bank has to predict how much it will need each day. Treasury manages this. Every morning treasury looks at the expected payment volumes, the balance in each nostro account and the funding needed. During the day, payments draw the balance down.
