If the balance runs low, treasury tops it up by buying dollars or moving funds. At end of day the bank reconciles the nostro

entries.title: How do correspondent banks work together on a cross-border payment?
entries.text: How do correspondent banks work together on a cross-border payment? A cross-border payment usually passes through more than one bank because no single bank has a presence in every country. The sending bank, for example a UK bank, sends the payment to its correspondent bank in the destination country. The correspondent is a bank that has agreed to process payments on behalf of the sending bank. The sending bank holds a nostro account with the correspondent, and the correspondent debits that account when it pays the beneficiary. If the beneficiary's bank is different from the correspondent, the payment hops again to the beneficiary's bank through the local clearing system. Each bank in the chain checks the payment, screens it and takes its fee if the charge option allows it. The payment

entries.title: A payment is sent through SWIFT to a correspondent bank. Explain the difference between the cover method and the serial method, and when you would use each.
entries.text: A payment is sent through SWIFT to a correspondent bank. Explain the difference between the cover method and the serial method, and when you would use each. In the **serial method**, the payment instruction travels from bank to bank along the whole chain. Each bank in the chain receives the **MT103** or **pacs.008**, checks it, and passes it to the next bank, until it reaches the beneficiary bank. The funds move with the instruction at each hop. This works well when the banks in the chain have direct relationships and the payment is straightforward. In the **cover method**, the instruction and the funds travel separately. The ordering bank sends the payment instruction directly to the beneficiary bank, usually as an **MT103** or **pacs.008**, and separately sends a **cover payment**, an

entries.title: Your bank uses SWIFT gpi. How does the gpi tracker know where a payment is, and what does the bank do when the tracker shows the payment stuck at an intermediary?
entries.text: Your bank uses SWIFT gpi. How does the gpi tracker know where a payment is, and what does the bank do when the tracker shows the payment stuck at an intermediary? **SWIFT gpi** gives the bank a tracker that shows where a payment is at each step. Every bank in the chain updates the tracker when it receives and forwards the payment, and the tracker shows the status, the fees deducted, and the time at each hop. When the tracker shows the payment stuck at an intermediary, the first step is to check the **UETR** and confirm the payment is genuinely stuck, not just slow. Some intermediaries take longer, especially if they run batch processing. If the payment is genuinely stuck, the bank contacts the intermediary directly, usually through a **SWIFT** message or a phone call to their operations

entries.title: A payment used the cover method. The pacs.008 instruction and the pacs.009 cover have both settled, and now the customer payment needs to be returned. How do you unwind the cover leg?
entries.text: A payment used the cover method. The pacs.008 instruction and the pacs.009 cover have both settled, and now the customer payment needs to be returned. How do you unwind the cover leg? The cover is a separate settlement, so it gets a separate return. Returning the customer payment does not automatically unwind the cover. I recognise the two legs. The **pacs.008 instruction** travelled to the beneficiary bank, while the **pacs.009 with settlement method COVE** settled the funds between correspondents. To return the payment, I need a **pacs.004** for the customer leg and a separate pacs.004 for the cover leg. I match each return to its original using the **UETR and settlement references**, so nothing gets misapplied. I watch for partial amounts, because the cover returned may differ from the

entries.title: What is a nostro account, and how does the payment hub interact with it? What happens if the nostro balance is too low?
entries.text: What is a nostro account, and how does the payment hub interact with it? What happens if the nostro balance is too low? A **nostro account** is your bank's account with a correspondent bank in a foreign currency. When you send a USD payment from India, your bank debits the customer's INR account, converts to USD, and then instructs its correspondent bank in the US to pay from the nostro account. The nostro balance goes down. When you receive a USD payment, the correspondent credits your nostro account and the balance goes up. The hub must check the **nostro balance** before releasing a payment, because if the balance is too low, the correspondent will reject it. Treasury manages nostro funding by moving money between accounts, and they need a **real time view** of every nostro balance.

entries.title: Walk through a clean SWIFT gpi payment. How does the UETR and the tracker give the customer visibility at every hop?
entries.text: Walk through a clean SWIFT gpi payment. How does the UETR and the tracker give the customer visibility at every hop? SWIFT gpi works because every payment carries a **UETR**, a unique end-to-end transaction reference, and every bank in the chain updates the status against that reference. The customer sends the payment, and the sending bank creates the UETR and includes it in the **pacs.008**. As the payment moves through each intermediary, each bank updates the **gpi Tracker** with its status, so the sending bank and the customer can see exactly where the payment is. The beneficiary bank credits the account and sends a **pacs.002** with ACSC status, which appears on the tracker. The customer can check the tracker and see the payment arrived, the amount credited, and any charges deducted

entries.title: Walk through a clean cover method payment. How do the pacs.008 instruction and the pacs.009 cover travel separately and come together at the beneficiary bank?
entries.text: Walk through a clean cover method payment. How do the pacs.008 instruction and the pacs.009 cover travel separately and come together at the beneficiary bank? The cover method works when the instruction and the money travel on separate tracks but arrive together. The sending bank creates two messages, both carrying the same **UETR**. The **pacs.008** instruction goes directly to the beneficiary bank, carrying the full customer and remittance details. The **pacs.009** with settlement method COVE goes through the correspondent chain, moving the funds between **Nostro accounts**. Each correspondent validates the cover, debits its Nostro account, and passes it on. The beneficiary bank receives the pacs.008 first, and waits for the cover to arrive. When both legs have arrived, the beneficiary

entries.title: Explain how the bank uses SWIFT gpi to track a payment when the pacs.002 has not arrived.
entries.text: Explain how the bank uses SWIFT gpi to track a payment when the pacs.002 has not arrived. **SWIFT gpi** gives the bank a tracker that is independent of the **pacs.002** flow. Every bank in the chain updates the tracker when it receives and forwards the payment, so the bank can see where the payment is even when the formal status message has not arrived. The operations team looks up the payment by its **UETR** in the gpi tracker and reads the latest status, the fees deducted at each hop, and the time the payment spent at each bank. If the tracker shows the payment was credited to the beneficiary, the bank knows the payment completed and the pacs.002 was simply lost or delayed, and the status can be updated from the tracker. If the tracker shows the payment is stuck at an intermediary, the

entries.title: The gpi tracker shows the payment as credited but the internal status is still pending. Which one is right and how do you fix it?
entries.text: The gpi tracker shows the payment as credited but the internal status is still pending. Which one is right and how do you fix it? When the **gpi tracker** and the internal status disagree, the bank must find out which one is right. The gpi tracker is updated by every bank in the chain, so it reflects what the banks in the chain reported. The internal status reflects what the bank's own **payment hub** recorded from the **pacs.002** messages it received. A mismatch usually means a pacs.002 was lost, delayed, or not processed by the hub. The operations team checks the settlement confirmation and the **camt.053** statement first. If the statement shows the funds left the bank and the gpi tracker shows the payment was credited, then the payment did complete and the internal status is wrong.

entries.title: What is MT202 COV?
entries.text: What is MT202 COV? An MT202 COV is the cover variant of the MT202 financial institution transfer, and it exists to solve a transparency problem. A plain MT202 moves money between banks for their own account, and it carries no customer details. If a plain MT202 were used to settle a customer payment, the intermediary banks and the creditor agent would see money moving with no idea who the underlying ordering customer or beneficiary was. That gap created a compliance and reconciliation risk, because banks could not screen the underlying parties or match the funds to the right customer instruction. The MT202 COV fixes this by carrying the cover details. It is sent through the correspondent chain to move the funds that settle an MT103 customer payment, and it includes the key customer

entries.title: What is a payment investigation (MT192/195/196)?
entries.text: What is a payment investigation (MT192/195/196)? A payment investigation is the formal process a bank uses to find out what happened to a payment that is missing, delayed, or incorrect, and in the MT system it uses three messages. MT192 is a Request for Cancellation, sent when the sender wants a payment stopped before it settles. MT195 is a general Query, sent when the sender wants information, for example asking the beneficiary bank whether the payment was credited and on what date. MT196 is the answer to a query, sent by the bank that received the MT195, giving the status of the payment. Together, these messages form the investigation trail. In ISO 20022, the same work is done with camt.056 for a cancellation request, camt.028 for a status report, and camt.029 for the resolution of an

entries.title: A beneficiary calls to say they cannot match a payment to an invoice because the remittance information is cut off. The MT103 field 70 only shows part of the invoice number. What went wrong and how do you prevent it?
entries.text: A beneficiary calls to say they cannot match a payment to an invoice because the remittance information is cut off. The MT103 field 70 only shows part of the invoice number. What went wrong and how do you prevent it? **Field 70** of the MT103, the remittance information field, holds a maximum of **four lines of 35 characters**, and anything longer is cut off. The sending bank put a long invoice reference into field 70, the message carried only the first 140 characters, and the beneficiary received a truncated reference they cannot match. The fix for this payment is to send the full reference to the beneficiary bank by a separate message, such as an **MT199** free format message, quoting the original MT103 reference so the beneficiary bank can link the two. The prevention is to use

entries.title: A corporate customer asks why their MT103 carries a field 72, sender to receiver information, and whether they can use it to add instructions for the beneficiary bank. Explain what field 72 is for and what it must never contain.
entries.text: A corporate customer asks why their MT103 carries a field 72, sender to receiver information, and whether they can use it to add instructions for the beneficiary bank. Explain what field 72 is for and what it must never contain. **Field 72** is the sender to receiver information field in the MT103. It carries instructions from the sending bank to the receiving bank, such as asking the beneficiary bank to phone the beneficiary, to hold the payment for collection, or to apply a specific value date. It is bank to bank information, and it is not part of the payment instruction to the beneficiary. The corporate customer cannot use field 72 to send a message to the beneficiary, because the beneficiary bank may not pass it on, and the beneficiary will never see it. Field 72 must never contain

entries.title: A payment travels through three correspondent banks. The operations team is unsure whether to send an MT202 or an MT202 COV to move the funds. Explain the difference and when each one is used.
entries.text: A payment travels through three correspondent banks. The operations team is unsure whether to send an MT202 or an MT202 COV to move the funds. Explain the difference and when each one is used. An **MT202** is a general financial institution transfer. It moves money between banks for their own account and carries no customer details. An **MT202 COV** is the cover variant, and it carries the underlying customer information from the related **MT103**, such as the ordering customer and the beneficiary. The rule is simple: if the funds being moved settle a customer payment, use the **MT202 COV**, because every bank in the chain needs to see who the underlying customer is for **sanctions screening** and reconciliation. If the funds are the bank own money, for example a treasury transfer or a

entries.title: A treasury analyst asks for an MT910 and an MT900 to check whether two nostro payments settled yesterday. Explain what these two messages are and how the analyst uses them.
entries.text: A treasury analyst asks for an MT910 and an MT900 to check whether two nostro payments settled yesterday. Explain what these two messages are and how the analyst uses them. An **MT900** is a confirmation of debit. It tells the account owner that their account has been debited, with the amount, the currency, the value date, and the reference of the original instruction. An **MT910** is a confirmation of credit, and it tells the account owner that their account has been credited, with the same details. The two messages are always sent by the **account servicing institution**, which is the bank that holds the account, to the account owner. The treasury analyst uses them to confirm that a payment actually left or arrived in the **nostro account**. If the bank sent a payment instruction and

entries.title: A reconciliation analyst is unsure whether to use the MT940 or the MT942 for intraday nostro checking. Explain the difference between the two statements and when each one is used.
entries.text: A reconciliation analyst is unsure whether to use the MT940 or the MT942 for intraday nostro checking. Explain the difference between the two statements and when each one is used. The **MT940** is the customer statement message. It is sent at **end of day** and gives the full statement for the account: the opening balance, every debit and credit during the day, and the closing balance. It is the official record used for end of day reconciliation. The **MT942** is the interim transaction report. It is sent **during the day**, often several times, and gives the transactions since the last report, with an interim balance. The analyst uses the MT942 for **intraday monitoring**, to check that expected payments have arrived, to spot unexpected debits early, and to manage liquidity during the

entries.title: A payment has not arrived after three days and the beneficiary bank is not responding to emails. The operations team wants to send an MT199 to chase it. Explain what an MT199 is, when it is the right message, and when a different message should be used instead.
entries.text: A payment has not arrived after three days and the beneficiary bank is not responding to emails. The operations team wants to send an MT199 to chase it. Explain what an MT199 is, when it is the right message, and when a different message should be used instead. An **MT199** is a free format message. It is the general purpose message banks use to send information that does not fit into a structured message type. It is the right message when you need to ask a question, give information, or chase a payment, and there is no specific message type for what you want to say. For a missing payment, the MT199 should quote the original payment **reference**, the **UETR**, the amount, the currency, the value date, and the date it was sent, so the receiving bank can find it without asking for more

entries.title: A customer asks their bank to cancel a payment that was sent yesterday. The bank sends an MT192 request for cancellation, but the beneficiary bank replies that the funds have already been credited to the beneficiary. What happens now?
entries.text: A customer asks their bank to cancel a payment that was sent yesterday. The bank sends an MT192 request for cancellation, but the beneficiary bank replies that the funds have already been credited to the beneficiary. What happens now? An **MT192** is a request for cancellation. It asks the receiving bank to stop the payment and return the funds, but it is only a request, not an instruction the receiving bank must obey. If the funds have already been **credited to the beneficiary**, the beneficiary bank cannot simply take the money back, because the beneficiary now owns it. The beneficiary bank should reply explaining the position, and the sending bank must then ask the beneficiary to agree to return the funds voluntarily. This is done through a **recall**, usually a **camt.056** message,

entries.title: A bank sends an MT195 to ask a correspondent bank about a missing payment. Three days later there is still no reply. Explain the MT195 and MT196 flow, what the deadlines are, and what the bank should do next.
entries.text: A bank sends an MT195 to ask a correspondent bank about a missing payment. Three days later there is still no reply. Explain the MT195 and MT196 flow, what the deadlines are, and what the bank should do next. The **MT195** is an enquiry message. A bank sends it to ask another bank a question about a payment, such as whether it was received, whether it was credited, or why it has not arrived. The receiving bank is expected to reply with an **MT196**, which is the answer to the enquiry. The MT195 should include the original payment **reference**, the **UETR**, the amount, the currency, and the value date, so the receiving bank can identify the payment immediately. There is no universal deadline in the SWIFT rules, but market practice and **gpi service levels** expect a reply within one to

entries.title: A corporate treasurer wants to send 500 salary payments to their bank in a single instruction instead of 500 separate payments. Explain how the MT101 helps and what the bank does with it.
entries.text: A corporate treasurer wants to send 500 salary payments to their bank in a single instruction instead of 500 separate payments. Explain how the MT101 helps and what the bank does with it. The **MT101** is a request for transfer. It is the message a corporate customer sends to their bank to instruct multiple payments in a single message. Instead of sending 500 separate instructions, the treasurer sends one MT101 containing all 500 payment instructions, each with its own beneficiary, account, amount, and value date. The bank validates the MT101, checks that the customer account has enough funds, and then processes each instruction inside it, usually by generating individual **MT103** messages for the cross border payments or domestic clearing instructions for the local ones. The MT101 is

entries.title: An operations analyst sees an MT205 and an MT202 for the same amount on the same day and thinks it is a duplicate. Explain the difference between the two messages and why both can be legitimate.
entries.text: An operations analyst sees an MT205 and an MT202 for the same amount on the same day and thinks it is a duplicate. Explain the difference between the two messages and why both can be legitimate. An **MT202** is a general financial institution transfer, used to move money between banks. An **MT205** is a financial institution transfer **execution**, and it is used when the transfer is executed by a financial institution on behalf of another financial institution. The difference is in the role of the sender. The MT202 is sent by the bank that owns the funds. The MT205 is sent by a bank that has been instructed by another bank to execute the transfer, for example when a bank uses a **correspondent** to move funds on its behalf. Both messages can appear for the same underlying movement

entries.title: The MT950 end of day statement shows three entries that do not appear in the bank nostro ledger. The amounts are small but the reconciliation cannot be signed off. Walk through how you investigate the break.
entries.text: The MT950 end of day statement shows three entries that do not appear in the bank nostro ledger. The amounts are small but the reconciliation cannot be signed off. Walk through how you investigate the break. Start by confirming the **MT950** is the correct statement for the correct account and the correct value date, because a wrong account or a wrong date is the most common cause of a phantom break. Next, pull the **MT900 and MT910** confirmations for the day and check whether the three entries appear there. If they do, the entries are real and the nostro ledger is missing them. If they do not, the entries may be **charges, interest, or fees** applied by the account servicing bank, which appear on the statement but are not payment instructions and therefore never hit the payment ledger.

entries.title: A bank agrees an FX rate with a customer for a cross border payment, but the MT300 confirmation from the counterparty shows a different rate and a different value date. What has gone wrong and how do you resolve it?
entries.text: A bank agrees an FX rate with a customer for a cross border payment, but the MT300 confirmation from the counterparty shows a different rate and a different value date. What has gone wrong and how do you resolve it? An **MT300** is a foreign exchange confirmation. It is the message one party sends to the other to confirm the details of an FX deal: the currencies, the amounts, the **exchange rate**, the **value date**, and the settlement instructions. If the MT300 shows a different rate and a different value date from what the bank agreed with the customer, there is a **confirmation mismatch**, and the deal cannot settle as it stands. The first step is to check the original deal record: the dealer ticket, the recorded conversation, or the electronic trading platform log. That record is the

entries.title: A customer reports a cheque as lost in the post and asks the bank to stop it. The bank sends an MT111. Explain what this message does and what the customer should expect.
entries.text: A customer reports a cheque as lost in the post and asks the bank to stop it. The bank sends an MT111. Explain what this message does and what the customer should expect. An **MT111** is a stop payment of a cheque. It is the message a bank sends to tell another bank, or to instruct its own systems, that a specific cheque must not be paid. The message carries the **cheque number**, the **amount**, the **currency**, the **account number**, and the **payee name**, so the paying bank can identify the exact cheque. Once the stop is in place, if the cheque is presented for payment, the paying bank will return it unpaid with a reason code indicating the stop. The customer should expect the stop to take effect quickly, usually the same day, but they should also know that a stop does not guarantee

entries.title: An MT103 arrives with field 50, the ordering customer field, containing only a name and no account number or address. The payment is held for compliance review. Explain why the field is incomplete, what the risks are, and how the payment gets released.
entries.text: An MT103 arrives with field 50, the ordering customer field, containing only a name and no account number or address. The payment is held for compliance review. Explain why the field is incomplete, what the risks are, and how the payment gets released. **Field 50** in the MT103 must identify the ordering customer fully. Under the **Funds Transfer Regulation** and the **travel rule**, the ordering customer information must include the name, the account number, and the address or another identifier, so that every bank in the chain can screen the real sender. A field 50 with only a name is incomplete, and the receiving bank cannot screen the payment properly, cannot identify the sender if there is a sanctions hit, and cannot return the funds to the right account if the payment is rejected.

entries.title: During the MT to MX migration, a bank converts an MT103 into a pacs.008. The conversion drops the remittance information because the MT103 field 70 is longer than the pacs.008 allows. Explain the data problem and how the bank handles it during coexistence.
entries.text: During the MT to MX migration, a bank converts an MT103 into a pacs.008. The conversion drops the remittance information because the MT103 field 70 is longer than the pacs.008 allows. Explain the data problem and how the bank handles it during coexistence. This is a **data truncation** problem, and it is one of the most common issues in the **MT to MX migration**. The MT103 field 70 allows four lines of 35 characters, and the pacs.008 unstructured remittance information allows 140 characters, so in theory they match. But the MT103 also carries information in other fields that have no direct equivalent in the pacs.008, and the **CBPR+ usage guidelines** define exactly how each MT field maps to the MX structure. When the mapping cannot carry all the data, the bank has three options. First,

entries.title: What is ISO 20022?
entries.text: What is ISO 20022? ISO 20022 is the global standard for exchanging electronic messages between financial institutions. It defines a common language that banks, payment systems, market infrastructures and corporates use to describe payments, securities, trade and card transactions. Instead of each system inventing its own format, ISO 20022 provides a shared dictionary of business concepts, such as debtor, creditor, amount and value date, plus a set of message definitions built on top of that dictionary. The standard is maintained by ISO Technical Committee 68 and is syntax independent in principle, but in practice almost all ISO 20022 messages today are expressed in XML. Each message type has a name, such as pacs.008 or pain.001, and a published schema that spells out exactly which

entries.title: What is CBPR+?
entries.text: What is CBPR+? CBPR+ stands for Cross Border Payments and Reporting Plus. It is the working group that defines how ISO 20022 is used for cross border payments on the SWIFT network. ISO 20022 itself is a broad standard with many optional elements, and different banks could implement it in different ways. CBPR+ exists to prevent that fragmentation: it publishes usage guidelines that say exactly which elements are mandatory, which are optional, and which rules apply for cross border payments, so that a pacs.008 sent by a bank in Singapore is understood the same way by a bank in Germany. The group is made up of banks, market infrastructures and SWIFT, and its guidelines are the practical rulebook for the migration. They cover message versions, character sets, address formats, charge bearer

entries.title: A payment engine produces ISO 20022 pacs.008 messages but the downstream clearing system still expects MT103. How do you handle the transformation, and what is the biggest risk?
entries.text: A payment engine produces ISO 20022 pacs.008 messages but the downstream clearing system still expects MT103. How do you handle the transformation, and what is the biggest risk? Start from the message the engine produces and the message the clearing house expects. The engine works in **ISO 20022** and produces a **pacs.008**. The clearing house may still expect **MT103** on the SWIFT network, or it may accept pacs.008 natively. The transformation happens in a **mapping layer** between the engine and the clearing interface. Every field in pacs.008 must map to a field in MT103, and the mapping is not one to one. For example, pacs.008 carries structured debtor and creditor addresses with separate fields for street, town and country. MT103 field 59 has a limited character set and no

entries.title: How do you explain ISO 20022 migration to a business stakeholder?
entries.text: How do you explain ISO 20022 migration to a business stakeholder? I explain ISO 20022 migration as a change of language, not a change of banking. Today the bank speaks one language for payments, the old MT messages, and it needs to learn a new language, the MX messages. The new language is richer: it carries more information, structured addresses, longer references and clearer data. The migration means the bank must be able to send and receive the new messages, translate between the old and the new during the transition, and handle the cases where the other bank has not migrated yet. I explain the business impact in plain terms: the new messages let the bank carry more information about a payment, which improves reconciliation and reduces exceptions. I explain the timeline: the migration

entries.title: What is SEPA?
entries.text: What is SEPA? SEPA, the Single Euro Payments Area, is the framework that makes euro payments work the same way across Europe. Before SEPA, a payment from Germany to France was a cross border payment with different formats, timelines and charges from a domestic payment. SEPA harmonised that: within the SEPA area, which covers the eurozone plus several other European countries, a euro payment is treated the same whether it stays inside one country or crosses a border. The framework is governed by the European Payments Council and supported by EU regulation. SEPA defines three main payment instruments. SEPA Credit Transfer, SCT, is the standard euro credit transfer, where the payer instructs their bank to send money to the beneficiary. SEPA Direct Debit, SDD, lets a creditor collect money

entries.title: What is SEPA Instant?
entries.text: What is SEPA Instant? SEPA Instant, formally SEPA Instant Credit Transfer or SCT Inst, is the real time version of the SEPA Credit Transfer. It is a scheme from the European Payments Council that lets euro payments settle within seconds, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, between accounts in the SEPA area. The target is a maximum of ten seconds from the payer bank sending the payment to the beneficiary bank confirming receipt, and most payments complete much faster. The scheme went live in 2017 and has grown steadily as more banks and payment service providers joined. The mechanics are straightforward in concept and demanding in practice. The payer bank sends an SCT Inst instruction, the beneficiary bank must respond within the time limit, confirming that the account exists and the funds

entries.title: Your bank is a direct participant in SEPA. A customer sends a SEPA Instant payment. Walk through what happens from instruction to settlement in under 10 seconds.
entries.text: Your bank is a direct participant in SEPA. A customer sends a SEPA Instant payment. Walk through what happens from instruction to settlement in under 10 seconds. The customer submits the payment through the channel, and the **payment hub** validates it, checks sanctions, and confirms the beneficiary bank is reachable for **SEPA Instant**. The hub formats the payment as a **pacs.008** and sends it to the beneficiary bank through the **SEPA Instant** clearing system, usually **TIPS** or a private clearing house. The whole journey must complete within 10 seconds, and the clearing system enforces a 20-second maximum. The beneficiary bank receives the pacs.008, validates the account, and must respond within the time limit. If it accepts, it credits the customer immediately and sends back a

entries.title: Walk through a clean SEPA credit transfer, from the customer instruction to the beneficiary credit. What makes the SEPA scheme work so smoothly?
entries.text: Walk through a clean SEPA credit transfer, from the customer instruction to the beneficiary credit. What makes the SEPA scheme work so smoothly? A SEPA credit transfer is clean because the scheme is standardised. The customer submits the instruction through their bank, and the bank validates it, checking the **IBAN** format, the balance, and the sanctions lists. The bank sends a **pacs.008** to the beneficiary bank, either directly or through a clearing system. The pacs.008 carries the IBAN, the amount, the end-to-end reference, and the remittance information. The beneficiary bank receives it, validates the IBAN, credits the customer account, and sends back a **pacs.002** with ACSC status. For a standard SEPA credit transfer, the funds arrive by the next business day. For a **SEPA

entries.title: A customer sends a SEPA credit transfer and it comes back rejected with reason code AC01. The customer insists the IBAN is correct. Explain what AC01 means and how you help the customer fix it.
entries.text: A customer sends a SEPA credit transfer and it comes back rejected with reason code AC01. The customer insists the IBAN is correct. Explain what AC01 means and how you help the customer fix it. **AC01** means incorrect account number. The receiving bank checked the **IBAN** in the payment and found that it does not match a valid account. The customer may have typed the IBAN correctly as they see it, but the problem is usually a small error: a digit transposed, a character missing, or the IBAN copied from an old document after the account changed. The first step is to ask the customer to check the IBAN against the source, such as the beneficiary invoice or the beneficiary bank statement, character by character. The IBAN has a built in **check digit**, so a typing error can be detected, but

entries.title: A customer sends a SEPA Instant payment. The money leaves their account, but the beneficiary bank does not confirm within 10 seconds and the payment times out. Explain what happens to the money and what the bank must do.
entries.text: A customer sends a SEPA Instant payment. The money leaves their account, but the beneficiary bank does not confirm within 10 seconds and the payment times out. Explain what happens to the money and what the bank must do. A **SEPA Instant** payment must complete within **10 seconds**. If the beneficiary bank does not confirm receipt in that time, the payment **times out**. The money has already left the payer account, so the bank must now find out what happened to it. The payer bank sends an **investigation** message to the beneficiary bank, asking whether the payment was credited, rejected, or never received. There are three outcomes. If the beneficiary bank credited the payment but the confirmation was delayed, the payment is complete and the payer bank tells the customer it arrived. If

entries.title: A customer sees a direct debit on their account that they do not recognise. They say they never signed a mandate. Explain how a SEPA Direct Debit works, what the customer rights are, and how the bank handles the dispute.
entries.text: A customer sees a direct debit on their account that they do not recognise. They say they never signed a mandate. Explain how a SEPA Direct Debit works, what the customer rights are, and how the bank handles the dispute. A **SEPA Direct Debit**, or SDD, lets a creditor, such as a utility company, collect money from the debtor account, but only if the debtor has signed a **mandate** giving permission. The mandate states the creditor name, the amount or the collection pattern, and the debtor account. Without a valid mandate, the collection is not authorised. If the customer says they never signed a mandate, the bank must ask the creditor bank for a copy of the **mandate** and check it against the customer details. The customer has strong rights: under the SEPA rules, they can request a

entries.title: A SEPA Instant payment is credited to the beneficiary, but the payer then discovers the payment was sent to the wrong account because of a typing error. The payer asks for the money back. Explain the recall process and why the beneficiary can refuse.
entries.text: A SEPA Instant payment is credited to the beneficiary, but the payer then discovers the payment was sent to the wrong account because of a typing error. The payer asks for the money back. Explain the recall process and why the beneficiary can refuse. A **SEPA Instant** payment is **irrevocable** once it is credited. The payer cannot cancel it through the payment system, because the money has already moved and the beneficiary bank has confirmed receipt. The only route is a **recall**, which is a request from the payer bank to the beneficiary bank, asking the beneficiary to return the funds voluntarily. The beneficiary bank contacts the beneficiary and explains the situation, but the beneficiary is **not obliged** to return the money. If the beneficiary agrees, the funds are sent back,

entries.title: A customer is about to send a SEPA payment and sees a warning that the payee name does not match the account number. The name is almost right, just one letter different. Explain what verification of payee does and what the customer should do.
entries.text: A customer is about to send a SEPA payment and sees a warning that the payee name does not match the account number. The name is almost right, just one letter different. Explain what verification of payee does and what the customer should do. **Verification of payee** is a check that runs before a SEPA payment is sent. The bank compares the **payee name** the payer typed against the name registered to the **IBAN**, and it returns one of three results: a **match**, a **close match**, or **no match**. A close match means the name is almost right, often because of a spelling difference, a missing middle name, or a company trading name instead of its legal name. The customer should stop and check: is this the right person, is the IBAN copied correctly, and does the close match make sense? If

entries.title: A customer submits a SEPA credit transfer on Friday evening and expects the money to arrive the same day. Explain how SEPA value dates and cut-off times work, and when the beneficiary will actually be paid.
entries.text: A customer submits a SEPA credit transfer on Friday evening and expects the money to arrive the same day. Explain how SEPA value dates and cut-off times work, and when the beneficiary will actually be paid. A standard **SEPA Credit Transfer**, or SCT, is not instant. It is processed on **business days**, and the value date, the day the beneficiary is credited, depends on when the payment is submitted and on the **cut-off time** of the payer bank. If the customer submits the payment on Friday evening after the cut-off, the bank will process it on the next business day, which is Monday, and the beneficiary will be credited on Monday, or Tuesday if the beneficiary bank takes a day to process it. The SEPA rule is that the payment must reach the beneficiary bank by the end of the next business

entries.title: A corporate customer needs to pay a supplier 150,000 euro immediately, but their bank SEPA Instant limit is 100,000 euro. Explain the options and the risks of splitting the payment.
entries.text: A corporate customer needs to pay a supplier 150,000 euro immediately, but their bank SEPA Instant limit is 100,000 euro. Explain the options and the risks of splitting the payment. The **SEPA Instant** scheme has a maximum amount per transaction, and many banks set their own lower limit, often **100,000 euro**, for risk and liquidity reasons. The customer has three options. First, ask the bank to raise the **limit** temporarily for this payment, which the bank may do after checking the customer and the beneficiary. Second, split the payment into two **SEPA Instant** payments, for example 100,000 euro and 50,000 euro. This works, but it creates a **reconciliation** problem, because the supplier receives two payments instead of one and must match both to the same invoice. Third, send the

entries.title: A biller collects a SEPA Direct Debit and the customer bank returns it. The biller wants to know why. Explain the SDD R-transactions: return, refund, reversal, and reject, and what each one means for the biller.
entries.text: A biller collects a SEPA Direct Debit and the customer bank returns it. The biller wants to know why. Explain the SDD R-transactions: return, refund, reversal, and reject, and what each one means for the biller. **R-transactions** are the exception messages in **SEPA Direct Debit**. Each one means something different, and the biller must handle them differently. A **reject** happens before the collection is processed, usually because the debtor account is closed, the IBAN is wrong, or the mandate is invalid. The biller receives the reject quickly and can fix the data. A **return** happens after the collection, because there were insufficient funds, or the debtor bank refused the debit. The biller can try to collect again, but should check with the debtor first. A **refund** is requested

entries.title: A bank in Sweden, which is in SEPA but does not use the euro, wants to offer SEPA Instant payments to its customers. Explain the challenges and what the bank must build.
entries.text: A bank in Sweden, which is in SEPA but does not use the euro, wants to offer SEPA Instant payments to its customers. Explain the challenges and what the bank must build. Sweden is in **SEPA** but does not use the euro, which creates a specific challenge: the customer account is in **Swedish krona**, but the SEPA Instant payment must settle in **euro**. The bank must therefore offer a **currency conversion** as part of the payment, converting krona to euro at the point of sending, and it must show the customer the exchange rate and the converted amount before they confirm. The bank must also be **reachable** for SEPA Instant, which means connecting to a clearing system such as **TIPS** or the EBA Clearing RT1 system, and being available 24 hours a day, because instant payments never sleep.

entries.title: A fraudster tricks a customer into sending a SEPA Instant payment to a mule account. The money is moved on within minutes. Explain why instant payments are attractive to fraudsters and what banks do to stop it.
entries.text: A fraudster tricks a customer into sending a SEPA Instant payment to a mule account. The money is moved on within minutes. Explain why instant payments are attractive to fraudsters and what banks do to stop it. **SEPA Instant** payments are attractive to fraudsters because they are **irrevocable** and they settle in **seconds**. Once the money is credited to the mule account, the fraudster can move it on to another account, withdraw it, or convert it, all before the victim realises they have been tricked. There is no time to stop the payment, because there is no clearing window to intervene in. Banks fight this in three ways. First, **verification of payee** checks the payee name against the IBAN before the payment is sent, and warns the customer if there is a mismatch. Second,

entries.title: Your bank is choosing how to settle SEPA Instant payments: through TIPS or through EBA Clearing RT1. Explain the difference between the two and how the bank decides.
entries.text: Your bank is choosing how to settle SEPA Instant payments: through TIPS or through EBA Clearing RT1. Explain the difference between the two and how the bank decides. **TIPS**, the TARGET Instant Payment Settlement service, is run by the **Eurosystem** and settles SEPA Instant payments in **central bank money**, in real time, 24 hours a day. Each payment is settled individually and immediately, with finality at the moment of settlement. **RT1**, run by **EBA Clearing**, is a clearing system that also settles in real time, but it uses a **prefunded** model: participating banks hold funds in a technical account, and payments are settled against those prefunded balances. The difference matters for **liquidity** and for **risk**. With TIPS, the bank needs liquidity in its central bank account,

entries.title: Your bank still runs a legacy domestic payment format alongside SEPA. The board wants to retire the legacy format and move everything to ISO 20022. Explain the migration and the risks of running two formats in parallel.
entries.text: Your bank still runs a legacy domestic payment format alongside SEPA. The board wants to retire the legacy format and move everything to ISO 20022. Explain the migration and the risks of running two formats in parallel. Migrating from a **legacy domestic format** to **ISO 20022** means changing the message format for every payment the bank sends and receives. The legacy format is usually a fixed length file or a proprietary message, while ISO 20022 uses **XML** with structured data, including structured addresses, purpose codes, and rich remittance information. The migration has three parts. First, the bank must **map** every field in the legacy format to the ISO 20022 equivalent, and decide what to do with fields that have no equivalent. Second, the bank must update its **customer

entries.title: What is settlement risk?
entries.text: What is settlement risk? Settlement risk is the risk that one party to a payment or transaction does not deliver what it owes when it is due, even though the other party has already delivered its side. In payments, it is the risk that a bank credits its customer or releases goods or securities before it has actually received the funds from the sending bank, and then the sending bank fails to pay. A simple example shows the problem. Bank A sends a payment instruction to Bank B, and Bank B credits its customer immediately in the expectation that Bank A will settle later that day. If Bank A becomes insolvent before settlement, Bank B has paid out money it will never receive. Bank B bears the loss, and its customer keeps the funds. Settlement risk is largest in systems where there is a long

entries.title: What is CHIPS netting?
entries.text: What is CHIPS netting? CHIPS netting is the process by which the Clearing House Interbank Payments System offsets payments between banks so that only the net amount needs to be settled at the end of the day. During the operating day, banks send payment instructions to CHIPS, which records them in a central queue. CHIPS does not settle each payment immediately. Instead, it keeps a running total of what each bank owes to every other bank. If Bank A owes Bank B 100 million dollars and Bank B owes Bank A 80 million dollars, the net position is 20 million dollars from A to B. CHIPS also uses a liquidity saving mechanism. It holds payments in a queue and releases them when an offsetting payment arrives, so that the net amount is smaller and less liquidity is needed. Each participant prefunds an

entries.title: How does a bank manage cut-off times across multiple clearing systems?
entries.text: How does a bank manage cut-off times across multiple clearing systems? A large bank connects to many clearing systems: Faster Payments, CHAPS, BACS, SEPA, Fedwire, CHIPS and SWIFT. Each one has its own cut off time, the last moment a payment can be sent and still settle that day. The bank manages this with a cut off calendar. For each clearing system, the bank records the cut off time, the time zone and the value date rule. The payment hub reads this calendar when it routes a payment. If a payment arrives before the cut off, it is sent the same day. If it arrives after the cut off, the hub either holds it for the next day or rejects it, depending on the product rules. The customer is told the value date so they know when the beneficiary will receive the money. The complexity comes when a

entries.title: How does your bank actually connect to a clearing house? Explain the technical path from the payment hub to the clearing system.
entries.text: How does your bank actually connect to a clearing house? Explain the technical path from the payment hub to the clearing system. The bank does not send payments directly from the branch or the app to the clearing house. The **channel** captures the instruction and passes it to the **payment hub**. The hub is the single control point. It validates the instruction, checks sanctions and fraud, applies the charge option, and decides the clearing route. Then it formats the payment into the clearing system's message standard, for example **ISO 20022 pacs.008** for most modern clearing systems, or the local format the clearing house requires. From the hub, the payment travels over a secure connection to the clearing house. For **SWIFT**, that connection is the SWIFT network, and the bank's

entries.title: The clearing house is down during a settlement window. What does the bank do with payments queued for that window?
entries.text: The clearing house is down during a settlement window. What does the bank do with payments queued for that window? The first step is to confirm the outage is real and not a problem on the bank's own side. The operations team checks the clearing house status page and contacts the clearing house service desk. Once confirmed, the **payment hub** holds all payments due for that window in the queue. Nothing is released, because there is nowhere to send it. The bank must not try an alternative route without checking, because the payment may already have been accepted by the clearing house before it went down. The bank then communicates. Clients with time-critical payments are told the clearing house is down and given a revised estimate. Treasury is told, because the funding plan for the day

entries.title: Your bank has a large FX payment settling through CLS. How does CLS remove settlement risk, and what happens if one leg fails?
entries.text: Your bank has a large FX payment settling through CLS. How does CLS remove settlement risk, and what happens if one leg fails? **CLS**, Continuous Linked Settlement, removes **Herstatt risk**, which is the risk that one side of an FX trade settles and the other side does not. The bank submits both legs of the FX payment to CLS. CLS holds both legs and settles them simultaneously, payment versus payment. If one leg cannot settle, neither leg settles. That is the core protection. The bank funds its CLS account in each currency before the settlement window, and CLS nets the flows so the bank only funds the net amount, not the gross. If one leg fails, CLS does not settle the trade. The bank is told which currency is short and by how much. The bank then has to fund the short leg, usually by

entries.title: A payment is stuck in the RTGS queue because the bank does not have enough balance. How does queue resolution work, and what can the bank do to release it?
entries.text: A payment is stuck in the RTGS queue because the bank does not have enough balance. How does queue resolution work, and what can the bank do to release it? When a bank sends a payment through **RTGS** and its **central bank settlement account** does not have enough balance, the payment does not fail. It sits in the **RTGS queue**. The central bank's queue resolution mechanism looks at all queued payments across all banks and tries to find a set that can settle together, because one bank's outgoing payment is another bank's incoming payment. If a group of queued payments can be settled by offsetting them against each other, the central bank releases them as a batch. This is called **gridlock resolution** or multilateral offset. The bank can also act on its own. It can add funds to the

entries.title: The bank receives a settlement confirmation from the clearing house. What does the bank do with it, and how does it update the payment status?
entries.text: The bank receives a settlement confirmation from the clearing house. What does the bank do with it, and how does it update the payment status? The settlement confirmation arrives as a status message, usually a **pacs.002** with **ACSC** status, meaning the payment has been accepted and settled. The **payment hub** receives it and matches it to the original payment using the message reference and the **UETR**. The hub checks that the amount, currency, and value date match the original instruction. If they match, the hub updates the payment status to settled and posts the accounting entries, debiting the customer account and crediting the settlement account. The hub then pushes the status update to the **channel**, so the customer can see the payment as completed. If the payment was a

entries.title: A payment is sent with the wrong settlement method in the pacs.008. What goes wrong downstream, and how do you fix it?
entries.text: A payment is sent with the wrong settlement method in the pacs.008. What goes wrong downstream, and how do you fix it? The **settlement method** in the **pacs.008** tells the clearing system how the payment should settle, for example through the central bank, through a correspondent, or through a clearing house. If it is wrong, the payment can go to the wrong settlement account or be rejected by the clearing system. The first sign is usually a **pacs.002** with an **RJCT** status, or the payment sitting in the hub with no settlement confirmation. The operations team checks the pacs.008 against the static data for that corridor. Each corridor, meaning each currency and destination combination, has a defined settlement method, and the hub should have picked it automatically. If the static

entries.title: A clearing house rejects a batch of payments for a formatting error. How does the bank find the error, fix it, and resubmit?
entries.text: A clearing house rejects a batch of payments for a formatting error. How does the bank find the error, fix it, and resubmit? When a clearing house rejects a batch, the first step is to read the rejection message carefully. It usually names the error, such as a schema failure, an invalid field, or a limit breach. The operations team pulls the rejected file and identifies which payments failed and which, if any, were accepted. The accepted ones are left alone, because resubmitting them would create duplicates. The team then finds the root cause. If it is a **formatting error**, the fix is in the hub's message mapping for that clearing system. If it is a data error, such as an invalid **BIC** or a missing mandatory field, the fix is in the source data or the validation rules. The failed

entries.title: A customer payment is due to settle on a day the clearing house is closed for a holiday. What happens to the value date and the customer?
entries.text: A customer payment is due to settle on a day the clearing house is closed for a holiday. What happens to the value date and the customer? When the clearing house is closed for a holiday, no settlement happens that day. The **payment hub** checks the clearing calendar before accepting the payment and warns the client that the value date will move. If the payment was already submitted, the hub holds it in the queue and releases it on the next working day. The value date becomes the next working day, and the customer is told the new date. The bank must be careful with the customer promise. If the client was told the payment would settle on the holiday, that promise is now broken, and the bank should have caught it at submission. The channel should show the correct value date before the

entries.title: Explain settlement finality. At what point can the bank be certain the money has moved and cannot be reversed by the clearing house?
entries.text: Explain settlement finality. At what point can the bank be certain the money has moved and cannot be reversed by the clearing house? **Settlement finality** means the payment has settled and cannot be reversed by the clearing system. For **RTGS** payments, finality happens the moment the payment settles across the **central bank settlement account**. The sending bank's account is debited and the receiving bank's account is credited, and that movement is final. The receiving bank can then credit its customer knowing the funds are genuinely there. For other systems, finality happens at different points. In **Faster Payments**, the beneficiary bank credits the customer immediately, but the interbank settlement is deferred, so the bank is taking a small risk until the net settlement cycle

entries.title: The clearing system is down during the settlement window. Payments are queuing in the payment hub and the cut-off is approaching. How do you handle a clearing system outage?
entries.text: The clearing system is down during the settlement window. Payments are queuing in the payment hub and the cut-off is approaching. How do you handle a clearing system outage? A clearing outage means payments cannot settle, but they can still be accepted, validated, and queued. The first job is to protect the queue and keep customers informed. I confirm the outage through the clearing system status page and the **pacs.002** responses, because a missing response can look like an outage when it is actually a timeout. I check which payments are affected, separating those already settled from those still queued. For queued payments, I verify that the payment hub is holding them safely with their original value dates and instructions intact. I switch on **manual monitoring** of the queue,

entries.title: How does a bank connect to a clearing house? What are the components of that connection, and what happens when it goes down?
entries.text: How does a bank connect to a clearing house? What are the components of that connection, and what happens when it goes down? A clearing house connection is not a single link, it is a set of components that must all work together. First, the **network connection** itself, usually SWIFT for cross border or a domestic network for local clearing. Second, the **message interface** that converts the hub's internal format to the clearing house format, ISO 20022 for modern clearing, MT for legacy. Third, the **security layer**: certificates, encryption and mutual authentication so the clearing house knows the message really came from your bank. Fourth, the **session management**: the connection must stay alive, handle logon and logoff, and recover from a dropped session without losing messages.

entries.title: How do cut-off times work across different clearing systems and time zones? What happens to a payment that arrives after cut-off?
entries.text: How do cut-off times work across different clearing systems and time zones? What happens to a payment that arrives after cut-off? Cut-off times are the deadlines after which a payment cannot settle on the same day. Every clearing system has its own cut-off, and the hub must know them all. The design uses a **cut-off calendar** that stores the cut-off time for each clearing system, each currency, and each value date. When a payment arrives, the hub checks the current time against the cut-off for its route. If the payment arrives before cut-off, it goes for same day settlement. If it arrives after, the hub has two choices: queue it for the next business day, or reject it and tell the customer to resubmit. Most banks queue it and tell the customer the new value date. The tricky part is

entries.title: How does same-day settlement work? Walk through a high-value payment that is submitted, settled, and credited on the same day.
entries.text: How does same-day settlement work? Walk through a high-value payment that is submitted, settled, and credited on the same day. Same-day settlement works because every part of the chain is aligned to the same clock. The customer submits the payment before the published **cut-off**, and the channel accepts it. The payment hub validates it immediately and sends the **pacs.008** to the clearing system. The clearing system processes it in its next settlement cycle. For a high-value system like **RTGS**, settlement is real time, so the funds move between the banks within minutes. For a batch system, the payment settles in the next batch window, which is still the same day if the cut-off was met. The beneficiary bank receives the instruction and the settlement, credits the customer account, and

entries.title: A corporate customer needs to send a 10 million pound payment today and it must settle today. Walk through how a high-value payment is processed cleanly.
entries.text: A corporate customer needs to send a 10 million pound payment today and it must settle today. Walk through how a high-value payment is processed cleanly. A high-value payment gets extra care at every stage, because the stakes are higher. The corporate customer submits the instruction, usually through a dedicated corporate channel, as a **pain.001**. The bank runs full validation, including sanctions screening, balance check, and a **four-eyes approval** if the amount exceeds the single-authoriser limit. The payment hub routes it to the high-value clearing system, such as **CHAPS** in the UK or **Fedwire** in the US, because these systems settle in real time with finality. The hub sends the **pacs.008** instruction, and the clearing system moves the funds between the banks settlement

entries.title: How does the bank handle a partial acceptance, where the clearing house accepts some payments in a file and rejects others?
entries.text: How does the bank handle a partial acceptance, where the clearing house accepts some payments in a file and rejects others? **Partial acceptance** happens when the bank sends a file of payments to the clearing system and the clearing system accepts some and rejects others. The bank receives a status report, usually a **pacs.002** per payment, or a file-level response that lists the accepted and rejected items separately. The **payment hub** must handle each payment individually, not treat the whole file as accepted or rejected. The accepted payments are processed normally. They settle, the status is updated, and the customer is told. The rejected payments are handled one by one. The hub reads the reason code on each rejection, classifies it as technical or business, and routes it to the

entries.title: What is a payment hub?
entries.text: What is a payment hub? A payment hub is a central platform inside a bank that receives payment instructions from all the bank's channels and systems, and routes each one to the right clearing system or payment rail. Before hubs existed, each product or channel often had its own connection to each payment system, so an online banking payment, a branch payment, and a corporate bulk file might each travel through different pipes with different controls. That was expensive to maintain, hard to change, and risky, because a control applied in one pipe might be missing in another. A hub replaces that tangle with a single layer. It takes in payments from every source, validates and enriches them, applies the bank's common controls such as sanctions screening, fraud checks, and limit checks, and

entries.title: What is a payment filter?
entries.text: What is a payment filter? A payment filter is the screening mechanism that checks payment messages against sanctions lists and internal watchlists before the payment is released. In a payment hub or SWIFT environment, the filter sits between message receipt and execution: it scans fields such as the payer and payee names, account numbers, addresses, and the payment narrative for matches against sanctions lists. Filters use fuzzy matching to catch spelling variations and can apply rules based on country, currency, and keywords, for example flagging payments that mention embargoed goods. When a payment matches, the filter stops it and creates an alert for an analyst to review. Filters operate in real time for instant payments and in near real time for batch and SWIFT traffic, so performance

entries.title: What is a payment hub architecture?
entries.text: What is a payment hub architecture? A payment hub is a centralized platform that processes all of a bank's payments, across channels, currencies, and payment types, through a single system. Its architecture typically has several layers. At the front, channels such as online banking, mobile apps, branches, and corporate host-to-host connections capture payment instructions. An orchestration layer validates, enriches, and routes each payment, applying business rules such as cut-off times, limits, and fraud checks. A processing layer executes the payment: it transforms the message into the format required by the clearing system, applies sanctions screening and compliance checks, and manages the payment lifecycle from initiation to settlement. A connectivity layer links the hub to clearing

entries.title: What is a payment engine?
entries.text: What is a payment engine? A payment engine is the core processing component inside a payment hub that executes payments once they have been validated and routed. Think of it as the factory floor: it takes an approved payment instruction and drives it through the steps needed to get the money to its destination. Its responsibilities include message transformation, where the internal payment format is converted into the clearing-specific format; sequencing, where the engine applies the right order of operations such as screening, liquidity checks, and settlement; state management, where it tracks the payment through its lifecycle, from received to validated, released, settled, or rejected; and exception handling, where payments that fail a check are routed to an operations queue. The engine

entries.title: How is a payment hub organised inside a large global bank?
entries.text: How is a payment hub organised inside a large global bank? A payment hub in a large bank like NatWest or JP Morgan is the central engine that takes payment instructions from every channel and moves them to the right clearing system. Think of it as one factory with several departments. The front door takes instructions from branches, online banking, corporate file uploads and APIs. The validation team checks the instruction is complete and the account has funds. The routing team decides which rail to use, Faster Payments, CHAPS, SEPA or SWIFT, based on currency, value date and cost. The clearing team sends the payment out and waits for the response. The exceptions team picks up anything that fails. Around all of this sit shared services: sanctions screening, fraud checks, reference data

entries.title: You are integrating a new payment hub with the core banking system and the core only accepts batch files at end of day, but the business wants real time payments. How do you design this?
entries.text: You are integrating a new payment hub with the core banking system and the core only accepts batch files at end of day, but the business wants real time payments. How do you design this? First, map the gap honestly. The core accepts batch files at end of day, so it cannot post a real time payment itself. That means you need a **payment hub** sitting between the channel and the core. The hub receives the instruction in real time, validates it, checks funds, runs sanctions screening, and then decides the route. For the customer, the hub gives an immediate acknowledgement that the payment is accepted. Behind the scenes, the hub holds the payment in a **pending settlement** state and releases it to the core in the next batch file. The customer sees the debit immediately because the hub places

entries.title: Design a payment flow from a mobile banking channel through to the clearing house. What are the layers, and how do they communicate?
entries.text: Design a payment flow from a mobile banking channel through to the clearing house. What are the layers, and how do they communicate? The first decision is whether the flow is **synchronous** or **asynchronous**. A customer facing payment that needs an immediate answer uses synchronous flow: the channel sends the instruction, waits for the response, and tells the customer the result in seconds. A bulk or batch payment uses asynchronous flow: the channel accepts the file, returns an acknowledgement, and the processing happens later. For the design, draw three layers. The **channel layer** receives the instruction and validates the format. The **payment hub** does the business validation, funds check, sanctions screening and routing. The **clearing layer** sends the message to the clearing

entries.title: Draw the architecture of a payment hub in a large bank. What systems connect to it, and what does each connection do?
entries.text: Draw the architecture of a payment hub in a large bank. What systems connect to it, and what does each connection do? The payment hub is the centre, and everything connects to it rather than to each other. The **channels** (mobile, internet, branch, corporate) send instructions to the hub. The hub validates the instruction, checks the account balance through a real time call to the **core banking system**, runs **sanctions screening** through a screening engine, and checks the **FX rate** if the payment is in a foreign currency. Once validated, the hub routes the payment. Domestic payments go to the local clearing house. Cross border payments go to **SWIFT** through the SWIFT interface. The hub then waits for the response. The clearing house sends a **pacs.002** status report, and the hub

entries.title: What is the difference between a payment engine and a payment hub? When would a bank have one, the other, or both?
entries.text: What is the difference between a payment engine and a payment hub? When would a bank have one, the other, or both? A **payment engine** and a **payment hub** are related but not the same. The engine is the component that processes a single payment: it validates the instruction, applies business rules, transforms the message format, and determines the route. The hub is the broader platform that contains the engine plus everything around it: the channel adapters, the sanctions screening integration, the FX service, the clearing interfaces, the ledger, the monitoring dashboard and the operations screens. Think of the engine as the heart and the hub as the whole body. In a large bank you may have one hub with multiple engines inside it, for example one engine for domestic payments and one for

entries.title: The core banking system is 30 years old and only accepts flat files. How do you integrate a modern payment hub with it without rewriting the core?
entries.text: The core banking system is 30 years old and only accepts flat files. How do you integrate a modern payment hub with it without rewriting the core? Legacy core banking systems are the hardest integration problem because they were built decades ago and they change slowly. The approach is to **never modify the core** if you can avoid it. Instead, build an **integration layer** between the hub and the core. The layer translates the hub's real time messages into whatever the core understands, usually batch files, flat files, or a proprietary API. If the core only accepts files, the layer collects the day's payments and writes a file at the agreed time. If the core has an API, the layer calls it for balance checks and postings. The layer also handles the **data mapping**: the core may store the

entries.title: How do you design a payment system that handles multiple currencies? What changes compared to a single currency system?
entries.text: How do you design a payment system that handles multiple currencies? What changes compared to a single currency system? Multi currency payments add three complications. First, the **account structure**. A customer may have separate accounts per currency, or one multi currency account. The hub must know which account to debit and whether the currency matches. If the payment currency differs from the account currency, the hub must apply an **FX conversion** before debiting. Second, the **routing**. Different currencies clear through different systems. EUR goes through TARGET2 or STEP2, USD goes through Fedwire or CHIPS, GBP goes through CHAPS. The hub must select the right clearing system based on the currency, not just the destination country. Third, the **settlement account**. The bank

entries.title: How do you design a payment hub for high availability and disaster recovery? What happens to payments in flight when a data centre fails?
entries.text: How do you design a payment hub for high availability and disaster recovery? What happens to payments in flight when a data centre fails? A payment hub must survive a failure, so design for **high availability** from the start. Run the hub in at least two **data centres** in active-active mode, so if one centre goes down, the other takes over immediately. The database must be **replicated** between the centres so no payment data is lost. Use a **load balancer** in front of the hub so traffic routes to whichever centre is healthy. The clearing house connections must exist from both centres, or the surviving centre cannot send payments. The most important part is the **state**. Every payment's status must be in the shared database, not in the memory of one server, so a failover does not

entries.title: What is the difference between a payment gateway and a payment hub? How do they work together when a customer pays on a merchant website?
entries.text: What is the difference between a payment gateway and a payment hub? How do they work together when a customer pays on a merchant website? A payment gateway is a service that accepts payment instructions from merchants or customers and routes them to the bank. A payment hub is the bank's internal platform that processes payments across all channels. The gateway is the front door, the hub is the engine room. In a typical flow, a customer pays on a merchant website, the gateway receives the card details or the bank transfer instruction, and then it calls the bank's **payment API** to initiate the payment. The hub picks it up, validates it, and routes it to clearing. The gateway does not hold money and does not settle anything, it just passes the instruction through securely. The hub does the

entries.title: What does good look like inside a payment hub? Describe a well-run hub and how you would know it is working properly.
entries.text: What does good look like inside a payment hub? Describe a well-run hub and how you would know it is working properly. A good payment hub looks boring from the outside, and that is the point. Payments flow in from every channel, mobile, corporate, branch, and file, and they all land in one queue. The hub validates each one against the same rules, enriches it with routing and static data, and sends it to the right clearing system. The **dashboard** shows the state of every payment in real time, accepted, processing, settled, or in exception, and each exception has an owner and a next action. The hub handles **cut-offs** cleanly, so payments submitted before the cut-off settle on the promised value date, and payments after it are queued for the next cycle with the customer told clearly.
