entries.title: A pacs.004 return was expected three days ago but it never arrived. The original payment settled, the beneficiary bank said it would return the funds, and now there is silence. What do you do?
entries.text: A pacs.004 return was expected three days ago but it never arrived. The original payment settled, the beneficiary bank said it would return the funds, and now there is silence. What do you do? A return that never arrives is an open item, and open items age badly. I start by confirming the original payment settled, using the **ACSC** status on the pacs.002 chain. Then I check whether the return was actually initiated. I look for the **pacs.004** in the message logs, and I check the gpi Tracker with the original UETR to see if a return leg exists. If no pacs.004 was ever sent, I contact the beneficiary bank with a structured query, giving the full references, the original amount, and the date the return was promised. I ask for the return status and the expected value date. If the

entries.title: A corporate customer calls, angry, because a 500,000 euro payment to a supplier has not arrived after two days. The supplier is threatening to stop deliveries. How do you handle this complaint?
entries.text: A corporate customer calls, angry, because a 500,000 euro payment to a supplier has not arrived after two days. The supplier is threatening to stop deliveries. How do you handle this complaint? The customer is angry because they have no information, not just because the money is late. So the first job is to get facts fast and communicate them. I take the payment reference and the **UETR** and check the **gpi Tracker** immediately, because the last confirmed hop tells me where the payment is. I read the **pacs.002 chain** to see the latest status, whether it is accepted, pending, rejected, or settled. I check whether the payment is held in **sanctions screening**, stuck on a beneficiary name mismatch, or waiting at an intermediary. Once I know the state, I call the customer back with a

entries.title: The beneficiary bank credited a customer account, then discovered the account was closed. The beneficiary bank itself initiates the return. Who sends the pacs.004 and how does it work?
entries.text: The beneficiary bank credited a customer account, then discovered the account was closed. The beneficiary bank itself initiates the return. Who sends the pacs.004 and how does it work? The beneficiary bank discovered the problem, so it becomes the return originator and sends the **pacs.004** itself. It does not wait for the sender to ask. The trigger is found post-credit, a closed account, a frozen account, or a similar problem discovered after the funds landed. The beneficiary bank initiates the pacs.004, and the return travels the **chain in reverse**, with each intermediary validating and passing it on. **Return charges** may be deducted at hops along the way, so the sender gets back the original amount minus charges. **Status reporting** on the return leg flows through pacs.002

entries.title: A customer says the money left their account but the beneficiary never received it. Walk through your investigation step by step.
entries.text: A customer says the money left their account but the beneficiary never received it. Walk through your investigation step by step. The payment was debited but the credit never arrived, so first confirm the debit actually happened by checking the **core banking posting**. Then check the **pacs.002** chain. If the clearing house returned an ACSC, settlement happened and the problem is downstream, likely at the beneficiary bank. If the pacs.002 shows RJCT, the payment was rejected before settlement and the funds should be returned automatically. If there is no pacs.002 at all, the payment is stuck between the hub and the clearing house. The most common cause is a **timeout** where the hub sent the message but never received an acknowledgement, so it does not know whether the clearing house

entries.title: How do you reconcile payments between the payment hub, the core banking system and the clearing house? What are the common breaks?
entries.text: How do you reconcile payments between the payment hub, the core banking system and the clearing house? What are the common breaks? Reconciliation between the hub and the core is a **three way match**. At end of day, you compare three sources: the **payment hub ledger** (every instruction the hub accepted), the **core banking postings** (every debit and credit the core recorded), and the **clearing house confirmations** (every payment the clearing house settled). The three must agree. Start with the hub ledger as the source of truth for what was initiated. For each payment, check that the core has a matching debit. Then check that the clearing house has a matching settlement. Any payment in the hub but not in the core is a **posting failure**. Any payment in the core but not in the hub is

entries.title: Walk through a clean reconciliation day. How does a bank prove that its books match the clearing confirmations and the bank statements?
entries.text: Walk through a clean reconciliation day. How does a bank prove that its books match the clearing confirmations and the bank statements? Clean reconciliation means the books agree, and it works because the comparison happens continuously, not once a month. The payment hub records every payment it sends, with the amount, the value date, and the status. The clearing system sends back a **pacs.002** confirmation for each payment, and the hub matches it against the original instruction. The correspondent bank sends a **camt.053** statement at end of day, and the reconciliation engine matches each statement line against the hub ledger. Any line that does not match becomes a **break**, and the break is assigned to an owner with a deadline. In a clean operation, the break rate is near zero,

entries.title: Walk through a clean end-of-day. How does the camt.053 statement get reconciled against the bank's books before the next business day?
entries.text: Walk through a clean end-of-day. How does the camt.053 statement get reconciled against the bank's books before the next business day? A clean end-of-day works because the statement and the books are compared the same day, not the next morning. The correspondent bank sends a **camt.053** statement at the end of the business day, listing every debit and credit on the Nostro account. The reconciliation engine takes the statement and matches each line against the payment hub ledger. Every payment the hub sent should appear as a debit on the statement, and every payment received should appear as a credit. The engine matches them by amount, value date, and reference. Lines that match are closed automatically. Lines that do not match become **breaks**, and each break gets an owner and a

entries.title: A company pays a supplier overseas and the supplier reconciles the payment against the invoice on the same day. How does full remittance data make that possible?
entries.text: A company pays a supplier overseas and the supplier reconciles the payment against the invoice on the same day. How does full remittance data make that possible? A clean cross-border payment with full remittance data works because the beneficiary can reconcile it without a phone call. The customer sends a **pain.001** with the full remittance information, the invoice number, the purchase order, and the payment reference, all in the structured fields. The bank sends the **pacs.008** with the remittance data intact, and the intermediary banks pass it through without stripping it. The beneficiary bank receives the payment, credits the account, and includes the **remittance information** in the credit notification to the beneficiary. The beneficiary's accounts team matches the payment against

entries.title: A pacs.002 comes back with ACCP status. What does that mean, and what does the bank do with it?
entries.text: A pacs.002 comes back with ACCP status. What does that mean, and what does the bank do with it? **ACCP** means the payment has been accepted by the clearing system or the next bank in the chain, and it is being processed. It does not mean the money has settled yet. It means the payment passed validation, the account exists, and the payment is on its way. When the **payment hub** receives a **pacs.002** with ACCP, it matches the message to the original payment using the reference and the **UETR**, checks the amount and currency, and updates the payment status from submitted to accepted. The hub then pushes the status to the **channel**, so the customer can see the payment is accepted and in progress. No accounting entries change at ACCP, because no money has moved yet. The hub keeps

entries.title: A pacs.002 comes back with RJCT. Walk me through the handling step by step.
entries.text: A pacs.002 comes back with RJCT. Walk me through the handling step by step. **RJCT** means the payment has been rejected before settlement, and no money has moved. That is the most important fact, because it means the fix is repair and resubmit, not a return. The first step is to read the **pacs.002** carefully. It carries a reason code that tells the bank exactly what failed, for example an invalid account number, a sanctions flag, or a formatting error. The operations team classifies the failure as technical or business. A technical failure, such as a schema error or an invalid field, is fixed in the hub's message mapping or the source data. A business failure, such as a sanctions flag or a regulatory restriction, goes to compliance. The team confirms no settlement happened, then

entries.title: The payment shows ACSC in the hub but the customer says they have not received the money. How do you investigate?
entries.text: The payment shows ACSC in the hub but the customer says they have not received the money. How do you investigate? The first step is to trust the **ACSC** status but verify it. ACSC means the clearing system confirmed settlement, so the funds left the bank. The operations team pulls the settlement confirmation and checks the amount, currency, value date, and beneficiary account against the original instruction. If everything matches, the bank's side is correct, and the problem is at the beneficiary bank or in the customer's expectation. The team then checks the **SWIFT gpi** tracker, if the payment went through gpi, to see whether the beneficiary bank confirmed credit. If the tracker shows the payment was credited, the customer may be looking at the wrong account or the credit may not have

entries.title: How does the bank reconcile its payment ledger against the camt.053 statement from its account servicer?
entries.text: How does the bank reconcile its payment ledger against the camt.053 statement from its account servicer? The **camt.053** is the account statement the bank receives from its account servicer, usually a correspondent bank or the central bank. It lists every debit and credit on the account for the period, with references. The reconciliation team loads the camt.053 into the reconciliation system and matches each line against the bank's own **payment ledger**. A match needs the same amount, currency, value date, and reference. Most items match automatically. The unmatched items fall into two groups. First, items on the statement that are not in the ledger, such as a credit the bank was not expecting, or a charge deducted by the correspondent. Second, items in the ledger that are not on the

entries.title: A camt.054 debit notification arrives but there is no matching payment in the hub. What do you do?
entries.text: A camt.054 debit notification arrives but there is no matching payment in the hub. What do you do? A **camt.054** is a debit or credit notification. It tells the bank that money has moved on its account, and it arrives separately from the statement. When a camt.054 debit arrives with no matching payment in the hub, the first step is to check whether it is a charge, a fee, or a settlement adjustment, rather than a customer payment. Correspondent banks deduct charges, and the central bank deducts fees, and those appear as debits with no matching customer instruction. If it is not a charge, the team checks the reference on the camt.054 against the payment records, the settlement confirmations, and the **nostro** account entries. The debit may relate to a payment that was processed through a

entries.title: The bank sent 1,000 payments today but only received 995 pacs.002 responses. How do you chase the missing five?
entries.text: The bank sent 1,000 payments today but only received 995 pacs.002 responses. How do you chase the missing five? The **payment hub** tracks every payment it sends and expects a **pacs.002** response for each one. At the end of the settlement window, the hub runs a check that lists every payment still waiting for a response. The operations team works through the list. For each missing response, the team checks whether the payment actually settled by looking at the clearing confirmation and the **camt.053** statement. Sometimes the payment settled but the pacs.002 was lost in transit, and the bank can update the status from the statement instead. If there is no settlement confirmation either, the team checks the **SWIFT gpi** tracker to see where the payment is. If the tracker shows the

entries.title: A duplicate pacs.002 arrives for a payment that is already ACSC. How does the bank handle it without double-posting?
entries.text: A duplicate pacs.002 arrives for a payment that is already ACSC. How does the bank handle it without double-posting? A duplicate **pacs.002** is not unusual. The clearing system or an intermediary may send the same status twice, especially after a retry or a system recovery. The **payment hub** must handle it without double-posting. The hub matches each incoming pacs.002 to the payment using the message reference and the **UETR**, and checks the current status of the payment. If the payment is already **ACSC** and the duplicate pacs.002 also says ACSC, the hub recognises it as a duplicate and discards it. No accounting entries are posted a second time. The hub uses the status sequence to decide. A status can only move forward, from accepted to settled, never backward. If a duplicate

entries.title: The customer channel still shows the payment as pending, but the hub shows ACSC. How do you fix the mismatch and what do you tell the customer?
entries.text: The customer channel still shows the payment as pending, but the hub shows ACSC. How do you fix the mismatch and what do you tell the customer? This is a status synchronisation problem between the **payment hub** and the **channel**. The hub is the system of record, so the ACSC status in the hub is correct. The channel, which is what the customer sees, has not received the update. The first step is to confirm the hub status is genuinely ACSC by checking the settlement confirmation. Then the operations team checks the interface between the hub and the channel. The status update may have failed, the channel may have been down when the update was sent, or the channel may be showing a cached status. The team forces a status refresh from the hub to the channel, so the customer sees the correct

entries.title: A reconciliation break appears: the ledger shows a debit the clearing confirmation does not have. How do you find the root cause?
entries.text: A reconciliation break appears: the ledger shows a debit the clearing confirmation does not have. How do you find the root cause? The first step is to confirm the break is real and not a timing difference. The team checks the value date and the settlement time. If the debit is in the ledger but the clearing confirmation has not arrived yet, it may simply be that the confirmation is still in transit, and the break will clear itself. If the confirmation should have arrived by now, the team investigates. The team pulls the original payment instruction and checks the amount, currency, and reference against the ledger entry. The most common causes are a **reference mismatch**, where the clearing confirmation carries a different reference from the ledger, a **duplicate posting** in the ledger,

entries.title: A payment is rejected with reason code AC01 (incorrect account number). What is the repair process and how do you stop it happening again?
entries.text: A payment is rejected with reason code AC01 (incorrect account number). What is the repair process and how do you stop it happening again? **AC01** means the account number is incorrect. The **pacs.002** carries this reason code, and it tells the bank the beneficiary account number in the instruction does not match any account at the beneficiary bank. The payment was rejected before settlement, so no money moved. The first step is to confirm the rejection and tell the customer the payment did not go through. The operations team then checks the account number against the source. The error usually comes from the customer typing the number wrong, from a stale beneficiary record in the bank's system, or from a data migration that corrupted the account number. The team corrects the account

entries.title: The camt.053 shows a credit the bank was not expecting. How do you identify what it is and post it correctly?
entries.text: The camt.053 shows a credit the bank was not expecting. How do you identify what it is and post it correctly? An unexpected credit on the **camt.053** means money arrived in the bank's account that the bank was not expecting. The reconciliation team must identify it before it can be posted correctly. The first step is to read the statement line carefully. It carries a reference, a value date, an amount, and sometimes a remittance description. The team searches the **payment hub** and the **nostro** records for a matching payment using the reference and the amount. The most common explanations are a return of a payment the bank sent, a refund from a correspondent, an interest payment, or a payment from a client that was not expected that day. If the team finds the match, the credit is

entries.title: How does the bank reconcile nostro accounts using MT950 or camt.053, and what are the common breaks?
entries.text: How does the bank reconcile nostro accounts using MT950 or camt.053, and what are the common breaks? **Nostro reconciliation** is the daily check that the bank's own record of its **nostro account**, the account it holds with a correspondent bank in a foreign currency, matches the correspondent bank's record. The bank receives a statement, usually an **MT950** or a **camt.053**, from the correspondent and compares each line against its own nostro ledger. A match needs the same amount, currency, value date, and reference. The common breaks are timing differences, where a payment is recorded in the bank's ledger but has not yet appeared on the correspondent's statement, charges deducted by the correspondent that the bank did not expect, and **value date** mismatches where the two sides

entries.title: A value date mismatch appears between the pacs.008 the bank sent and the settlement confirmation. How do you resolve it?
entries.text: A value date mismatch appears between the pacs.008 the bank sent and the settlement confirmation. How do you resolve it? A **value date** mismatch means the bank expected the payment to settle on one date but the settlement confirmation shows a different date. The first step is to check the original instruction. The **pacs.008** carries the requested execution date, and the hub should have applied the correct value date based on the clearing calendar and the cut-off. If the hub applied the wrong value date, for example because it used the wrong calendar or ignored a holiday, the fix is in the hub's value date logic. If the hub was right, the mismatch may come from the clearing system. The payment may have missed the cut-off and been pushed to the next working day, or the beneficiary bank

entries.title: The bank receives a pacs.002 with a status it does not recognise. What is the handling?
entries.text: The bank receives a pacs.002 with a status it does not recognise. What is the handling? When a **pacs.002** arrives with a status the hub does not recognise, the hub should not crash and it should not ignore the message. It should park the message in an exception queue and alert the operations team. The team reads the raw pacs.002 and identifies the status code. It may be a new status introduced by the clearing system, a proprietary status from an intermediary, or a code the hub's mapping table does not cover. The team checks the clearing system's documentation to understand what the status means and whether it represents an acceptance, a rejection, or a settlement. The team then updates the payment status manually in the hub, so the customer can see the correct status, and tells the

entries.title: An investigation is opened with a camt.056 for a payment the beneficiary says never arrived. Walk through the investigation.
entries.text: An investigation is opened with a camt.056 for a payment the beneficiary says never arrived. Walk through the investigation. When a beneficiary says a payment never arrived, the bank opens a formal investigation. The first step is to check the bank's own records. The **payment hub** shows the status, and the settlement confirmation shows whether the funds left the bank. If the payment shows **ACSC**, the funds did leave, and the investigation moves to the next bank in the chain. The bank sends a **camt.056** cancellation request or an investigation message, usually an **MT199**, to the next bank, asking for the status of the payment and whether it was credited. Each bank in the chain responds in turn, and the bank traces the payment hop by hop until it finds where it stopped. The bank

entries.title: A reconciliation item sits in the suspense account for three days. What is the process to clear it, and who owns it?
entries.text: A reconciliation item sits in the suspense account for three days. What is the process to clear it, and who owns it? A **suspense account** is where the bank parks money it cannot yet explain. When a reconciliation item sits in suspense for three days, it is already overdue. The reconciliation team owns the item and must clear it. The first step is to re-investigate. The team checks the payment record, the settlement confirmation, the **camt.053** statement, and any messages from the correspondent or the clearing house. The team also checks whether the item is a duplicate, a charge, or a timing difference that should have cleared. If the item can be identified, it is posted to the correct account and removed from suspense. If it cannot be identified, it is escalated to the operations

entries.title: The bank's auto-reconciliation matches 98 percent of items. What happens to the other 2 percent, and how are they worked?
entries.text: The bank's auto-reconciliation matches 98 percent of items. What happens to the other 2 percent, and how are they worked? **Auto-reconciliation** matches most items automatically, usually 95 to 99 percent, because most payments match on amount, currency, value date, and reference. The remaining 2 percent do not match, and they are the ones that need human attention. The reconciliation system puts the unmatched items in an exceptions queue, and the reconciliation team works through them. Each exception is one of a few types. A timing difference, where the item will match tomorrow when the other side posts it. A reference mismatch, where the two sides used different references for the same payment. A charge or a fee that one side recorded and the other did not. Or a genuine error, where a

entries.title: A customer is charged a fee that does not match the charge option on the pacs.008. How do you investigate and correct it?
entries.text: A customer is charged a fee that does not match the charge option on the pacs.008. How do you investigate and correct it? The charge option on the **pacs.008** tells the banks in the chain who pays the fees. **OUR** means the sender pays all charges, **SHA** means the sender and the beneficiary share them, and **BEN** means the beneficiary pays them all. When the customer is charged a fee that does not match the charge option, the first step is to check the pacs.008 and confirm what was instructed. Then the team checks the **camt.053** statement and the correspondent's messages to see what was actually deducted. The most common cause is a correspondent bank deducting a fee that was not in the agreed schedule, or the beneficiary bank deducting a fee when the charge option said OUR. The

entries.title: How does end-of-day reconciliation sign-off work, and what happens if the team cannot sign off?
entries.text: How does end-of-day reconciliation sign-off work, and what happens if the team cannot sign off? **End-of-day reconciliation sign-off** is the formal confirmation that the bank's books balance for the day. The reconciliation team checks that every payment sent and received is accounted for, that the **nostro** accounts reconcile to the correspondent statements, that the **central bank settlement account** matches the central bank's record, and that the **suspense account** contains no unexplained items beyond the agreed limit. Each reconciliation is reviewed and signed by the team lead, and the sign-off is recorded. If the team cannot sign off, it means there is an unresolved break. The team identifies the break, quantifies it, and escalates to the operations manager. The manager decides

entries.title: A pacs.002 arrives after the bank has already sent a pacs.004 return for the same payment. How do you resolve the conflict?
entries.text: A pacs.002 arrives after the bank has already sent a pacs.004 return for the same payment. How do you resolve the conflict? This is a conflict that should not happen, but it does. A **pacs.004** return means the bank already sent the money back, but a **pacs.002** arriving afterwards says something about the original payment's status. The **payment hub** must handle this carefully. The hub checks the sequence. If the pacs.004 was already sent and the return is in progress, the pacs.002 is usually a late status update on the original payment, and it does not change the fact that the return is underway. The operations team checks whether the pacs.002 status contradicts the return. For example, if the pacs.002 says the original payment was **RJCT**, meaning it never settled, then the return

entries.title: A duplicate payment is sent because the channel submitted it twice. How does the bank detect it, stop the second one, and recover the funds if it settled?
entries.text: A duplicate payment is sent because the channel submitted it twice. How does the bank detect it, stop the second one, and recover the funds if it settled? A duplicate payment usually happens when the **channel** submits the same instruction twice, for example because the customer clicked submit twice, or because the channel retried a submission after a timeout without checking whether the first one went through. The **payment hub** should catch it. The hub checks each incoming instruction against recent payments using the customer, the amount, the beneficiary, and the reference. If it finds a match within a short window, it blocks the second submission as a suspected duplicate and alerts the operations team. If the duplicate was not caught and both payments settled, the bank must recover

entries.title: How does the bank reconcile charges and fees deducted by correspondent banks against what was instructed in the pacs.008?
entries.text: How does the bank reconcile charges and fees deducted by correspondent banks against what was instructed in the pacs.008? When a payment travels through correspondent banks, each bank in the chain can deduct a fee. The **pacs.008** carries the charge option, **OUR**, **SHA**, or **BEN**, and the instructed amount. The bank reconciles the charges by comparing three things. First, what was instructed in the pacs.008. Second, what the correspondent deducted, as shown on the **camt.053** statement and the **camt.054** notifications. Third, what the beneficiary actually received, as shown on the **gpi tracker** or the beneficiary bank's confirmation. If the deductions match the charge option and the agreed fee schedule, the reconciliation is clean. If a correspondent deducted more than agreed,

entries.title: A payment is sent twice by mistake. How do you handle it?
entries.text: A payment is sent twice by mistake. How do you handle it? A duplicate payment is serious because the beneficiary has been paid twice and the bank may not get the second payment back easily. First, I confirm it is a real duplicate: same amount, same beneficiary, same reference, sent twice. I check whether both payments settled or only one did. Second, I stop any further duplicates: I check if the source system is sending the payment twice, if a retry loop is firing, or if an operator resubmitted manually. I make sure the root cause is fixed before more duplicates go out. Third, I start the recovery for the duplicate: the bank sends a recall request to the beneficiary bank asking for the second payment back. entries.title: What is sanctions screening?
entries.text: What is sanctions screening? Sanctions screening is the process of checking every party and detail in a payment against lists of people, companies, countries, and vessels that governments have sanctioned. If a payment involves a sanctioned person or country, the bank must not process it, or must process it only under a specific licence. Screening happens before the payment is released, and it is one of the most important controls in a bank, because a single missed sanction can lead to fines running into billions and serious reputational damage. The screening engine compares the payment message against sanctions lists, such as the OFAC list in the United States, the EU consolidated list, and the UN list, plus the bank's own internal lists. It checks the sender and receiver names, and

entries.title: How does a bank handle a sanctions hit on a payment?
entries.text: How does a bank handle a sanctions hit on a payment? When a payment hits a sanctions list, the system stops it automatically before it leaves the bank. No one can override this by hand. The payment goes to a sanctions queue where a compliance analyst reviews it. The analyst checks the name, the address and the details of the payment against the sanctions list to decide if it is a true match or a false positive. A false positive is common: a customer name that is similar to a sanctioned person but is not the same person. In that case the analyst clears the payment and releases it, and records the decision. A true match is different. If the payment is to a sanctioned person or country, the payment is blocked and the bank must not release it. The bank reports the blocked payment to the

entries.title: A payment is sent to a bank in a country under sanctions screening. It is held at the clearing stage. Walk through what happens next.
entries.text: A payment is sent to a bank in a country under sanctions screening. It is held at the clearing stage. Walk through what happens next. When a payment is held at the clearing stage for **sanctions screening**, it means a name, a country, or a word in the payment matched a sanctions list or a screening rule. The payment does not fail, it is held for review. The bank's compliance team receives the alert and investigates. They check the names against the sanctions lists, look at the full payment details, and decide whether the match is real or a false positive, for example a common name that happens to match a listed person. If it is a false positive, compliance clears the payment and releases it, but the value date may have moved, and the client must be told. If the match is real, the payment

entries.title: A payment is held mid-flight because the beneficiary name fuzzy-matches a sanctions list. It could be a real hit or a false positive. What happens next?
entries.text: A payment is held mid-flight because the beneficiary name fuzzy-matches a sanctions list. It could be a real hit or a false positive. What happens next? The payment is held immediately and no funds move while the review is open. That is the first rule, because a held payment can be released but a released payment cannot be un-sent. The analyst escalates to the **compliance officer** with the match evidence attached, including which list matched, the match score, and the payment details. Then comes **true-match verification**. The compliance team compares the beneficiary details against the list entry, name, date of birth, address, nationality, to decide whether this is the same person or just a similar name. entries.title: Screening flags the ultimate beneficiary details as doubtful, but not definitively wrong. Do you reject the payment immediately or investigate first?
entries.text: Screening flags the ultimate beneficiary details as doubtful, but not definitively wrong. Do you reject the payment immediately or investigate first? When the data is doubtful but not definitively wrong, I ask before I kill the payment. I park it, request the information, and decide on facts. An instant reject could kill a legitimate payment, and a wrongly rejected payment damages the customer relationship. I send a **request for additional information** back up the chain to the sender bank, asking for the specific detail that is unclear. I **park the payment** with a clear status so it is visible in the queue, not lost in a pile. I give the sender a **bounded window** to respond, because open-ended parks become forgotten parks. entries.title: A letter of credit worth 28 million dirhams is delayed eight working days because sanctions screening fuzzy-matched a common surname. There is no fraud and no real risk, just bad screening logic. How do you fix false positives without missing real hits?
entries.text: A letter of credit worth 28 million dirhams is delayed eight working days because sanctions screening fuzzy-matched a common surname. There is no fraud and no real risk, just bad screening logic. How do you fix false positives without missing real hits? About 95 percent of sanctions alerts are false positives, but every one still delays real business. The client in this case faced **cash-flow strain** because a legitimate letter of credit sat parked for eight working days on a common surname match. I fix it by **triaging by risk**. Exact matches and high-risk corridors get senior review first. Common-name matches go through a fast lane with a clear checklist. I **fine-tune the matching rules**, adjusting fuzzy-match thresholds per corridor and per name frequency, instead of one global

entries.text: A 500,000 dollar wire is blocked when the beneficiary name fuzzy-matches the OFAC SDN list. The analyst escalates to compliance, the payment is held, and a SAR is filed. Walk through what happens. The payment is held immediately when **screening flags** the beneficiary name as a fuzzy match against the SDN list. No funds move while the review is open. The analyst **escalates to the compliance officer** with the match evidence attached, including the list entry, the match score, and the full payment details. Then comes **true-match verification**. The compliance team compares the beneficiary against the list entry, checking name, date of birth, address, and nationality, to decide whether this is the same person or just a similar name. entries.title: Transaction monitoring flags multiple accounts. The pattern is small inward transfers from unrelated sources, funds moved out within minutes of credit, minimal balance retention, and common device linkage. What is this and how do you respond?
entries.text: Transaction monitoring flags multiple accounts. The pattern is small inward transfers from unrelated sources, funds moved out within minutes of credit, minimal balance retention, and common device linkage. What is this and how do you respond? This is a **mule account network**. The red flags are clear. Small-value inward transfers from unrelated sources, rapid outward movement within minutes of credit, minimal balance retention, and common device or IP linkage across accounts. One account with this pattern is a case. Linked accounts with the same pattern are a network. I act fast. A **debit freeze** on the suspect accounts stops the flow immediately, because every hour of delay is more money moved. entries.title: Where does sanctions screening fit in the payment flow, and how do you design it so it does not slow down real time payments?
entries.text: Where does sanctions screening fit in the payment flow, and how do you design it so it does not slow down real time payments? Sanctions screening sits in the payment flow between validation and routing, and it must be fast enough not to break real time payments. The flow is: the channel sends the instruction to the hub, the hub extracts the **debtor name, creditor name, and any address fields**, and sends them to the screening engine. The engine compares them against sanctions lists and returns a result: clear, potential match, or confirmed match. If clear, the payment continues. If potential match, the payment goes to a **manual review queue** and an analyst checks it. If confirmed match, the payment is **blocked** and reported. The design challenge is speed. Screening must return in

entries.title: Transaction monitoring flags an account that receives several small transfers from unrelated people, then sends the full amount abroad within an hour. Explain the pattern, what it suggests, and what the bank does next.
entries.text: Transaction monitoring flags an account that receives several small transfers from unrelated people, then sends the full amount abroad within an hour. Explain the pattern, what it suggests, and what the bank does next. This is a classic **money mule** pattern. The account receives multiple small **inward transfers** from people who have no connection to the account holder, and then sends the money out almost immediately, usually to an account abroad. The small amounts are designed to stay below the **monitoring thresholds**, and the speed is designed to move the money before the bank can react. The pattern suggests the account holder is either a willing mule, paid to move criminal money, or an unwitting mule, tricked into receiving and forwarding money, often through a fake job advert or

entries.title: A sanctions list is updated at midday and a new name is added. Several payments are already in flight that involve that name. Explain what the bank must do with the payments that are already moving.
entries.text: A sanctions list is updated at midday and a new name is added. Several payments are already in flight that involve that name. Explain what the bank must do with the payments that are already moving. When a **sanctions list** is updated, the new entry applies **immediately**. The bank must screen all payments against the updated list, including payments that are already in flight. The first step is to identify which payments are affected: the bank checks the **payment queue** for payments sent but not yet settled and payments received but not yet credited. Any payment that matches must be **held**, which means stopping it before it settles or before it is credited to the beneficiary. If the payment has already settled and the funds have been credited, the bank cannot take the money back

entries.title: A customer calls in tears. They were tricked by a fraudster posing as their bank into sending 15,000 pounds to a criminal account. Explain how the bank handles the case, what the customer can expect, and what the bank does to try to recover the money.
entries.text: A customer calls in tears. They were tricked by a fraudster posing as their bank into sending 15,000 pounds to a criminal account. Explain how the bank handles the case, what the customer can expect, and what the bank does to try to recover the money. This is **authorised push payment fraud**, where the customer was tricked into authorising the payment themselves. The bank must act with **empathy** first: the customer is a victim, and the first thing they need is to be believed and to be told what will happen next. The bank must immediately contact the **receiving bank** and ask it to freeze the criminal account, because the fraudster moves the money within hours. The bank must also raise a **fraud case**, record all the evidence, such as the phone number the fraudster used and the

entries.title: A customer makes cash deposits of 9,500 pounds every few days, always just below the 10,000 pound reporting threshold. Explain what the bank suspects, how it investigates, and what happens if the suspicion is confirmed.
entries.text: A customer makes cash deposits of 9,500 pounds every few days, always just below the 10,000 pound reporting threshold. Explain what the bank suspects, how it investigates, and what happens if the suspicion is confirmed. The bank suspects **structuring**, which is the deliberate splitting of transactions to avoid a **reporting threshold**. The threshold exists so that large cash transactions are reported to the authorities, and a customer who consistently deposits just below it is likely trying to avoid that report. The pattern is suspicious because there is no normal business reason to deposit 9,500 pounds repeatedly instead of the full amount. The bank investigates by looking at the customer **profile**: what is their normal activity, what is their source of income, and does the cash

entries.title: A payment is held because the beneficiary name fuzzy matches a sanctions list entry. The name is a common one, like Mohammed Khan, and the customer is angry about the delay. Explain fuzzy matching, why the payment was held, and how it gets released.
entries.text: A payment is held because the beneficiary name fuzzy matches a sanctions list entry. The name is a common one, like Mohammed Khan, and the customer is angry about the delay. Explain fuzzy matching, why the payment was held, and how it gets released. **Fuzzy matching** is the technique sanctions screening systems use to catch names that are spelled differently, transliterated from another alphabet, or entered with a typo. The system does not look for an exact match. It looks for names that are **similar enough** to be the same person, and it scores the similarity. A common name like Mohammed Khan will match many entries on a sanctions list, because the list contains many people with that name, and the system cannot tell them apart from the name alone. entries.title: A bank trade finance team notices that the invoice value for a shipment of electronics is three times the market price, and the goods are shipped through three countries for no clear reason. Explain trade based money laundering and how the bank responds.
entries.text: A bank trade finance team notices that the invoice value for a shipment of electronics is three times the market price, and the goods are shipped through three countries for no clear reason. Explain trade based money laundering and how the bank responds. **Trade based money laundering** is the use of international trade to move criminal money across borders by disguising it as legitimate business. The techniques include **over invoicing**, where the invoice value is inflated so that extra money moves with the shipment, **under invoicing**, where the value is reduced, and **phantom shipments**, where the goods do not exist at all. In this case, the invoice is three times the market price and the goods take an unnecessarily complex route, which are both red flags. The bank responds by

entries.title: A customer adds a new payee to their online banking, then immediately sends a large payment to that payee. The bank transaction monitoring flags it. Explain what the bank suspects and what controls should have stopped it.
entries.text: A customer adds a new payee to their online banking, then immediately sends a large payment to that payee. The bank transaction monitoring flags it. Explain what the bank suspects and what controls should have stopped it. The bank suspects **account takeover**. A fraudster has gained access to the customer account, added a new payee, which is an account the fraudster controls, and then sent a large payment to it. The pattern is a red flag because genuine customers rarely add a payee and send a large payment in the same session. The controls that should have stopped it include **strong customer authentication** when the payee is added, a **cooling off period** where a new payee cannot receive a large payment for 24 hours, **confirmation of payee** to check the payee name against the

entries.title: A customer wants to send a large payment to a cryptocurrency exchange. The bank compliance team is unsure whether to allow it. Explain the risks, what the bank should check, and how it makes the decision.
entries.text: A customer wants to send a large payment to a cryptocurrency exchange. The bank compliance team is unsure whether to allow it. Explain the risks, what the bank should check, and how it makes the decision. A payment to a **cryptocurrency exchange** carries specific risks. Cryptocurrency can be used to move money quickly and anonymously, which makes it attractive for **money laundering**, **fraud**, and **sanctions evasion**. The bank must check several things before it allows the payment. First, is the exchange **regulated** and does it carry out **customer due diligence** on its own users. A regulated exchange in a reputable jurisdiction is lower risk than an unregulated exchange in a high risk country. Second, what is the **purpose** of the payment: is the customer investing, trading, or

entries.title: Walk through a clean card payment, from the customer tapping the card to the merchant being settled. What happens at authorisation, clearing, and settlement?
entries.text: Walk through a clean card payment, from the customer tapping the card to the merchant being settled. What happens at authorisation, clearing, and settlement? A card payment has three stages, authorisation, clearing, and settlement, and in a clean flow each one happens on time. The customer taps their card, and the merchant sends an **authorisation request** to the acquiring bank. The acquirer routes it through the card scheme to the issuing bank. The issuing bank checks the balance, the card status, and the fraud rules, then approves the transaction and places a hold on the funds. The customer sees the transaction immediately. At the end of the day, the merchant sends a **clearing file** with all the day transactions. The scheme nets the amounts between banks and calculates the

entries.title: A customer taps their card at a cafe and the terminal declines it, even though they have plenty of money in the account. The customer is embarrassed and angry. How do you investigate the decline and what do you tell the customer?
entries.text: A customer taps their card at a cafe and the terminal declines it, even though they have plenty of money in the account. The customer is embarrassed and angry. How do you investigate the decline and what do you tell the customer? Start with the **authorisation response code**, because it tells you exactly why the issuer said no. A code like **05 do not honour** is a generic issuer decline, **51** means insufficient funds, **54** means an expired card, and **91** means the issuer is temporarily unavailable. Ask the merchant for the code from the terminal receipt or the acquirer log before you guess anything. Next, check the **card status** in the issuer system. entries.title: A merchant receives a chargeback 60 days after a sale. The reason code says the cardholder did not authorise the transaction, but the merchant has signed delivery proof and a photo of the goods being handed over. How does the merchant fight the chargeback, and what are the chances?
entries.text: A merchant receives a chargeback 60 days after a sale. The reason code says the cardholder did not authorise the transaction, but the merchant has signed delivery proof and a photo of the goods being handed over. How does the merchant fight the chargeback, and what are the chances? The merchant fights it through **representment**, which is the formal reply to a chargeback sent through the acquirer to the card scheme. The acquirer has a strict deadline, usually **30 to 45 days** from the chargeback date, and missing it means the money is lost automatically, so the first step is to confirm the deadline and start the clock. The merchant must submit **compelling evidence**: the signed delivery note, the photo, the order details, the delivery address matching the cardholder address, and any

entries.title: A small retailer has not received card settlement for two days. Takings were normal, the terminal shows the sales went through, but no money has arrived in the bank account. Walk through how you find the problem.
entries.text: A small retailer has not received card settlement for two days. Takings were normal, the terminal shows the sales went through, but no money has arrived in the bank account. Walk through how you find the problem. Start by checking whether the terminal **batched and closed** for those two days. Card payments are authorised in real time, but they are only sent for clearing when the terminal closes its **batch**, usually at end of day. If the batch was never closed, the money is sitting authorised but uncleared, and closing the batch releases it. Next, ask the acquirer to confirm it received the **clearing file** and check the **settlement account** details on the merchant account. A changed bank account, a closed account, or a wrong sort code means the acquirer tried to pay and the payment

entries.title: An online shopper starts a purchase, gets a 3-D Secure challenge on their phone, fails it twice, and abandons the checkout. The merchant loses the sale and blames the bank. Explain what happened and how the merchant reduces abandoned checkouts without increasing fraud.
entries.text: An online shopper starts a purchase, gets a 3-D Secure challenge on their phone, fails it twice, and abandons the checkout. The merchant loses the sale and blames the bank. Explain what happened and how the merchant reduces abandoned checkouts without increasing fraud. The shopper hit **3-D Secure**, the extra authentication step that asks the cardholder to confirm the payment, usually through their banking app or a one time passcode. Failing it twice means the issuer could not verify the shopper, so the payment was not authenticated and the merchant correctly did not proceed. Under **PSD2 strong customer authentication** rules, the issuer must challenge payments that look risky, and the merchant cannot skip that step. The merchant can reduce abandonment by using **frictionless flow**

entries.title: Your bank stores card numbers for one-click checkout. The team wants to move from stored PANs to network tokens. Explain what changes, what the risks are, and how you migrate without breaking existing customers.
entries.text: Your bank stores card numbers for one-click checkout. The team wants to move from stored PANs to network tokens. Explain what changes, what the risks are, and how you migrate without breaking existing customers. Moving to **network tokens** means replacing the stored **PAN**, the 16 digit card number, with a token issued by the card scheme, such as Visa or Mastercard. The token works like the card number for payments, but it is useless if stolen, because it only works with the merchant it was issued for and can be suspended without reissuing the card. The migration starts with the **token requestor** setup: the bank or its processor registers with the scheme, agrees the token rules, and builds the token vault that maps each token back to the real PAN. entries.title: A customer taps their card several times during the day and suddenly the terminal asks for a PIN. They have never been asked for a PIN on contactless before. Explain why this happens and what the customer should do.
entries.text: A customer taps their card several times during the day and suddenly the terminal asks for a PIN. They have never been asked for a PIN on contactless before. Explain why this happens and what the customer should do. This is the **contactless cumulative limit** doing its job. Under **strong customer authentication** rules, a card can only be used contactless for a certain total value, or a certain number of taps, before the terminal must ask for a **PIN** to prove the person holding the card is the real cardholder. In the UK the single tap limit is **100 pounds**, and the cumulative limit means that after several taps the card needs a PIN even if each individual tap was small. The limit resets once the PIN is entered correctly. The terminal is not broken, the card is not blocked, and the

entries.title: A customer pays by card while on holiday abroad and later complains that the amount taken from their account is higher than the price on the receipt. The shop offered to charge them in their home currency. Explain what happened and what the customer should have done.
entries.text: A customer pays by card while on holiday abroad and later complains that the amount taken from their account is higher than the price on the receipt. The shop offered to charge them in their home currency. Explain what happened and what the customer should have done. The shop offered **dynamic currency conversion**, known as DCC, which means the card payment is converted into the customer home currency at the point of sale, using the exchange rate set by the merchant or their acquirer. That rate is almost always worse than the rate the card scheme, Visa or Mastercard, would apply, and it often includes an extra **markup** of 3 to 5 percent. The customer accepted the conversion, probably without realising the cost, and the higher amount is the result. The right choice is almost always to

entries.title: A card scheme raises its interchange rates. The acquirer passes the increase to merchants, and a large retailer threatens to leave. Explain what interchange is, why the merchant pays it, and how the acquirer handles the negotiation.
entries.text: A card scheme raises its interchange rates. The acquirer passes the increase to merchants, and a large retailer threatens to leave. Explain what interchange is, why the merchant pays it, and how the acquirer handles the negotiation. **Interchange** is the fee the merchant bank, the acquirer, pays to the cardholder bank, the issuer, on every card transaction. It is the largest part of the **merchant service charge**, the total fee the merchant pays to accept cards, and it is set by the card scheme, not by the acquirer. The acquirer cannot remove it, it can only decide how much of its own margin to add on top. When the scheme raises interchange, the acquirer cost rises on every transaction, so passing it on is normal, but the merchant sees only a higher bill. Explain to the merchant that

entries.title: An authorisation is approved at the till, the customer leaves with the goods, but the merchant settlement for that day is short by exactly that amount. The clearing file has no record of the transaction. What went wrong and how do you fix it?
entries.text: An authorisation is approved at the till, the customer leaves with the goods, but the merchant settlement for that day is short by exactly that amount. The clearing file has no record of the transaction. What went wrong and how do you fix it? The authorisation and the clearing are two separate steps, and this case shows the second step failed. The card was authorised in real time, which is why the customer left with the goods, but the transaction was never **presented for clearing**. In a **dual message** system, the authorisation holds the funds and the clearing message, the presentment, actually moves the money. entries.title: A customer subscription payment fails the month after their card is reissued with a new expiry date. The customer did not update the card details with the merchant. Explain why the payment failed and how it should have worked.
entries.text: A customer subscription payment fails the month after their card is reissued with a new expiry date. The customer did not update the card details with the merchant. Explain why the payment failed and how it should have worked. The payment failed because the merchant tried to charge the **old card details**. A reissued card has a new expiry date and sometimes a new card number, and the stored details the merchant holds are now out of date. The subscription should have kept working through the **account updater** service, run by Visa and Mastercard. When a card is reissued, the issuer sends the new details to the scheme, and merchants enrolled in the updater service receive the new card number and expiry date automatically, before the next payment is due. entries.title: A merchant is charged more for card acceptance than expected. When you investigate, you find the merchant category code on the account is wrong. Explain what a merchant category code is, why it matters, and how you fix it.
entries.text: A merchant is charged more for card acceptance than expected. When you investigate, you find the merchant category code on the account is wrong. Explain what a merchant category code is, why it matters, and how you fix it. The **merchant category code**, or MCC, is a four digit code that describes what type of business the merchant is, such as a supermarket, a restaurant, or an airline. The code is set when the merchant account is opened, and it drives two things: the **interchange rate** the merchant pays, because different business types have different rates, and the **risk rules** applied to the account, because some categories, like travel or electronics, carry higher chargeback risk. A wrong MCC can mean the merchant pays a higher interchange rate than they should, or that their

entries.title: A fraudster uses a stolen card at a terminal. The chip fails to read, the terminal falls back to the magnetic stripe, and the transaction goes through. Who bears the loss, and what should the merchant and the acquirer have done?
entries.text: A fraudster uses a stolen card at a terminal. The chip fails to read, the terminal falls back to the magnetic stripe, and the transaction goes through. Who bears the loss, and what should the merchant and the acquirer have done? This is an **EMV fallback** transaction, where the chip could not be read and the terminal used the **magnetic stripe** instead. The magnetic stripe is easy to copy, which is why the industry moved to chip, and fallback transactions are a known fraud route. Under the **liability shift** rules, the party that has not adopted EMV bears the loss. If the merchant terminal is chip enabled but the card chip was faulty, the issuer usually bears the loss.
