entries.title: A customer returns goods to a shop and the refund is issued to a card that has since expired. The customer worries the money is lost. Explain where the refund goes and what the customer should expect.
entries.text: A customer returns goods to a shop and the refund is issued to a card that has since expired. The customer worries the money is lost. Explain where the refund goes and what the customer should expect. The money is not lost. When a refund is issued to an **expired card**, the issuer routes it using the card account behind the card number, not the plastic card itself. The card number stays linked to the same account even after the expiry date passes, so the refund lands in the account that the old card belonged to. If the customer has been issued a **replacement card**, the refund usually appears on the new card statement, because the issuer maps the old card number to the new one. If the account itself is closed, the issuer cannot post the refund and will return it to the merchant, who

entries.title: A new online merchant wants to start accepting card payments. The acquirer asks for business details, trading history, and a reserve. The merchant thinks this is unnecessary paperwork. Explain why the acquirer does this and what the merchant should expect.
entries.text: A new online merchant wants to start accepting card payments. The acquirer asks for business details, trading history, and a reserve. The merchant thinks this is unnecessary paperwork. Explain why the acquirer does this and what the merchant should expect. The acquirer is doing **merchant underwriting**, which is the risk check every acquirer must do before letting a business take card payments. Card payments carry a risk the acquirer takes on: if the merchant takes money and then fails to deliver the goods, or goes out of business, the acquirer must refund the cardholders through **chargebacks**. The acquirer therefore checks the business model, the trading history, the expected volumes, and the **chargeback risk** before agreeing terms. For a new business with no history, or a high risk

entries.title: Explain the difference between single message and dual message card clearing, and why a merchant might be paid at a different time depending on which system their acquirer uses.
entries.text: Explain the difference between single message and dual message card clearing, and why a merchant might be paid at a different time depending on which system their acquirer uses. In a **dual message** system, a card payment has two separate steps. The **authorisation** message checks the funds and holds the amount, and hours later a **clearing** message, the presentment, actually moves the money. Visa and Mastercard credit cards mostly work this way, and the merchant is paid after the clearing file is processed, usually the next working day. In a **single message** system, the authorisation and the clearing happen in one message, so the money moves at the same time as the approval. Many debit card systems work this way, and the merchant can be paid faster, sometimes the same day. The

entries.title: What is a payment exception queue?
entries.text: What is a payment exception queue? A payment exception queue is the worklist where payments that cannot be processed automatically are held for manual handling by operations staff. Payments land in the exception queue for many reasons: a sanctions screening alert, a failed validation such as an invalid account number, a missing beneficiary address, a limit breach, a liquidity shortfall, or a technical error such as a rejected message from a clearing system. Each item in the queue shows the payment details, the reason it failed, and the actions available: repair and resubmit, release, return to sender, or escalate. Operations teams work the queue in priority order, guided by service level agreements based on value date and cut-off times, because a payment that misses its cut-off may settle

entries.title: What is a payment operations dashboard?
entries.text: What is a payment operations dashboard? A payment operations dashboard is a real-time view of payment processing health that lets operations teams see what is happening and act quickly when something goes wrong. It typically shows volumes by payment type, channel, and currency; the straight through processing rate; the size and ageing of exception queues; payments approaching cut-off times; settlement and nostro balances; and the status of connections to clearing systems. Good dashboards use traffic-light indicators: green for normal, amber for warning, and red for breach, so an operator can spot a problem at a glance. They also support drill-down: clicking on a red exception count shows the underlying payments and their failure reasons. Dashboards serve different audiences: operators

entries.title: What is a payment test case?
entries.text: What is a payment test case? A payment test case is a documented scenario that verifies a specific behavior of a payment system, with defined inputs, expected results, and pass or fail criteria. A good test case starts with a clear objective, for example verifying that a SEPA payment with an invalid IBAN is rejected with the correct error code. It specifies the preconditions, such as the test account setup and reference data; the test steps, such as entering the payment details and submitting; the test data, including amounts, currencies, and dates; and the expected result, such as the exact error message and the payment status. Payment test cases cover happy paths, such as a standard domestic payment settling on time, and edge cases, such as a payment on a bank holiday, a payment above a

entries.title: How does a large bank handle peak volumes on a salary day or month end?
entries.text: How does a large bank handle peak volumes on a salary day or month end? A large bank plans for peak days weeks in advance. The operations team looks at the calendar and knows which days will be heavy: month end, salary days, tax payment deadlines and the days before a public holiday. First, they check capacity. The payment hub, the core banking system and the clearing interfaces all have throughput limits, and the team confirms they can handle the expected volume. Second, they staff up. More people are put on the exceptions queue and the helpdesk because more payments means more failures. Third, treasury pre-funds the nostro accounts with extra liquidity, because more payments going out means more money leaving the accounts. Fourth, the bank may ask large corporate clients to send their

entries.title: How are payments operations teams structured in a large bank?
entries.text: How are payments operations teams structured in a large bank? In a large bank like BNY Mellon or Goldman Sachs, payments operations is split into teams by function, not by product. The intake team receives payment files and instructions from channels and checks they are complete. The processing team monitors the payment hub and makes sure payments flow through without getting stuck. The exceptions team investigates payments that fail validation, get rejected by clearing or come back with an error. The reconciliation team matches what the bank sent against what clearing confirmed, and matches the nostro accounts against the ledger. The investigations team handles customer queries about missing or delayed payments. The treasury operations team manages liquidity and funding. Above these

entries.title: What happens when a payment is stuck in a queue at a large bank?
entries.text: What happens when a payment is stuck in a queue at a large bank? A payment gets stuck in a queue when it cannot move to the next step. The most common reasons are a missing field, a failed validation, a sanctions hold or a system that is down. The payment hub holds the payment in a queue and flags it for the operations team. The operations team looks at the queue regularly during the day. They open the payment, read the error or the hold reason and decide what to do. If it is a data problem, they fix the data or send it back to the channel team to fix at source. If it is a sanctions hold, they pass it to the compliance team for review. If it is a system problem, they raise it with engineering and wait for a fix. While the payment is stuck, the customer may call to ask where their money

entries.title: How does a large bank test a payment change before it goes live?
entries.text: How does a large bank test a payment change before it goes live? Testing a payment change in a large bank has several layers because a defect can stop real money. First, the engineers run unit tests on the code they wrote. Second, the QA team runs system integration tests in a test environment that mirrors production, checking that the payment hub talks correctly to the core banking system, the sanctions screening and the clearing interfaces. Third, the BA writes end to end test scenarios based on real payment flows: a normal payment, a payment with a missing field, a payment that gets rejected, a payment that hits sanctions, a payment that needs to be returned. These scenarios are run with test data that looks like real customer data. Fourth, operations run user acceptance testing. They

entries.title: What is the role of a payments operations manager during a system outage?
entries.text: What is the role of a payments operations manager during a system outage? When a payment system goes down, the operations manager becomes the incident owner. The first job is to assess the impact: which payments are affected, how many, and whether customers are impacted. The manager opens an incident, calls the engineering team and the duty manager, and starts a bridge call. Second, the manager decides whether to stop taking new payments or to queue them. Stopping intake prevents a backlog building up, but it means customers cannot pay. Queuing keeps the intake open but risks a large backlog when the system comes back. Third, the manager communicates. The manager updates the business, the helpdesk and the customer communications team so that customers get a consistent message. Fourth, the

entries.title: How does a bank handle a failed file from a corporate client?
entries.text: How does a bank handle a failed file from a corporate client? A corporate client sends a payment file, usually a bulk file with hundreds or thousands of payments. The bank's file gateway receives the file and checks it. First, it checks the file format: is it a valid file, does it have the right structure, are the headers correct. If the format is wrong, the whole file is rejected and the client is told to fix it and resend. Second, it checks each payment inside the file: is the account number valid, is the amount present, is the currency supported. Payments that fail this check are rejected individually, and the good payments in the file still go through. Third, it checks for duplicates: has this file been sent before, are there duplicate payments inside it. The bank sends a response

entries.title: How does a large bank measure payment performance and what are the key metrics?
entries.text: How does a large bank measure payment performance and what are the key metrics? A large bank tracks payment performance with a small set of metrics that everyone watches. The first is the straight-through processing rate: the percentage of payments that go through without manual intervention. A high STP rate means the system is working well. The second is the average processing time: how long from instruction to settlement. For instant payments this is measured in seconds, for cross border it is measured in hours. The third is the exception rate: the percentage of payments that land in a repair or investigation queue. A rising exception rate signals a data quality or system problem. The fourth is the reconciliation break rate: how many payments fail to match at end of day. The fifth is

entries.title: A corporate customer submits a payment one minute after the cut-off. The channel accepts it, but the clearing system rejects it because the settlement window has closed. The customer expects same-day value. What do you do?
entries.text: A corporate customer submits a payment one minute after the cut-off. The channel accepts it, but the clearing system rejects it because the settlement window has closed. The customer expects same-day value. What do you do? A cut-off is a contract between the bank, the clearing system, and every downstream batch. When a payment misses it, the channel and the clearing system disagree, and the customer is caught in between. I first check the **pacs.002** status to confirm the rejection and the reason. If the payment was rejected pre-settlement, no funds have moved, so I can repair and resubmit for the next value date. I tell the customer plainly that the value date has shifted to the next business day, and I explain why, because a customer who understands the cut-off will plan around it next

entries.title: Customers report duplicate debits, but no alerts fired. The root cause is a messaging failure, the broker acknowledged a message before replication finished, then died, and the retry charged again. How do you debug this?
entries.text: Customers report duplicate debits, but no alerts fired. The root cause is a messaging failure, the broker acknowledged a message before replication finished, then died, and the retry charged again. How do you debug this? The failure is in the interaction between systems, not in any single component, which is why no alert fired. Each part behaved as designed. The producer used **acks equals 1**, so only the leader broker acknowledged the message. The broker died before replication finished, so the message was lost. But the payment had already been charged, and the system believed it had failed, so the retry charged a second time. I debug it by tracing the full flow, from the payment request through the message broker to the debit posting, and I look for the gap between what the system

entries.title: A payment timeout keeps recurring but the network is healthy and the servers look fine. Where do you look for the root cause?
entries.text: A payment timeout keeps recurring but the network is healthy and the servers look fine. Where do you look for the root cause? The timeout is the symptom, not the cause. I stop fixating on where the error surfaced and start from where the message was created. I trace the **full end-to-end lifecycle** hop by hop, with timestamps and message copies at every step. In this kind of case the real culprit is often a small deviation from **message standards** upstream, not an infrastructure problem. A field that is slightly out of spec, a format that is almost right, or a value that is technically valid but unexpected. Small deviations **compound downstream**. A tolerant receiver today becomes a hard failure after the next release, when the receiving system tightens its validation. I validate

entries.title: A release passes QA, staging, and a small rollout. Hours after full release, volumes spike and failures spike with them. What went wrong?
entries.text: A release passes QA, staging, and a small rollout. Hours after full release, volumes spike and failures spike with them. What went wrong? Testing never hit the fringe edge case. The root cause was one parameter that everyone assumed was always populated, but in a small number of real cases it came back empty. QA, staging, and a small rollout all passed because the edge case only appeared at full volume. The cascade was fast. **Partner API calls failed**, reconciliation mismatched, and war rooms opened with stakeholders. Recovery needs calm coordination across engineering, operations, and partner support, without blame. The first job is to stop the failures, then fix the code, then fix the **assumption**. I validate every input, especially the ones labelled always present, because those

entries.title: Payments fail intermittently, but only during peak hours. The system is fine at all other times. How do you find the root cause?
entries.text: Payments fail intermittently, but only during peak hours. The system is fine at all other times. How do you find the root cause? I run the **5-Why chain** from the symptom down. The payments time out, so why. Processing is slow, so why. Database queries are lagging, so why. Server load is high, so why. The servers are not sized for peak traffic. That chain points at capacity, not code. **Peak-only failures mean capacity**. All-day failures mean code or data. I fix the root, not the symptom. I add **database indexing** on the slow queries, increase server capacity, and add **load balancing** so traffic spreads evenly. Then I **monitor after the fix** to confirm the failures actually stopped, not just moved to a different time of day. I **document the RCA** so the next incident starts from

entries.title: A payment left the channel but never arrived at the clearing house. The customer is asking where their money is. How do you trace it and what do you tell them?
entries.text: A payment left the channel but never arrived at the clearing house. The customer is asking where their money is. How do you trace it and what do you tell them? Start by checking the **pacs.002** status reports. If the clearing house sent an ACSC, the payment settled and the problem is in the feedback loop. If there is no pacs.002, the payment never reached the clearing house. Next, check the **payment hub logs** for that UETR. The hub records every hop: received from channel, validated, sent to clearing. Find the last hop that succeeded. Then check the **clearing interface**. The message may be stuck in the outbound queue because the clearing house connection dropped, or the interface may have rejected it for a format error. Also check the **cut-off**. If the payment arrived after the

entries.title: A corporate customer sends a bulk file with 5,000 salary payments. Walk through how the file is processed without errors, from receipt to settlement.
entries.text: A corporate customer sends a bulk file with 5,000 salary payments. Walk through how the file is processed without errors, from receipt to settlement. A clean bulk file starts before the file even arrives. The corporate customer prepares a **pain.001** file with hundreds or thousands of payments, and the bank publishes a clear file specification so the customer knows the exact format. When the file arrives, the hub validates the file structure first, checking the header, the record count, and the control totals. Then it validates each payment inside, the account numbers, the amounts, the beneficiary details, and the sanctions lists. If every payment passes, the hub processes the whole file as a batch, sending each payment to the clearing system and tracking the **pacs.002** status on each

entries.title: A customer submits a payment at 3 PM and the cut-off is 4 PM. Walk through how the payment meets the cut-off and settles on the same value date.
entries.text: A customer submits a payment at 3 PM and the cut-off is 4 PM. Walk through how the payment meets the cut-off and settles on the same value date. Meeting the cut-off works because the whole chain is aligned to the same clock. The customer submits the payment before the published **cut-off time**, and the channel accepts it. The payment hub validates it immediately and sends the **pacs.008** to the clearing system before the clearing cut-off. The clearing system processes it in the current settlement cycle, and the beneficiary bank credits the account on the same **value date**. The customer sees the credit the same day, and the sender gets a **pacs.002** with ACSC status. The keys to making it work are a published cut-off that the customer can see in the channel, a hub that processes fast

entries.title: A corporate customer sends a payment file that passes validation on the first attempt. What does the bank do to make first-time-right files the norm?
entries.text: A corporate customer sends a payment file that passes validation on the first attempt. What does the bank do to make first-time-right files the norm? A file that passes validation the first time is a sign that the customer onboarding and the file specification both work. The corporate customer prepares the file using the bank's **published specification**, which defines the exact format, the mandatory fields, and the validation rules. Before sending the file, the customer runs it through the bank's **pre-validation tool**, which checks the format and flags any errors. The customer fixes the errors and sends the file. The bank hub validates the file structure, checking the header, the record count, and the control totals, and then validates each payment, the account numbers, the amounts,

entries.title: Walk through a clean bulk salary run. How does an employer pay 5,000 employees on payday with every payment landing on time?
entries.text: Walk through a clean bulk salary run. How does an employer pay 5,000 employees on payday with every payment landing on time? A clean salary run works because the file, the funding, and the timing are all agreed in advance. The employer sends a **pain.001** file with every employee payment, the account numbers, the amounts, and the value date, which is payday. The bank validates the file, checking each payment against the account details and the sanctions lists. The bank checks that the employer account has **enough funds** to cover the total, and if not, it alerts the employer before the value date. On payday, the bank releases the file, sending each payment to the clearing system. The clearing system settles them, and each employee bank credits the salary to the employee account. The

entries.title: A production incident hits during a release. What is your role?
entries.text: A production incident hits during a release. What is your role? My role in a production incident is to own the business impact and the communication, while engineering owns the technical fix. First, I find out what is affected: which payments, how many customers, whether money is stuck or just delayed. I write this down clearly so everyone is working from the same facts. Second, I join the incident bridge and stay on it, translating between engineering and the business. When engineering says the message queue is backed up, I turn that into the business impact: 200 payments are delayed and the oldest is 45 minutes old. Third, I help the operations manager decide the priority: which payments to release first when the system comes back, usually the urgent and high value ones. Fourth, I draft

entries.title: How do you prioritise when five payment issues land at once?
entries.text: How do you prioritise when five payment issues land at once? I triage by impact first, then by urgency. I look at all five issues and ask three questions about each one: how many customers are affected, is money stuck or at risk, and is there a deadline like a cut off or a regulatory report. The issue that affects the most customers and has money at risk comes first. I am explicit about the order and I tell the stakeholders what I am working on and what is queued. I do not try to do all five at once. I pick the top one, work it until it is stable or handed to the right owner, then move to the next. For each issue I identify the owner: is it a data fix I can do, an engineering defect, or an operations problem. I delegate what is not mine. I also look for a common cause: five issues landing

entries.title: A payment is failing in production and nobody knows why. Walk me through your investigation.
entries.text: A payment is failing in production and nobody knows why. Walk me through your investigation. I start with the facts, not guesses. First, I find a failing payment and get its reference number and UETR. I check the payment hub to see where it stopped and what error was recorded. I look at the message that was sent and the response that came back. If the response is a pacs.002 rejection, I read the reason code: it tells me exactly what failed. Second, I check whether the failure is isolated or widespread. I look at the same time window and see if other payments failed the same way. If many failed, it is likely a system or configuration issue. If only one failed, it is likely a data issue with that payment. Third, I check the recent changes: was there a deployment, a configuration change or a

entries.title: A user acceptance test fails on the last day before go-live. What do you do?
entries.text: A user acceptance test fails on the last day before go-live. What do you do? I would not sign off a go live with a failing test on the last day. First, I find out what failed and how serious it is. Is it a defect that stops payments, or a minor display issue. If it stops payments or risks wrong payments, the go live must be delayed or the scope reduced. I would explain this to the stakeholders with the evidence: the failing test, the impact and the risk of going live with it. Second, I look for a workaround: can the affected payment type be excluded from the first release, can operations handle it manually for a short period, can we go live for a limited set of customers. Third, I work with engineering on the fix and the retest: how long will the fix take, can it be tested properly in the

entries.title: A test environment does not match production. How do you handle it?
entries.text: A test environment does not match production. How do you handle it? A test environment that does not match production is a common and dangerous problem, because a test can pass and the change can still fail in production. First, I identify the differences: is the data different, is the configuration different, is a system missing or a different version. I document the gaps precisely so everyone knows what the test did and did not cover. Second, I work with engineering to close the gaps that matter most: the configuration of the payment hub, the reference data, the clearing system simulators and the test data. I prioritise the gaps that affect the payment flow being tested. Third, for the gaps that cannot be closed quickly, I note them as test limitations and I plan additional checks: a

entries.title: How do you prepare for a payment system cutover weekend?
entries.text: How do you prepare for a payment system cutover weekend? A cutover weekend is planned in detail because the bank cannot afford to get it wrong. The preparation starts weeks before. I write the cutover plan with every step, who does it, how long it takes and what the rollback is. I run a dress rehearsal in a test environment following the exact steps, and I time each step to confirm the plan fits in the window. I prepare the test scenarios for the go live validation: a set of payments that will be run immediately after cutover to prove the system works. I confirm the communications plan: who is told, when and by whom, including customers if they are affected. On the weekend, I am on the bridge call from the start. I track each step against the plan and note any deviation. After each major

entries.title: What controls does a large bank put around payments to manage risk?
entries.text: What controls does a large bank put around payments to manage risk? A large bank layers controls around payments because the risk is real money leaving the bank. The first control is authentication: the person giving the instruction must prove who they are, through a password, a token or a biometric. The second is authorisation: the payment must be approved by someone with the right limit, and large payments need two approvers. The third is sanctions screening: every payment is checked against sanctions lists before it is released, and a hit stops the payment automatically. The fourth is fraud detection: the bank looks for unusual patterns, a new beneficiary, a large amount, a payment at an odd hour, and holds the payment for review. The fifth is limits: each customer and each channel has

entries.title: A stakeholder wants a change that breaks a regulatory rule. What do you do?
entries.text: A stakeholder wants a change that breaks a regulatory rule. What do you do? I would not agree to it, but I would not just say no either. First I would understand what the stakeholder actually needs. Often the request that breaks a rule is a shortcut to a genuine business need, and there is a compliant way to meet that need. I would explain the rule in plain language: what the regulation says, why it exists and what happens if the bank breaks it, including fines and reputational damage. I would bring the evidence, the exact regulation and the control that would fail. Then I would propose an alternative. For example, if the stakeholder wants to skip a sanctions check to speed up payments, I would suggest ways to make the check faster, like improving the screening rules to reduce false

entries.title: A regulatory change lands with a tight deadline. How do you respond?
entries.text: A regulatory change lands with a tight deadline. How do you respond? A regulatory change with a tight deadline is a common situation in payments. First, I read the regulation and the regulator's guidance to understand exactly what must change and by when. I do not rely on a summary from someone else. Second, I assess the impact: which payment types are affected, which systems, which customer journeys and which reports. I map the change to the current process and identify the gaps. Third, I bring the right people together: compliance to confirm the interpretation, operations to confirm the operational impact, engineering to estimate the build and testing effort, and the business to confirm the customer impact. Fourth, I build a plan working backwards from the deadline: design, build, test,

entries.title: How do you handle a situation where the business and compliance disagree?
entries.text: How do you handle a situation where the business and compliance disagree? When the business and compliance disagree, the BA is in the middle and has to help both sides reach a decision that is compliant and workable. First, I make sure I understand both positions precisely. The business usually wants speed or simplicity for the customer. Compliance wants the control that protects the bank and meets the regulation. I write down both positions and the underlying reason for each, so the conversation is about the reasons, not the positions. Second, I check the regulation itself, not someone's interpretation of it. I read the rule and the guidance, and I ask compliance to point to the specific requirement. Third, I look for a solution that meets the regulatory requirement and still works for

entries.title: A customer tries to pay online and the bank asks them to approve the payment in their banking app. The customer complains that this is an extra step and asks why it is needed. Explain strong customer authentication under PSD2 and when the bank can skip it.
entries.text: A customer tries to pay online and the bank asks them to approve the payment in their banking app. The customer complains that this is an extra step and asks why it is needed. Explain strong customer authentication under PSD2 and when the bank can skip it. **Strong customer authentication**, or SCA, is a requirement under **PSD2**, the European payment services law. It means the customer must prove their identity using at least two of three factors: something they know, such as a password, something they have, such as their phone, and something they are, such as a fingerprint. The bank asks for approval in the app because the app combines something the customer has with something they know or are. SCA applies to most electronic payments, including online card payments and account access.

entries.title: Your bank operates in the euro area. The Instant Payments Regulation now requires you to offer SEPA Instant payments and to check the payee name before sending. Explain what the regulation requires and what your bank must build to comply.
entries.text: Your bank operates in the euro area. The Instant Payments Regulation now requires you to offer SEPA Instant payments and to check the payee name before sending. Explain what the regulation requires and what your bank must build to comply. The **Instant Payments Regulation** requires banks in the euro area to offer **SEPA Instant Credit Transfer**, or SCT Inst, so that customers can send and receive euro payments within **10 seconds**, 24 hours a day, every day of the year. The bank must also offer instant payments at a price no higher than a standard credit transfer, which means it cannot charge a premium for speed. The second requirement is **verification of payee**. Before the payer confirms the payment, the bank must check that the payee name matches the account number, the IBAN, and

entries.title: Your bank payment platform goes down for four hours during a busy morning. The regulator asks for a report under the operational resilience rules. Explain what DORA requires, what the bank must show, and how the operations team prepares for this.
entries.text: Your bank payment platform goes down for four hours during a busy morning. The regulator asks for a report under the operational resilience rules. Explain what DORA requires, what the bank must show, and how the operations team prepares for this. **DORA**, the Digital Operational Resilience Act, requires financial firms in the EU to be able to withstand, respond to, and recover from technology disruptions. A four hour payment outage is exactly the kind of incident DORA covers. The bank must report the incident to the regulator within a strict timeline, usually an **initial notification within 4 hours** and a fuller report within 72 hours, describing what happened, which services were affected, how many customers were impacted, and what was done to recover. The bank must also show that it

entries.title: A customer is tricked by a fraudster into sending 20,000 pounds to a criminal account. The customer reports it to the bank the same day. Under the UK PSR rules on authorised push payment fraud, who pays, and what does the bank have to do?
entries.text: A customer is tricked by a fraudster into sending 20,000 pounds to a criminal account. The customer reports it to the bank the same day. Under the UK PSR rules on authorised push payment fraud, who pays, and what does the bank have to do? Under the **PSR reimbursement rules**, the sending bank must reimburse the customer for **authorised push payment fraud**, where the customer was tricked into authorising the payment. The cost is split **50/50** between the sending bank and the receiving bank, unless the receiving bank can show it did not meet its obligations. The customer must be reimbursed within **five business days** of the claim, and the maximum reimbursement is **85,000 pounds**. The bank must first check whether the customer acted with **gross negligence**, which is a very high

entries.title: The SWIFT CBPR+ migration deadline has passed and MT messages are no longer accepted for cross border payments. A small bank in your network is still sending MT103 messages. What happens to those messages and what must the bank do?
entries.text: The SWIFT CBPR+ migration deadline has passed and MT messages are no longer accepted for cross border payments. A small bank in your network is still sending MT103 messages. What happens to those messages and what must the bank do? When the **CBPR+ migration** deadline passes, the SWIFT network stops accepting **MT103** messages for cross border payments and requires **ISO 20022** messages, such as the **pacs.008**. An MT103 sent after the deadline is **rejected** by the network, and the sending bank receives a rejection notice. The payment does not travel, the beneficiary is not paid, and the sending bank must fix the problem before the customer payment can go through. The small bank must complete its migration: build or buy the ability to create and receive **pacs.008** messages, map

entries.title: A payment is blocked because the beneficiary name matches a name on the OFAC sanctions list. The customer says it is a different person with the same name. Explain what happens next and why the bank cannot simply release the payment.
entries.text: A payment is blocked because the beneficiary name matches a name on the OFAC sanctions list. The customer says it is a different person with the same name. Explain what happens next and why the bank cannot simply release the payment. **OFAC**, the US Office of Foreign Assets Control, maintains the **SDN list**, a list of people and entities that US persons and banks must not deal with. When a payment matches a name on the list, the bank must **block** it, which means holding the funds and not releasing them, while it investigates. The customer saying it is a different person is not enough, because the bank must prove it. The compliance team compares the **full details**: the date of birth, the address, the nationality, the passport number, and any other identifiers, against the listing.

entries.title: A customer asks why the bank needs their full address for a cross border payment, and whether the bank is sharing their personal data. Explain the GDPR position and what the bank must do with payment data.
entries.text: A customer asks why the bank needs their full address for a cross border payment, and whether the bank is sharing their personal data. Explain the GDPR position and what the bank must do with payment data. Under **GDPR**, the bank can only collect and use personal data when it has a **lawful basis**. For a cross border payment, the lawful basis is that the data is necessary to perform the contract, the payment instruction, and to comply with a **legal obligation**, because payment regulations require the bank to include the payer name, account, and address in the payment message. The bank must include this data in the **pacs.008** or MT103, because the receiving bank and the intermediary banks need it for **sanctions screening** and reconciliation. The bank must tell the customer what

entries.title: Transaction monitoring flags a customer who has received several cash deposits just below the reporting threshold, then sent the money abroad. Explain what the bank suspects, what it must do, and what it must never tell the customer.
entries.text: Transaction monitoring flags a customer who has received several cash deposits just below the reporting threshold, then sent the money abroad. Explain what the bank suspects, what it must do, and what it must never tell the customer. The bank suspects **structuring**, which is the deliberate splitting of transactions into smaller amounts to avoid a reporting threshold. It is a classic **money laundering** technique: the criminal breaks a large sum into deposits just below the threshold, so no single transaction triggers a report, then moves the money abroad where it is harder to trace. The bank must investigate the pattern: who is the customer, what is their normal activity, what is the source of the cash, and does the behaviour make business sense. If the investigation cannot explain the

entries.title: The Bank of England migrates CHAPS to ISO 20022. A corporate customer asks what changes for them. Explain the migration, what the customer must do, and what improves once it is live.
entries.text: The Bank of England migrates CHAPS to ISO 20022. A corporate customer asks what changes for them. Explain the migration, what the customer must do, and what improves once it is live. The **Bank of England** migrated **CHAPS**, the UK high value payment system, to **ISO 20022** message formats. The change means CHAPS payments now use the same structured data standard as the rest of the world, instead of the older MT format. For the corporate customer, the main change is in the **data** they must provide. The payment instruction now needs a **structured address**, with separate fields for street, town, and postcode, instead of free text. It also needs a **purpose code** that says what the payment is for, and richer **remittance information** so the beneficiary can reconcile it. The customer

entries.title: An Indian company wants to pay a supplier in Germany. The payment is delayed because the bank asks for FEMA documentation. Explain what FEMA is, why the bank asks, and what the company should prepare.
entries.text: An Indian company wants to pay a supplier in Germany. The payment is delayed because the bank asks for FEMA documentation. Explain what FEMA is, why the bank asks, and what the company should prepare. **FEMA**, the Foreign Exchange Management Act, is the Indian law that governs how money moves in and out of India. It requires that cross border payments are made for a **permitted purpose**, that the amount is genuine, and that the transaction is reported to the **Reserve Bank of India** through the bank. The bank asks for documentation because it is the **authorised dealer** and it is legally responsible for checking that the payment complies with FEMA before it releases the funds. For a supplier payment, the company should prepare the **invoice**, the **purchase order**, the **shipping

entries.title: A bank receives a payment instruction where the beneficiary information is missing. The payment cannot be processed. Explain the travel rule and what the bank must do.
entries.text: A bank receives a payment instruction where the beneficiary information is missing. The payment cannot be processed. Explain the travel rule and what the bank must do. The **travel rule** requires that certain information about the payer and the payee **travels with** the payment, from the sending bank all the way to the beneficiary bank. Under the EU **Funds Transfer Regulation**, the payer information must include the name, the account number, and the address, and the payee information must include the name and the account number. When a payment arrives with the beneficiary information missing, the receiving bank cannot complete its **sanctions screening**, because it does not know who the money is going to, and it cannot reconcile the payment, because it does not know who to credit.

entries.title: Your bank has identified its payment platform as a critical business service under the operational resilience rules. The board asks what impact tolerance means and what happens if it is breached. Explain it in plain language.
entries.text: Your bank has identified its payment platform as a critical business service under the operational resilience rules. The board asks what impact tolerance means and what happens if it is breached. Explain it in plain language. **Impact tolerance** is the maximum disruption the bank is willing to accept for a **critical business service** before the harm to customers, to the market, or to the bank itself becomes unacceptable. For a payment platform, the board might set a tolerance of **two hours**: the platform can be down for up to two hours, but beyond that, customers cannot pay, businesses cannot settle, and the damage is severe. The tolerance is not a target, it is a limit. The bank must be able to **recover** within the tolerance, which means the backup systems, the recovery

entries.title: What is a payment workshop and what questions do you ask?
entries.text: What is a payment workshop and what questions do you ask? A payment workshop is a facilitated session where a BA brings business stakeholders, operations staff, and technical teams together to define requirements for a payment change. It is more effective than one-to-one interviews for payments because a payment flow crosses many teams, and a workshop surfaces disagreements early. A typical workshop starts with the current state: how does the payment flow work today, and where does it break? Then it moves to the future state: what should change, and what does success look like? Key questions include: which payment types and channels are in scope, and which are out of scope? entries.title: How does a BA work with engineering and operations in a large bank?
entries.text: How does a BA work with engineering and operations in a large bank? A BA in a large bank is the bridge between the business and the engineers. The work starts with operations. The BA sits with the operations team and watches how they process payments today, where they struggle and what they need. The BA writes down the current process, the pain points and the requirements for the new system. Then the BA works with engineering. The BA explains the business requirement in a way engineers can build: the data fields, the validation rules, the expected behaviour when something fails. The BA writes user stories, acceptance criteria and test scenarios. During development, the BA answers questions from engineers and makes decisions when the requirement is unclear. entries.title: How is a change delivered in a large bank: release, testing and cutover?
entries.text: How is a change delivered in a large bank: release, testing and cutover? Change in a large bank follows a strict path because a mistake can stop payments for thousands of customers. First, the change is designed and the requirements are written and signed off by the business, operations and risk. Second, the engineers build it in a development environment. Third, the change goes to a test environment where the QA team runs functional tests, regression tests and performance tests. The BA writes the test scenarios based on real payment flows, including the unhappy paths like a rejected payment or a missing field. Fourth, the change goes to user acceptance testing where operations run it with real scenarios and confirm it works. Fifth, the change is scheduled for a release window, usually a

entries.title: How does a large bank onboard a new corporate client onto its payment platform?
entries.text: How does a large bank onboard a new corporate client onto its payment platform? Onboarding a corporate client onto a payment platform is a project that takes weeks, not days. First, the bank does due diligence: it checks the client's identity, its business, its owners and its risk profile. This is the know your customer process, and it must be complete before the client can send a payment. Second, the bank sets up the client's static data: the accounts, the users, the approval limits, the payment types the client can use and the file formats they will send. Third, the bank and the client agree on the connectivity: will the client send files through a secure portal, an API or a direct host to host connection. entries.title: What is the role of a business analyst in a payments transformation programme?
entries.text: What is the role of a business analyst in a payments transformation programme? A payments transformation programme in a large bank replaces old systems with new ones, often moving from legacy mainframe payment engines to a modern payment hub. The BA is central to this work. First, the BA documents the current state: how payments work today, which systems are involved, where the manual workarounds are and what breaks. Second, the BA works with the business to define the future state: what should the new hub do, which payment types will it support, what are the target STP rates and exception handling rules. Third, the BA writes the requirements for the new system in a form engineers can build from, including the data model, the validation rules, the message formats and the reconciliation

entries.title: You have two conflicting requirements from operations and engineering. How do you resolve it?
entries.text: You have two conflicting requirements from operations and engineering. How do you resolve it? I would start by bringing both sides into the same room with the facts in front of them. Operations wants the payment to be processed a certain way because that is how their team works today. Engineering wants a different way because it is simpler to build or fits the system architecture better. I would first check whether the conflict is real or a misunderstanding. Often operations describes a need and engineering hears a different requirement. I would write down both requirements side by side and trace each one back to its source: is it a regulatory rule, a customer promise, an operational need or a preference. Regulatory and customer promises are not negotiable. Preferences can be discussed.

entries.title: How do you gather requirements for a new payment product?
entries.text: How do you gather requirements for a new payment product? I start by understanding the problem the product is solving, not the solution someone has already imagined. I talk to the business sponsor and ask: who is the customer, what payment are they making, what goes wrong today, what does good look like. Then I talk to operations, because they process the payments today and they know where the pain is. I watch them work and note the manual steps, the workarounds and the exceptions. Then I talk to the customers if possible, or read the customer complaints and the helpdesk tickets to see what customers actually struggle with. I also look at the existing systems and data: what payment types exist, what volumes, what the failure rates are. From all of this I write the requirements, starting

entries.title: How do you explain a complex payment failure to a non-technical stakeholder?
entries.text: How do you explain a complex payment failure to a non-technical stakeholder? I start with the outcome, not the technical detail. I would say: the payment did not reach the beneficiary on time, and here is what that means for the customer. Then I explain the cause in plain terms, using an analogy if it helps. For example, I might say: think of the payment like a letter. The letter was written correctly, but the post office could not read the address because one line was missing, so the letter was returned. In the same way, our system rejected the payment because a required field was blank, and the payment was sent back to us. I would then explain what we are doing about it: we have fixed the missing information, we have resent the payment, and the beneficiary should receive it by tomorrow.

entries.title: How do you handle a requirement that keeps changing?
entries.text: How do you handle a requirement that keeps changing? Changing requirements are normal in payments because the business learns as the build progresses. I handle it by making the change process visible and controlled. First, I understand the change: what is different, why is it needed, and what is the impact on what is already built. I write the change down as a change request with the old requirement, the new requirement and the reason. Second, I assess the impact with engineering: how much work to change it, does it affect testing already done, does it affect the go live date. Third, I take the impact to the decision maker, usually the product owner, with a clear recommendation and the cost of the change. Fourth, once approved, I update the requirements, the test scenarios and the

entries.title: A vendor delivers a payment component late. What do you do?
entries.text: A vendor delivers a payment component late. What do you do? First, I assess the impact: what is delayed, who is affected and whether there is a workaround. I tell the stakeholders immediately so they hear it from me, not from a missed deadline. Second, I understand the reason for the delay from the vendor: is it a resource problem, a technical blocker or a scope misunderstanding. I ask for specifics, not a vague new date. Third, I look at the options. Can we descope the component and use a manual workaround for the first release. Can we use a different vendor component. Can we reorder the work so other parts of the build continue while we wait. Fourth, I replan with engineering: what is the new realistic date, what is the critical path and what can be done in parallel. Fifth, I manage the

entries.title: How do you validate that a payment requirement is complete?
entries.text: How do you validate that a payment requirement is complete? I validate a requirement by testing it against real examples. First, I take a real payment and walk it through the requirement end to end: does the requirement cover every step, every field, every decision point and every error. If I find a step with no requirement, the requirement is incomplete. Second, I test the unhappy paths: what happens when a field is missing, when the amount is zero, when the currency is unsupported, when the beneficiary bank rejects the payment. If the requirement only describes the happy path, it is incomplete. Third, I check the non functional side: performance, security, audit, reconciliation and reporting. entries.title: How do you work with a difficult stakeholder?
entries.text: How do you work with a difficult stakeholder? I start by understanding what the stakeholder actually cares about, not what they are demanding. A difficult stakeholder is often someone under pressure from their own manager or client, and the demand is a symptom of that pressure. I listen without interrupting and I repeat back what I heard so they know I understood. Then I separate the person from the problem: I focus on the requirement and the facts, not on the tone. I bring evidence: the data, the process, the options and the trade offs. Evidence is hard to argue with. I also find common ground: we both want the payment to work and the customer to be happy, and I say that out loud. entries.title: How do you document a payment flow for both business and technical readers?
entries.text: How do you document a payment flow for both business and technical readers? I write two versions of the same flow, because business and technical readers need different things. For the business reader, I write a simple step by step flow in plain language: the customer gives the instruction, the bank checks it, the bank sends it, the beneficiary receives it. I use a diagram with boxes and arrows, and I label each box with what happens and who does it. I include the timing: when the payment is sent, when it settles and when the customer is told. For the technical reader, I write the same flow but with the detail: the message types, the field names, the validation rules, the API calls, the error codes and the expected responses. entries.title: Tell me about a time you found a defect in a payment flow.
entries.text: Tell me about a time you found a defect in a payment flow. I found it during user acceptance testing, before go live, which is exactly when you want to find it. We were testing a new payment type and the test scenario was a payment with a special character in the beneficiary name. The payment hub rejected it, which was correct, but the error message that came back to the user was a raw system code that meant nothing to anyone in operations. The payment was stuck and nobody could tell why without calling engineering. I traced the flow: the hub rejected the payment, the rejection reason was passed to the front end without translation, and the front end displayed the code as it was. entries.title: Tell me about a time you had to say no to a stakeholder.
entries.text: Tell me about a time you had to say no to a stakeholder. I had a stakeholder who wanted a new payment feature built in two weeks, but the design needed six weeks because it touched the sanctions screening and the reconciliation. I said no to the two week date, but I did not leave it there. First, I understood why two weeks mattered: the stakeholder had promised a client a date. I explained clearly what was involved and why two weeks was not safe: the sanctions change needed compliance sign off, the reconciliation needed testing, and skipping those steps risked a regulatory breach. I showed the work broken down so the stakeholder could see it was not padding. entries.title: Tell me about a time you improved a payment process.
entries.text: Tell me about a time you improved a payment process. I noticed that the exceptions team was spending a large part of their day manually correcting payments that failed because the beneficiary account number had a space or a dash in it. The payment hub rejected these as invalid, and an operator had to open each one, remove the space and resubmit it. I counted the volume: about 200 payments a day were failing for this reason, taking roughly two hours of operator time. I proposed a simple fix: strip spaces and dashes from the account number field at the point of entry, before validation. The rule was safe because spaces and dashes carry no meaning in an account number. I wrote the requirement, got it approved and worked with engineering to implement it. We tested it with the common

entries.title: Tell me about a time you had to learn a new payment system quickly.
entries.text: Tell me about a time you had to learn a new payment system quickly. I was asked to work on a new instant payments system that I had never used before. I started by reading the scheme rules and the message specifications so I understood the standard. Then I asked operations to show me the current system and walked through a real payment with them, asking questions at each step. I mapped the flow on paper: where the instruction comes from, how it is validated, how it is routed, how the response comes back and what happens when it fails. I read the existing requirements and test cases to see what the system was expected to do. entries.title: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager about a payment design.
entries.text: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager about a payment design. My manager wanted to build a new payment feature as a custom addition to the existing system. I thought that was the wrong approach because the existing system was already hard to maintain, and adding a custom feature would make it worse. I did not just disagree in a meeting. I prepared the evidence: the current system's complexity, the cost of maintaining custom code, the risk of breaking existing payments, and an alternative approach using the payment hub's standard configuration. I presented both options side by side with the pros and cons and the cost of each. entries.title: Tell me about a time you spotted a risk nobody else saw.
entries.text: Tell me about a time you spotted a risk nobody else saw. During a testing cycle, I noticed that the test scenarios only covered payments where the beneficiary bank was in the same country. No one had tested a payment where the beneficiary bank was in a different time zone and the value date crossed a weekend. I raised it because I knew from experience that value dating across a weekend is a common source of errors: a payment sent on Friday for a Monday value date can be processed as Friday if the system does not handle the weekend correctly. I wrote a test scenario for it and ran it. The test failed: the system applied the wrong value date, which would have meant the beneficiary received the money a day early and the bank's liquidity forecast was wrong. entries.title: In a job interview for a payments business analyst role, the interviewer says: tell me about yourself. How do you structure a strong answer that is not just a list of your jobs?
entries.text: In a job interview for a payments business analyst role, the interviewer says: tell me about yourself. How do you structure a strong answer that is not just a list of your jobs? Use a simple three part structure: **present, past, future**. Start with the present: what you do now, in one sentence, such as I am a senior business analyst working on payments transformation at a large bank. Then go to the past: pick two or three experiences that prove you can do this job, such as I spent three years on cross border payments, I led the ISO 20022 migration analysis, and I worked with operations to cut exception rates. Keep each one short and tie it to a result. Then finish with the future: why this role, such as I want to apply that experience to your payment hub programme because it is the next

entries.title: The interviewer asks: tell me about the biggest payments failure you have handled. How do you answer honestly without making yourself look bad?
entries.text: The interviewer asks: tell me about the biggest payments failure you have handled. How do you answer honestly without making yourself look bad? Use the **STAR** structure: situation, task, action, result. Describe the situation briefly, such as a cross border payment of 125,000 pounds that vanished between banks and the customer was waiting. Explain your task: to find the payment, keep the customer informed, and prevent a repeat. Then describe the **actions** you took: you traced the payment through the gpi tracker, you found it stuck at an intermediary bank because of a missing field, you raised an MT199 to the intermediary, and you gave the customer a daily update. entries.title: The interviewer asks why you are leaving your current bank. You are unhappy there, but you know you should not criticise your employer. How do you answer?
entries.text: The interviewer asks why you are leaving your current bank. You are unhappy there, but you know you should not criticise your employer. How do you answer? Keep the answer **forward looking**, not backward looking. Talk about what you want to move towards, not what you want to escape from. A good answer is: I have learned a great deal in my current role, I have built deep experience in payments operations and ISO 20022, and now I want to apply that experience to a larger transformation programme, which is what this role offers. That is honest, positive, and it connects your experience to the job. Never criticise your current employer, your manager, or your colleagues, even if the interviewer invites you to. entries.title: The hiring manager is not technical. They ask you to explain ISO 20022 migration in plain language. How do you explain it without jargon?
entries.text: The hiring manager is not technical. They ask you to explain ISO 20022 migration in plain language. How do you explain it without jargon? Start with an analogy the manager already understands. Say: imagine every bank in the world writes payment instructions in a different language, and ISO 20022 is the agreement to use one common language. Then explain the **problem**: the old MT messages carry limited information, so payments often need manual repair, reconciliation is slow, and fraud screening misses things. Explain the **change**: ISO 20022 messages, such as the **pacs.008**, carry richer, structured data, including full addresses, purpose codes, and longer remittance information, so the receiving bank can process the payment automatically. entries.title: The interviewer asks about your salary expectations. You do not want to price yourself out, but you also do not want to accept less than you are worth. How do you handle the question?
entries.text: The interviewer asks about your salary expectations. You do not want to price yourself out, but you also do not want to accept less than you are worth. How do you handle the question? Do your **research** before the interview. Find out the market rate for the role, the location, and your experience level, using salary surveys, job adverts, and conversations with recruiters. When the question comes, give a **range**, not a single number, and anchor the range to the market and to your experience. A good answer is: based on the market for this role and my experience in payments transformation, I am looking for a range of X to Y, and I am flexible depending on the full package. entries.title: The interviewer asks: tell me about a time you worked with a difficult stakeholder. How do you answer with a payments example?
entries.text: The interviewer asks: tell me about a time you worked with a difficult stakeholder. How do you answer with a payments example? Pick a real example where a stakeholder disagreed with you and you resolved it professionally. Use the **STAR** structure. The situation: the operations team wanted to delay a payment hub release because they were worried about exception handling, while the programme wanted to go live on schedule. Your task: to find a solution that protected operations without missing the deadline. The action: you listened to the operations concerns first, you ran a **workshop** to map the exact exception scenarios they were worried about, you showed them the test evidence, and you agreed a phased go live where the riskiest payment types moved later. entries.title: The interviewer asks how you keep up with changes in payments regulation and technology. What is a convincing answer?
entries.text: The interviewer asks how you keep up with changes in payments regulation and technology. What is a convincing answer? Give a **specific** answer, not a vague one. Name the sources you actually use: the **SWIFT** standards releases and the CBPR+ usage guidelines, the **Bank of England** and **European Payments Council** publications, the **PSR** and **FCA** updates, and the industry newsletters you read regularly. Explain your **routine**: you set aside time each week to read the updates, you attend industry webinars and conferences when you can, and you discuss changes with colleagues in operations and compliance. entries.title: The interviewer gives you a scenario: three payment projects are competing for your time. One is a regulatory deadline, one is a revenue opportunity, and one is a fix for a recurring operations problem. How do you prioritise them?
entries.text: The interviewer gives you a scenario: three payment projects are competing for your time. One is a regulatory deadline, one is a revenue opportunity, and one is a fix for a recurring operations problem. How do you prioritise them? Start by stating your **framework**, then apply it. A good framework is: regulatory deadlines first, because missing them means fines and the risk of losing the ability to operate; revenue second, because it funds the business; and operational fixes third, unless the operations problem is causing customer harm or financial loss. Apply it to the scenario: the **regulatory** project goes first, because the deadline is fixed and the consequences of missing it are severe. entries.title: The interviewer asks how you would handle a production incident where payments are failing and nobody knows why. Walk through your answer.
entries.text: The interviewer asks how you would handle a production incident where payments are failing and nobody knows why. Walk through your answer. Show a calm, structured approach. First, **assess the impact**: how many payments are failing, which customers are affected, and whether money is at risk. Second, **communicate**: tell the operations manager, the incident team, and the customer service team what is happening, so nobody is guessing. Third, **investigate** systematically: check the payment hub logs, check whether the failures started at a specific time, check whether a release went out recently, check the clearing house status, and check whether the failures share a pattern, such as one currency, one channel, or one message type. entries.title: At the end of the interview, the interviewer asks if you have any questions. What should you ask, and what should you avoid asking?
entries.text: At the end of the interview, the interviewer asks if you have any questions. What should you ask, and what should you avoid asking? Ask questions that show you are **genuinely interested** in the role and that you have done your **research**. Good questions are: what does success look like in this role in the first six months; what is the biggest challenge facing the payments programme right now; how does the team work with operations and engineering; and what is the plan for the ISO 20022 migration or the next major change. These questions show you are thinking about the job, not just about getting an offer.
